abstract: A bit - serial VLSI neural network is described from an initial architecture for a synapse array through to silicon layout and board design. The issues surrounding bit - serial computation, and analog/digital arithmetic are discussed and the parallel development of a hybrid analog/digital neural network is outlined. Learning and recall capabilities are reported for the bit - serial network along with a projected specification for a 64 - neuron, bit - serial board operating at 20 MHz. This tech(cid:173) nique is extended to a 256 (2562 synapses) network with an update time of 3ms, using a "paging" technique to time - multiplex calculations through the synapse array.

paragraphs: This paper develops a bit-serial neural network implementation from the architecture of its synapse array through silicon layout and board design. Bit-serial computation handles the bits of a value over successive steps. The paper considers this computational organization alongside the choice between analog and digital arithmetic.

The authors report learning and recall capabilities for the bit-serial network and outline a parallel effort on a hybrid analog/digital network. They also provide a projected specification for a 64-neuron board operating at 20 MHz. The projected board specification is a hardware design target, while the reported learning and recall concern the network's computational capabilities.

The approach extends to 256 neurons and 256 squared synapses through a paging technique, with an update time of 3 milliseconds. Paging time-multiplexes calculations through the synapse array, letting the same computational hardware serve different parts of the larger network at different times. This illustrates how scheduling and reuse of an array can be part of scaling a neural implementation, alongside the physical circuit design.
summary.tldr: The paper develops bit-serial neural hardware and uses time-multiplexed paging to extend a synapse array to a larger network.

title: Bit-Serial Neural Networks

abstract: The concept of the stochastic Boltzmann machine (BM) is auractive for decision making and pattern classification purposes since the probability of attaining the network states is a function of the network energy. Hence, the probability of attaining particular energy minima may be associated with the probabilities of making certain decisions (or classifications). However, because of its stochastic nature, the complexity of the BM is fairly high and therefore such networks are not very likely to be used in practice. In this paper we suggest a way to alleviate this drawback by converting the sto(cid:173) chastic BM into a deterministic network which we call the Boltzmann Per(cid:173) ceptron Network (BPN). The BPN is functionally equivalent to the BM but has a feed-forward structure and low complexity. No annealing is required. The conditions under which such a convmion is feasible are given. A learning algorithm for the BPN based on the conjugate gradient method is also provided which is somewhat akin to the backpropagation algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational complexity of stochastic Boltzmann machines. Their appeal for classification comes from the relationship between network energy and the probability of reaching particular states. That relationship allows probabilities of different outcomes to be associated with decisions, but the authors regard stochastic operation as a practical obstacle.

They propose converting a Boltzmann machine into a deterministic feedforward model called the Boltzmann Perceptron Network. The resulting network is described as functionally equivalent while having lower complexity and requiring no annealing. The paper gives conditions under which the conversion is possible, so the equivalence is tied to those conditions.

The authors also provide a learning algorithm based on conjugate gradients that resembles backpropagation. The contribution combines a change in computational structure with a way to train the resulting model. It aims to retain the decision-making function associated with the Boltzmann machine while expressing that function through a deterministic forward computation, reducing the operational burden identified in the stochastic formulation.
summary.tldr: Under stated conversion conditions, a deterministic feedforward network reproduces a Boltzmann machine’s function without annealing.

title: The Boltzmann Perceptron Network: A Multi-Layered Feed-Forward Network Equivalent to the Boltzmann Machine

abstract: We describe a multi-network, or modular, connectionist architecture that captures that fact that many tasks have structure at a level of granularity intermediate to that assumed by local and global function approximation schemes. The main innovation of the architecture is that it combines associative and competitive learning in order to learn task decompositions. A task decomposition is discovered by forcing the networks comprising the architecture to compete to learn the training patterns. As a result of the competition, different networks learn different training patterns and, thus, learn to partition the input space. The performance of the architecture on a "what" and "where" vision task and on a multi-payload robotics task are presented.

The main innovation of the architecture is that it combines associative and competitive learning in order to learn task decompositions. A task decomposition is discovered by forcing the networks comprising the architecture to compete to learn the training patterns. As a result of the competition, different networks learn different training patterns and, thus, learn to partition the input space. paragraphs: This paper develops a neural architecture in which several networks share a task by learning different parts of it. The motivation is that useful task structure can lie between highly local relationships and a single global relationship. A collection of specialized networks offers a way to represent this intermediate level of organization.

The central mechanism combines associative learning with competition. The component networks compete to learn training examples, and different networks consequently become responsible for different patterns. This process partitions the input space through training. The division of work is therefore something the architecture discovers, rather than a task decomposition that must be fully specified beforehand.

The paper presents performance on a vision task involving object identity and location, and on a robotics task involving multiple payloads. These applications illustrate the intended role of learned specialization across different settings. The contribution is an architecture that makes discovering the task's internal organization part of learning how to perform it.
summary.tldr: Competing neural modules learn to divide a task into specialized parts by taking responsibility for different training examples.

title: A competitive modular connectionist architecture

abstract: We describe single-transistor silicon synapses that compute, learn, and provide non-volatile memory retention. The single transistor synapses simultaneously perform long term weight storage, com(cid:173) pute the product of the input and the weight value, and update the weight value according to a Hebbian or a backpropagation learning rule. Memory is accomplished via charge storage on polysilicon floating gates, providing long-term retention without refresh. The synapses efficiently use the physics of silicon to perform weight up(cid:173) dates; the weight value is increased using tunneling and the weight value decreases using hot electron injection. The small size and low power operation of single transistor synapses allows the devel(cid:173) opment of dense synaptic arrays. We describe the design, fabri(cid:173) cation, characterization, and modeling of an array of single tran(cid:173) sistor synapses. When the steady state source current is used as the representation of the weight value, both the incrementing and decrementing functions are proportional to a power of the source current. The synaptic array was fabricated in the standard 21'm double - poly, analog process available from MOSIS.

paragraphs: The paper describes silicon synapses that combine weight storage, computation, and learning in a single transistor. Each synapse retains its weight, multiplies an input by that weight, and updates the weight according to a Hebbian or backpropagation learning rule. Combining these functions makes the device itself an active part of the learning mechanism.

Memory is stored as charge on a polysilicon floating gate, providing long-term retention without refresh. Weight increases use tunneling, while decreases use hot-electron injection. The circuit therefore uses physical charge-transfer processes to implement learning updates. Its small size and low-power operation support the construction of dense arrays of such synapses.

The authors describe the design, fabrication, characterization, and modeling of a synaptic array. When steady-state source current represents the weight, both increase and decrease functions follow powers of that current. This connects the abstract weight-update rule to the device’s measurable electrical behavior. The contribution is a fabricated implementation in which persistent memory and adaptive computation share the same compact physical element.
summary.tldr: Single-transistor synapses combine non-volatile weight storage, multiplication, and learning through floating-gate charge dynamics.

title: Single Transistor Learning Synapses

abstract: A new model for chemosensory reception is presented. It models reacti(cid:173) ons between odor molecules and receptor proteins and the activation of second messenger by receptor proteins. The mathematical formulation of the reaction kinetics is transformed into an artificial neural network (ANN). The resulting feed-forward network provides a powerful means for parameter fitting by applying learning algorithms. The weights of the network corresponding to chemical parameters can be trained by presen(cid:173) ting experimental data. We demonstrate the simulation capabilities of the model with experimental data from honey bee chemosensory neurons. It can be shown that our model is sufficient to rebuild the observed data and that simpler models are not able to do this task.

paragraphs: The paper models how odor molecules interact with receptor proteins and how those proteins activate a second messenger. It treats chemosensory reception as a sequence of chemical reactions whose behavior can be described mathematically. The aim is to connect these reaction mechanisms to experimental measurements of sensory neurons.

The authors transform the reaction-kinetics equations into a feedforward artificial neural network. This makes neural network learning algorithms available for fitting the model's parameters. Crucially, the adjustable weights correspond to chemical parameters, so training changes quantities with a meaning in the underlying reaction model. Experimental observations become examples from which those parameter values can be learned.

The model is demonstrated using data from honey bee chemosensory neurons. The authors report that it can reproduce the observed data, whereas simpler models cannot do so. This supports the adequacy of the proposed reaction model for those observations. The broader methodological contribution is using a neural network representation to fit a mechanistic chemical model directly to experimental evidence.
summary.tldr: A neural network representation of chemical reaction kinetics fits honey bee sensory data that simpler models cannot reproduce.

title: A Model for Chemosensory Reception

abstract: This paper investigates learning in a lifelong context. Lifelong learning addresses situations in which a learner faces a whole stream of learn(cid:173) ing tasks. Such scenarios provide the opportunity to transfer knowledge across multiple learning tasks, in order to generalize more accurately from less training data. In this paper, several different approaches to lifelong learning are described, and applied in an object recognition domain. It is shown that across the board, lifelong learning approaches generalize consistently more accurately from less training data, by their ability to transfer knowledge across learning tasks.
originalAbstract: This paper investigates learning in a lifelong context. Lifelong learning addresses situations in which a learner faces a whole stream of learn(cid:173) ing tasks. Such scenarios provide the opportunity to transfer knowledge across multiple learning tasks, in order to generalize more accurately from less training data. In this paper, several different approaches to lifelong learning are described, and applied in an object recognition domain. It is shown that across the board, lifelong learning approaches generalize consistently more accurately from less training data, by their ability to transfer knowledge across learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning as an ongoing sequence of tasks. A learner that has already solved earlier tasks has accumulated knowledge that might help with later ones. The central question is whether that experience allows it to learn a new task from fewer examples while making more accurate predictions on unseen cases.

The authors describe several approaches to lifelong learning and apply them to object recognition. Their common purpose is to transfer knowledge between tasks. The relevant unit of experience is therefore the stream of tasks: learning on one part of that stream can influence how effectively the learner handles another part.

Across the approaches examined, the paper reports consistently better generalization with less training data, attributed to knowledge transfer. The finding supports treating previous learning as a resource for future learning. In the reported object-recognition setting, experience across tasks improves the relationship between how much new data is needed and how accurately the resulting model generalizes.
summary.tldr: Across the tested object-recognition approaches, transferring knowledge between tasks improves generalization while reducing training-data needs.

title: Is Learning The n-th Thing Any Easier Than Learning The First?

abstract: The process of machine learning can be considered in two stages: model selection and parameter estimation. In this paper a technique is presented for constructing dynamical systems with desired qualitative properties. The approach is based on the fact that an n-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system can be decomposed into one gradient and (n - 1) Hamiltonian sys(cid:173) tems. Thus, the model selection stage consists of choosing the gradient and Hamiltonian portions appropriately so that a certain behavior is obtainable. To estimate the parameters, a stably convergent learning rule is presented. This algorithm has been proven to converge to the desired system trajectory for all initial conditions and system inputs. This technique can be used to design neural network models which are guaranteed to solve the trajectory learning problem.

In this paper a technique is presented for constructing dynamical systems with desired qualitative properties. The approach is based on the fact that an n-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system can be decomposed into one gradient and (n - 1) Hamiltonian sys(cid:173) tems. Thus, the model selection stage consists of choosing the gradient and Hamiltonian portions appropriately so that a certain behavior is obtainable. To estimate the parameters, a stably convergent learning rule is presented. This algorithm has been proven to converge to the desired system trajectory for all initial conditions and system inputs. paragraphs: This paper separates learning a dynamical system into choosing its structure and estimating its parameters. The goal is to construct systems with desired qualitative behavior and then train them to follow a desired trajectory. This makes model selection part of the design problem, rather than leaving all desired behavior to emerge from parameter adjustment.

The approach uses a decomposition of an n-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system into one gradient system and n minus one Hamiltonian systems. The designer selects these portions so that the intended behavior is obtainable. The decomposition therefore supplies a structured way to build the model before learning its numerical parameters.

For parameter estimation, the authors present a learning rule with a stable-convergence guarantee. They state that it converges to the desired system trajectory for all initial conditions and system inputs. Within this construction, the result provides a route to neural network models guaranteed to solve trajectory learning, connecting a deliberately chosen dynamical structure with a provably convergent training process.
summary.tldr: A gradient–Hamiltonian decomposition supports dynamical model design together with a learning rule guaranteed to converge to desired trajectories.

title: Gradient and Hamiltonian Dynamics Applied to Learning in Neural Networks

abstract: We have combined an artificial neural network (ANN) character classifier with context-driven search over character segmentation, word segmentation, and word recognition hypotheses to provide robust recognition of hand-printed English text in new models of Apple Computer's Newton MessagePad. We present some innovations in the training and use of ANNs al; character classifiers for word recognition, including normalized output error, frequency balancing, error emphasis, negative training, and stroke warping. A recurring theme of reducing a priori biases emerges and is discussed.
originalAbstract: We have combined an artificial neural network (ANN) character classifier with context-driven search over character segmentation, word segmentation, and word recognition hypotheses to provide robust recognition of hand-printed English text in new models of Apple Computer's Newton MessagePad. We present some innovations in the training and use of ANNs al; character classifiers for word recognition, including normalized output error, frequency balancing, error emphasis, negative training, and stroke warping. A recurring theme of reducing a priori biases emerges and is discussed.

paragraphs: The paper describes a system for recognizing hand-printed English text in Apple’s Newton MessagePad. A neural network supplies character classifications, while a context-driven search considers alternative interpretations of the writing. That search covers character segmentation, word segmentation, and word recognition, making the character classifier one component of a broader recognition process.

This arrangement allows the system to consider where characters and words begin and end alongside what they mean as text. The abstract presents the combination as providing robust recognition. Its focus is therefore on training and using a character classifier effectively within a system that must manage multiple competing segmentation and recognition hypotheses.

The authors introduce normalized output error, frequency balancing, error emphasis, negative training, and stroke warping as innovations in this setting. A recurring theme is reducing prior biases that affect recognition. Together, the contributions concern both the classifier’s preparation and its use in contextual search: successful word recognition depends on how character evidence is learned and how that evidence participates in interpreting the complete handwritten input.
summary.tldr: The paper combines improved neural-network character training with contextual search to recognize hand-printed words in the Newton MessagePad.

title: Effective Training of a Neural Network Character Classifier for Word Recognition

abstract: Unsupervised learning algorithms have been derived for several sta(cid:173) tistical models of English grammar, but their computational com(cid:173) plexity makes applying them to large data sets intractable. This paper presents a probabilistic model of English grammar that is much simpler than conventional models, but which admits an effi(cid:173) cient EM training algorithm. The model is based upon grammat(cid:173) ical bigrams, i.e. , syntactic relationships between pairs of words. We present the results of experiments that quantify the represen(cid:173) tational adequacy of the grammatical bigram model, its ability to generalize from labelled data, and its ability to induce syntactic structure from large amounts of raw text.
originalAbstract: Unsupervised learning algorithms have been derived for several sta(cid:173) tistical models of English grammar, but their computational com(cid:173) plexity makes applying them to large data sets intractable. This paper presents a probabilistic model of English grammar that is much simpler than conventional models, but which admits an effi(cid:173) cient EM training algorithm. The model is based upon grammat(cid:173) ical bigrams, i.e. , syntactic relationships between pairs of words. We present the results of experiments that quantify the represen(cid:173) tational adequacy of the grammatical bigram model, its ability to generalize from labelled data, and its ability to induce syntactic structure from large amounts of raw text.

paragraphs: Learning statistical grammar from unlabeled text can require computations that become impractical on large datasets. This paper addresses that obstacle by proposing a simpler probabilistic model of English grammar. The aim is to retain a useful representation of syntax while making unsupervised training computationally manageable.

The model is organized around grammatical bigrams: syntactic relationships between pairs of words. These pairwise relationships provide the building blocks for its grammar representation. The simplified structure admits an efficient expectation-maximization training algorithm, connecting the representational choice directly to the feasibility of learning from large amounts of text.

The experiments examine three distinct questions: how adequately the model represents grammar, how well it generalizes from labeled examples, and whether it can induce syntactic structure from raw text. Together, these evaluations address the usefulness of the representation as well as its learnability. The contribution is a tractable grammar-modeling approach with empirical assessment along these dimensions; the abstract does not characterize the reported results as uniformly successful or superior to conventional models.
summary.tldr: A simpler grammar model built from pairwise syntactic relationships enables efficient EM training and is evaluated on representation and learning tasks.

title: Grammatical Bigrams

abstract: We describe a new algorithm for computing a Nash equilibrium in graphical games, a compact representation for multi-agent systems that we introduced in previous work. The algorithm is the first to compute equilibria both efficiently and exactly for a non-trivial class of graphical games.
originalAbstract: We describe a new algorithm for computing a Nash equilibrium in graphical games, a compact representation for multi-agent systems that we introduced in previous work. The algorithm is the first to compute equilibria both efficiently and exactly for a non-trivial class of graphical games.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an algorithm for computing a Nash equilibrium in a class of graphical games with tree structure. Graphical games provide a compact representation of systems involving multiple agents. The computational task is to turn that representation into an equilibrium, rather than merely use it to describe the agents’ interactions.

A Nash equilibrium is a configuration of strategies in which no individual agent can improve its outcome by changing its own strategy alone. Computing such a configuration is therefore a way to identify mutually stable choices. The paper’s stated contribution combines exact equilibrium computation with efficiency for the class of games it addresses.

Both parts of that claim matter: exactness concerns the solution obtained, while efficiency concerns the work needed to obtain it. The authors describe their algorithm as the first to achieve both properties for a non-trivial class of graphical games. The tree-structured scope is central to interpreting that result; the claim establishes a tractable setting rather than covering graphical games in general.
summary.tldr: The paper presents an efficient, exact Nash-equilibrium algorithm for a non-trivial class of tree-structured graphical games.

title: An Efficient, Exact Algorithm for Solving Tree-Structured Graphical Games

abstract: Model selection is linked to model assessment, which is the problem of comparing different models, or model parameters, for a speciﬁc learning task. For supervised learning, the standard practical technique is cross- validation, which is not applicable for semi-supervised and unsupervised settings. In this paper, a new model assessment scheme is introduced which is based on a notion of stability. The stability measure yields an upper bound to cross-validation in the supervised case, but extends to semi-supervised and unsupervised problems. In the experimental part, the performance of the stability measure is studied for model order se- lection in comparison to standard techniques in this area.
originalAbstract: Model selection is linked to model assessment, which is the problem of comparing different models, or model parameters, for a speciﬁc learning task. For supervised learning, the standard practical technique is cross- validation, which is not applicable for semi-supervised and unsupervised settings. In this paper, a new model assessment scheme is introduced which is based on a notion of stability. The stability measure yields an upper bound to cross-validation in the supervised case, but extends to semi-supervised and unsupervised problems. In the experimental part, the performance of the stability measure is studied for model order se- lection in comparison to standard techniques in this area.

paragraphs: The paper addresses model assessment: comparing candidate models or parameter choices for a particular learning task. Such assessment supports model selection by providing a basis for choosing among alternatives. The authors seek a criterion that can extend beyond the supervised setting in which cross-validation is a standard practical tool.

They introduce an assessment scheme based on a notion of stability. In supervised learning, its measure gives an upper bound on cross-validation. The same scheme also extends to semi-supervised and unsupervised problems, where the abstract identifies ordinary cross-validation as inapplicable. The mathematical connection to supervised assessment provides an anchor for this broader use.

Experiments investigate the stability measure for model order selection and compare it with standard techniques for that task. The contribution is a shared assessment approach across learning settings with different access to supervision. The upper-bound result describes a relationship between assessment quantities; it does not by itself establish that stability will choose the best model in every application.
summary.tldr: A stability-based assessment measure upper-bounds supervised cross-validation and extends to semi-supervised and unsupervised model selection.

title: Stability-Based Model Selection

abstract: Consider a number of moving points, where each point is attached to a joint of the human body and projected onto an image plane. Johannson showed that humans can eﬀortlessly detect and recog- nize the presence of other humans from such displays. This is true even when some of the body points are missing (e.g. because of occlusion) and unrelated clutter points are added to the display. We are interested in replicating this ability in a machine. To this end, we present a labelling and detection scheme in a probabilistic framework. Our method is based on representing the joint prob- ability density of positions and velocities of body points with a graphical model, and using Loopy Belief Propagation to calculate a likely interpretation of the scene. Furthermore, we introduce a global variable representing the body’s centroid. Experiments on one motion-captured sequence suggest that our scheme improves on the accuracy of a previous approach based on triangulated graph- ical models, especially when very few parts are visible. The im- provement is due both to the more general graph structure we use and, more signiﬁcantly, to the introduction of the centroid variable.

Experiments on one motion-captured sequence suggest that our scheme improves on the accuracy of a previous approach based on triangulated graph- ical models, especially when very few parts are visible. paragraphs: Johansson displays depict a moving person using only points attached to body joints. Humans can recognize the person even when some points disappear and unrelated moving points are present. This paper develops a probabilistic method intended to reproduce that ability by detecting the body and assigning interpretations to the observed points.

The method uses a graphical model to represent the joint distribution of body-point positions and velocities. Loopy belief propagation computes a likely interpretation of the scene from these relationships. The authors also introduce a variable for the body’s centroid, giving the model an explicit representation of the body’s overall center alongside its individual parts.

Experiments on one motion-captured sequence suggest greater accuracy than a previous method based on triangulated graphical models, especially when very few body parts remain visible. The authors attribute the improvement to both the more general graph structure and, more strongly, the centroid variable. The evidence supports the usefulness of this shared body-level information in the tested sequence, with the experimental scope explicitly limited to that sequence.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic body-point model with a centroid variable improves detection and labeling on one tested motion sequence, especially with few visible parts.

title: An Improved Scheme for Detection and Labelling in Johansson Displays

abstract: In this paper, sparse representation (factorization) of a data matrix is ﬁrst discussed. An overcomplete basis matrix is estimated by using the K(cid:0)means method. We have proved that for the estimated overcom- plete basis matrix, the sparse solution (coefﬁcient matrix) with minimum l1(cid:0)norm is unique with probability of one, which can be obtained using a linear programming algorithm. The comparisons of the l1(cid:0)norm so- lution and the l0(cid:0)norm solution are also presented, which can be used in recoverability analysis of blind source separation (BSS). Next, we ap- ply the sparse matrix factorization approach to BSS in the overcomplete case. Generally, if the sources are not sufﬁciently sparse, we perform blind separation in the time-frequency domain after preprocessing the observed data using the wavelet packets transformation. Third, an EEG experimental data analysis example is presented to illustrate the useful- ness of the proposed approach and demonstrate its performance. Two almost independent components obtained by the sparse representation method are selected for phase synchronization analysis, and their peri- ods of signiﬁcant phase synchronization are found which are related to tasks. Finally, concluding remarks review the approach and state areas that require further study.

paragraphs: This paper develops sparse matrix factorization and applies it to blind source separation in the overcomplete case. The method first estimates an overcomplete basis using K-means, then obtains coefficients through minimum-l1-norm optimization. The authors prove that, for the estimated basis, this solution is unique with probability one and can be found using linear programming.

They also compare minimum-l1 and minimum-l0 solutions to support analysis of source recoverability. The uniqueness result and the comparison play different roles: a uniquely determined optimization solution still needs to be related to the source-recovery problem. When sources are insufficiently sparse, the approach uses wavelet-packet preprocessing and performs separation in the time-frequency domain.

An EEG example illustrates the method's use. The authors select two almost independent components recovered by sparse representation and examine their phase synchronization. They find periods of significant synchronization associated with tasks. This connects the factorization procedure to analysis of relationships between recovered signals, alongside the theoretical work on uniqueness and recoverability.
summary.tldr: Sparse factorization combines a K-means basis with l1 optimization for overcomplete source separation and illustrates task-related synchronization in EEG components.

title: Sparse Representation and Its Applications in Blind Source Separation

abstract: Synapses are a critical element of biologically-realistic, spike-based neu- ral computation, serving the role of communication, computation, and modiﬁcation. Many different circuit implementations of synapse func- tion exist with different computational goals in mind. In this paper we describe a new CMOS synapse design that separately controls quiescent leak current, synaptic gain, and time-constant of decay. This circuit im- plements part of a commonly-used kinetic model of synaptic conduc- tance. We show a theoretical analysis and experimental data for proto- types fabricated in a commercially-available 1.5µm CMOS process.

This circuit im- plements part of a commonly-used kinetic model of synaptic conduc- tance. We show a theoretical analysis and experimental data for proto- types fabricated in a commercially-available 1.5µm CMOS process.

paragraphs: This paper presents a CMOS circuit for implementing synapses in systems that compute using neural spikes. Synapses are important because they do more than transmit signals: they also shape computation and modification of neural activity. Different circuit designs capture different aspects of that behavior, so the contribution concerns a specific set of controllable synaptic properties.

The design separately controls the quiescent leak current, synaptic gain, and decay time constant. These correspond to the current present at rest, the strength of the synaptic response, and how quickly that response fades. Separating these controls matters because they describe distinct features of the circuit’s behavior, allowing each to be adjusted as its own design parameter.

The circuit implements part of a commonly used kinetic model of synaptic conductance and provides summating, exponentially decaying responses. The authors support the design with theoretical analysis and experimental measurements from prototypes fabricated using a commercially available 1.5-micrometer CMOS process. The work thus connects a synaptic model to a physically fabricated implementation.
summary.tldr: A fabricated CMOS synapse separately controls resting leakage, response strength, and exponential decay time.

title: A Summating, Exponentially-Decaying CMOS Synapse for Spiking Neural Systems

abstract: This paper reports on a family of computationally practical classiﬁers that converge to the Bayes error at near-minimax optimal rates for a va- riety of distributions. The classiﬁers are based on dyadic classiﬁcation trees (DCTs), which involve adaptively pruned partitions of the feature space. A key aspect of DCTs is their spatial adaptivity, which enables lo- cal (rather than global) ﬁtting of the decision boundary. Our risk analysis involves a spatial decomposition of the usual concentration inequalities, leading to a spatially adaptive, data-dependent pruning criterion. For any distribution on (X, Y ) whose Bayes decision boundary behaves locally like a Lipschitz smooth function, we show that the DCT error converges to the Bayes error at a rate within a logarithmic factor of the minimax optimal rate. We also study DCTs equipped with polynomial classiﬁca- tion rules at each leaf, and show that as the smoothness of the boundary increases their errors converge to the Bayes error at a rate approaching n−1/2, the parametric rate. We are not aware of any other practical classi- ﬁers that provide similar rate of convergence guarantees. Fast algorithms for tree pruning are discussed.

The goal is a computationally practical classifier whose error approaches the Bayes error, the best achievable error for the underlying distribution, at a theoretically strong rate.

summary.tldr: Spatially adaptive classification trees achieve near-minimax convergence under local boundary smoothness conditions.

title: Near-Minimax Optimal Classification with Dyadic Classification Trees

abstract: We introduce supervised latent Dirichlet allocation (sLDA), a statistical model of labelled documents. The model accommodates a variety of response types. We derive a maximum-likelihood procedure for parameter estimation, which relies on variational approximations to handle intractable posterior expectations. Prediction problems motivate this research: we use the fitted model to predict response values for new documents. We test sLDA on two real-world problems: movie ratings predicted from reviews, and web page popularity predicted from text descriptions. We illustrate the benefits of sLDA versus modern regularized regression, as well as versus an unsupervised LDA analysis followed by a separate regression.

Prediction problems motivate this research: we use the fitted model to predict response values for new documents. We test sLDA on two real-world problems: movie ratings predicted from reviews, and web page popularity predicted from text descriptions. We illustrate the benefits of sLDA versus modern regularized regression, as well as versus an unsupervised LDA analysis followed by a separate regression.

paragraphs: Supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, or sLDA, is a statistical model for documents accompanied by response labels. The goal is to fit a model that can predict response values for new documents, while accommodating several kinds of response. This brings document modeling and the prediction task into the same supervised framework.

The authors derive a maximum-likelihood procedure to estimate the model’s parameters. Some posterior expectations required by that procedure are intractable, so the method uses variational approximations to handle them. Approximate inference is therefore part of how the model is fitted, enabling the proposed estimation procedure to address the quantities it needs.

The paper evaluates prediction in two real-world settings: estimating movie ratings from reviews and estimating web page popularity from text descriptions. The reported comparisons illustrate benefits over regularized regression and over fitting unsupervised LDA before a separate regression step. These findings support using the document responses within the topic-modeling framework, rather than relying solely on topics learned without the prediction target.
summary.tldr: Supervised LDA models labeled documents for response prediction, showing benefits on movie-rating and web-popularity tasks.

title: Supervised Topic Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose an efficient algorithm for estimating the natural policy gradient with parameter-based exploration; this algorithm samples directly in the parameter space. Unlike previous methods based on natural gradients, our algorithm calculates the natural policy gradient using the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix. The computational cost of this algorithm is equal to that of conventional policy gradients whereas previous natural policy gradient methods have a prohibitive computational cost. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms several policy gradient methods.

Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms several policy gradient methods.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an efficient way to estimate natural policy gradients for control tasks using parameter-based exploration. Exploration samples directly in the policy's parameter space. The learning procedure therefore combines variation in policy parameters with a natural-gradient calculation, addressing how to make that calculation computationally practical in the proposed setting.

The defining computational feature is use of the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix. The authors report that their algorithm has the same computational cost as conventional policy-gradient methods, while the previous natural-gradient approaches they discuss have prohibitive costs. The contribution is thus a particular combination of exploration and gradient estimation that makes exact Fisher-based calculation affordable.

Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms several policy-gradient methods. Those findings provide empirical support for the algorithm alongside its stated computational advantage. Taken together, the results indicate that parameter-based exploration can support an effective natural policy-gradient procedure without increasing computational cost beyond the conventional policy-gradient comparison made in the paper.
summary.tldr: Parameter-based exploration enables exact Fisher-based natural policy-gradient estimation at conventional policy-gradient cost, with better results in the reported experiments.

title: Natural Policy Gradient Methods with Parameter-based Exploration for Control Tasks

abstract: In discriminative machine learning one is interested in training a system to optimize a certain desired measure of performance, or loss. In binary classification one typically tries to minimizes the error rate. But in structured prediction each task often has its own measure of performance such as the BLEU score in machine translation or the intersection-over-union score in PASCAL segmentation. The most common approaches to structured prediction, structural SVMs and CRFs, do not minimize the task loss: the former minimizes a surrogate loss with no guarantees for task loss and the latter minimizes log loss independent of task loss. The main contribution of this paper is a theorem stating that a certain perceptron-like learning rule, involving features vectors derived from loss-adjusted inference, directly corresponds to the gradient of task loss. We give empirical results on phonetic alignment of a standard test set from the TIMIT corpus, which surpasses all previously reported results on this problem.

paragraphs: Structured prediction tasks often have specialized measures of success, such as translation quality or segmentation overlap. Training objectives do not necessarily match these measures. The paper highlights that structural SVMs optimize a surrogate objective, while conditional random fields optimize log loss independently of the chosen task measure. It asks how training can target task loss more directly.

The main contribution is a theorem connecting a particular perceptron-like learning rule to the gradient of task loss. The rule uses feature vectors obtained through loss-adjusted inference, meaning that the task's loss participates in the inference used to form an update. This provides a mathematical connection between the learning procedure and the performance measure of interest.

The authors evaluate the approach on phonetic alignment using a standard TIMIT test set and report results exceeding previously published results for that problem. The empirical finding supports the method in that setting, while the theorem supplies the central rationale for using task-aware updates in structured prediction.
summary.tldr: A theorem links a perceptron-like update based on loss-adjusted inference directly to the gradient of structured task loss.

title: Direct Loss Minimization for Structured Prediction

abstract: The ability to learn a policy for a sequential decision problem with continuous state space using on-line data is a long-standing challenge. This paper presents a new reinforcement-learning algorithm, called iKBSF, which extends the benefits of kernel-based learning to the on-line scenario. As a kernel-based method, the proposed algorithm is stable and has good convergence properties. However, unlike other similar algorithms,iKBSF's space complexity is independent of the number of sample transitions, and as a result it can process an arbitrary amount of data. We present theoretical results showing that iKBSF can approximate (to any level of accuracy) the value function that would be learned by an equivalent batch non-parametric kernel-based reinforcement learning approximator. In order to show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in practice, we apply iKBSF to the challenging three-pole balancing task, where the ability to process a large number of transitions is crucial for achieving a high success rate.

paragraphs: The paper introduces iKBSF for learning sequential decisions from incoming data in a continuous state space. It extends kernel-based reinforcement learning to an online setting. A central concern is memory: processing more experience becomes difficult when the representation must keep growing with the number of observed transitions.

iKBSF has space complexity independent of the number of sample transitions, allowing it to process an arbitrary amount of data without sample-count-driven memory growth. The authors also describe stability and favorable convergence properties. Their theoretical result shows that it can approximate, to any desired accuracy, the value function learned by an equivalent batch kernel-based approximator.

That comparison links the incremental procedure to the output of a corresponding batch method; it is not a claim of arbitrary accuracy relative to the optimal policy itself. The authors apply iKBSF to three-pole balancing, where processing many transitions is crucial for high success rates. This application illustrates why bounded dependence on accumulated data matters operationally.
summary.tldr: iKBSF processes online reinforcement-learning experience with memory independent of sample count while approximating an equivalent batch kernel method.

title: On-line Reinforcement Learning Using Incremental Kernel-Based Stochastic Factorization

abstract: A brain-computer interface (BCI) allows users to “communicate” with a computer without using their muscles. BCI based on sensori-motor rhythms use imaginary motor tasks, such as moving the right or left hand to send control signals. The performances of a BCI can vary greatly across users but also depend on the tasks used, making the problem of appropriate task selection an important issue. This study presents a new procedure to automatically select as fast as possible a discriminant motor task for a brain-controlled button. We develop for this purpose an adaptive algorithm UCB-classif based on the stochastic bandit theory. This shortens the training stage, thereby allowing the exploration of a greater variety of tasks. By not wasting time on inefficient tasks, and focusing on the most promising ones, this algorithm results in a faster task selection and a more efficient use of the BCI training session. Comparing the proposed method to the standard practice in task selection, for a fixed time budget, UCB-classif leads to an improve classification rate, and for a fix classification rate, to a reduction of the time spent in training by 50%.

paragraphs: A brain-controlled button needs an imagined motor task whose brain signals can be distinguished reliably. Tasks such as imagining movement of a hand do not work equally well for every user. The paper therefore focuses on choosing an effective task during training, rather than assuming that the same task will suit everyone.

The authors introduce UCB-classif, an adaptive selection algorithm based on stochastic bandit theory. It directs training toward promising tasks and spends less time on ineffective ones. This adaptive allocation makes better use of the available training session and allows a wider variety of candidate motor tasks to be explored.

Compared with standard task-selection practice, the reported results show two benefits. With training time held fixed, UCB-classif improves classification performance. With classification performance held fixed, it reduces training time by 50%. These are complementary ways of expressing the practical gain: the procedure can use a session to obtain better discrimination or reach a given level of discrimination sooner.
summary.tldr: Adaptive bandit-based motor-task selection improves BCI classification for a fixed training budget and halves training time at a fixed classification rate in the reported comparison.

title: Bandit Algorithms boost Brain Computer Interfaces for motor-task selection of a brain-controlled button

abstract: The l1-regularized Gaussian maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) has been shown to have strong statistical guarantees in recovering a sparse inverse covariance matrix even under high-dimensional settings. However, it requires solving a difficult non-smooth log-determinant program with number of parameters scaling quadratically with the number of Gaussian variables. State-of-the-art methods thus do not scale to problems with more than 20,000 variables. In this paper, we develop an algorithm BigQUIC, which can solve 1 million dimensional l1-regularized Gaussian MLE problems (which would thus have 1000 billion parameters) using a single machine, with bounded memory. In order to do so, we carefully exploit the underlying structure of the problem. Our innovations include a novel block-coordinate descent method with the blocks chosen via a clustering scheme to minimize repeated computations; and allowing for inexact computation of specific components. In spite of these modifications, we are able to theoretically analyze our procedure and show that BigQUIC can achieve super-linear or even quadratic convergence rates.

paragraphs: Estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix is statistically well supported, but its optimization problem becomes enormous as the number of variables grows. The number of parameters increases quadratically, and the objective combines a log-determinant term with a nonsmooth sparsity penalty. This paper addresses the resulting computational barrier with an algorithm called BigQUIC.

BigQUIC exploits the structure of the optimization problem through block-coordinate descent. A clustering scheme chooses blocks to reduce repeated computation, and selected components are allowed to be computed inexactly. These changes target both computational work and memory demands. The authors report solving problems with one million variables on a single machine using bounded memory, despite the corresponding trillion-parameter scale.

The paper also analyzes the modified procedure theoretically and shows that it can achieve super-linear or even quadratic convergence rates. This matters because the computational shortcuts retain strong convergence properties in the analysis. The contribution concerns making the sparse Gaussian estimation problem tractable at much larger scales while preserving a theoretically analyzed optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: BigQUIC scales sparse inverse covariance estimation to one million variables on a single machine through structured block updates and selective inexact computation.

title: BIG & QUIC: Sparse Inverse Covariance Estimation for a Million Variables

abstract: We develop an automated variational method for approximate inference in Gaussian process (GP) models whose posteriors are often intractable. Using a mixture of Gaussians as the variational distribution, we show that (i) the variational objective and its gradients can be approximated efficiently via sampling from univariate Gaussian distributions and (ii) the gradients of the GP hyperparameters can be obtained analytically regardless of the model likelihood. We further propose two instances of the variational distribution whose covariance matrices can be parametrized linearly in the number of observations. These results allow gradient-based optimization to be done efficiently in a black-box manner. Our approach is thoroughly verified on 5 models using 6 benchmark datasets, performing as well as the exact or hard-coded implementations while running orders of magnitude faster than the alternative MCMC sampling approaches. Our method can be a valuable tool for practitioners and researchers to investigate new models with minimal effort in deriving model-specific inference algorithms.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models often have posterior distributions that cannot be computed tractably. This paper develops an automated variational method that approximates those posteriors using a mixture of Gaussian distributions. The aim is to make inference practical without requiring a separately derived inference algorithm for every new model.

The authors show that the variational objective and its gradients can be efficiently approximated by sampling from univariate Gaussians. They also derive analytic gradients for Gaussian process hyperparameters regardless of the likelihood. Two proposed covariance parameterizations require a number of parameters that grows linearly with the observation count. Together, these results support efficient gradient optimization through a general-purpose procedure.

The method is evaluated on five models and six benchmark datasets. The authors report performance comparable to exact or specially implemented alternatives, while running orders of magnitude faster than the MCMC approaches considered. These findings support its intended role as a practical tool for investigating Gaussian process models with less model-specific inference work.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-mixture variational method automates approximate inference for Gaussian process models and performs efficiently across the reported evaluations.

title: Automated Variational Inference for Gaussian Process Models

abstract: We introduce local expectation gradients which is a general purpose stochastic variational inference algorithm for constructing stochastic gradients by sampling from the variational distribution. This algorithm divides the problem of estimating the stochastic gradients over multiple variational parameters into smaller sub-tasks so that each sub-task explores intelligently the most relevant part of the variational distribution. This is achieved by performing an exact expectation over the single random variable that most correlates with the variational parameter of interest resulting in a Rao-Blackwellized estimate that has low variance. Our method works efficiently for both continuous and discrete random variables. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm has interesting similarities with Gibbs sampling but at the same time, unlike Gibbs sampling, can be trivially parallelized.

This is achieved by performing an exact expectation over the single random variable that most correlates with the variational parameter of interest resulting in a Rao-Blackwellized estimate that has low variance. paragraphs: Variational inference uses an adjustable probability distribution to approximate a distribution of interest. Stochastic optimization can update that approximation using sampled gradients, but noisy estimates complicate the updates. This paper introduces local expectation gradients, a general-purpose method that organizes gradient estimation around the particular variational parameter being updated.

The method divides a gradient-estimation problem involving many parameters into smaller tasks. For each task, it computes an exact expectation over the single random variable most correlated with the parameter of interest. Sampling still supplies information from the variational distribution, while this targeted averaging produces a Rao-Blackwellized estimate with low variance.

The approach works efficiently with both continuous and discrete random variables, giving it scope across different kinds of probabilistic models. Its local computations resemble aspects of Gibbs sampling, but the proposed algorithm can also be straightforwardly parallelized. The significance is the combination of focused exact averaging and stochastic estimation: each subtask spends computation on the part of the distribution most relevant to its parameter, while remaining suitable for parallel execution.
summary.tldr: Local expectation gradients use targeted exact averaging to obtain low-variance, parallelizable stochastic gradients for variational inference.

title: Local Expectation Gradients for Black Box Variational Inference

abstract: Learning to predict multi-label outputs is challenging, but in many problems there is a natural metric on the outputs that can be used to improve predictions. In this paper we develop a loss function for multi-label learning, based on the Wasserstein distance. The Wasserstein distance provides a natural notion of dissimilarity for probability measures. Although optimizing with respect to the exact Wasserstein distance is costly, recent work has described a regularized approximation that is efficiently computed. We describe an efficient learning algorithm based on this regularization, as well as a novel extension of the Wasserstein distance from probability measures to unnormalized measures. We also describe a statistical learning bound for the loss. The Wasserstein loss can encourage smoothness of the predictions with respect to a chosen metric on the output space. We demonstrate this property on a real-data tag prediction problem, using the Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons dataset, outperforming a baseline that doesn't use the metric.

paragraphs: In multi-label prediction, some possible outputs are naturally closer to one another than others. A learning objective can use that relationship instead of treating all output differences alike. This paper develops a loss based on Wasserstein distance, which measures dissimilarity between probability measures using a chosen metric on the output space.

Exact Wasserstein optimization is costly, so the authors build an efficient learning algorithm around a regularized approximation. They also extend the distance to unnormalized measures, broadening the kinds of output representations it can compare. A statistical learning bound provides theoretical support for the proposed loss alongside the computational method.

The Wasserstein loss can encourage predictions to vary smoothly with respect to the selected output metric. On a tag-prediction task using the Yahoo Flickr Creative Commons dataset, the approach outperforms a baseline that does not use that metric. The result demonstrates a practical benefit of incorporating output relationships into training, with the chosen metric supplying the structure that the loss uses.
summary.tldr: A regularized Wasserstein loss incorporates relationships between labels into efficient learning and improves a reported image-tag prediction task.

title: Learning with a Wasserstein Loss

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse in machine learning, yet it is also known to be slow relative to steepest descent. Recently, variance reduction techniques such as SVRG and SAGA have been proposed to overcome this weakness. With asymptotically vanishing variance, a constant step size can be maintained, resulting in geometric convergence rates. However, these methods are either based on occasional computations of full gradients at pivot points (SVRG), or on keeping per data point corrections in memory (SAGA). This has the disadvantage that one cannot employ these methods in a streaming setting and that speed-ups relative to SGD may need a certain number of epochs in order to materialize. This paper investigates a new class of algorithms that can exploit neighborhood structure in the training data to share and re-use information about past stochastic gradients across data points. While not meant to be offering advantages in an asymptotic setting, there are significant benefits in the transient optimization phase, in particular in a streaming or single-epoch setting. We investigate this family of algorithms in a thorough analysis and show supporting experimental results. As a side-product we provide a simple and unified proof technique for a broad class of variance reduction algorithms.

paragraphs: Variance reduction can accelerate stochastic gradient descent by reducing noise in its updates. Existing methods such as SVRG and SAGA achieve this through occasional full-gradient computations or stored corrections for individual data points. The paper highlights that these requirements impede streaming use and can delay practical speedups until several passes through the data.

The proposed algorithm family uses neighborhood structure in the training data to share and reuse information from past stochastic gradients across data points. Rather than treating all stored gradient information as useful only for its original example, it exploits relationships between examples. This targets the early part of optimization, when information has not yet accumulated through many training epochs.

The authors analyze the algorithms and provide supporting experiments, reporting significant benefits in the transient optimization phase, especially for streaming or single-epoch settings. They explicitly do not position the methods as offering asymptotic advantages. A further contribution is a simple, unified proof technique covering a broad class of variance-reduction algorithms, connecting the proposed methods to a wider analytical framework.
summary.tldr: Sharing gradient information across neighboring examples improves early-stage optimization, particularly in streaming and single-epoch settings.

title: Variance Reduced Stochastic Gradient Descent with Neighbors

abstract: The Teacher Forcing algorithm trains recurrent networks by supplying observed sequence values as inputs during training and using the network’s own one-step-ahead predictions to do multi-step sampling. We introduce the Professor Forcing algorithm, which uses adversarial domain adaptation to encourage the dynamics of the recurrent network to be the same when training the network and when sampling from the network over multiple time steps. We apply Professor Forcing to language modeling, vocal synthesis on raw waveforms, handwriting generation, and image generation. Empirically we find that Professor Forcing acts as a regularizer, improving test likelihood on character level Penn Treebank and sequential MNIST. We also find that the model qualitatively improves samples, especially when sampling for a large number of time steps. This is supported by human evaluation of sample quality. Trade-offs between Professor Forcing and Scheduled Sampling are discussed. We produce T-SNEs showing that Professor Forcing successfully makes the dynamics of the network during training and sampling more similar.

paragraphs: Teacher forcing trains a recurrent network with observed sequence values as inputs, while generating a sequence requires feeding back the network's own predictions. These two modes can produce different internal dynamics. Professor Forcing addresses this mismatch by encouraging the recurrent network to behave similarly during training and during generation over multiple steps.

The method uses adversarial domain adaptation to align those dynamics. The authors apply it to language modeling, raw-waveform vocal synthesis, handwriting generation, and image generation. Its target is the network's evolving behavior across a sequence, making the relationship between training and extended sampling an explicit part of the learning procedure.

Empirically, Professor Forcing acts as a regularizer and improves test likelihood on character-level Penn Treebank and sequential MNIST. Generated samples also improve qualitatively, especially for longer sequences, with human evaluations supporting the quality findings. Visualizations show more similar dynamics between training and sampling. These observations support the proposed alignment mechanism, while the paper also discusses tradeoffs with Scheduled Sampling.
summary.tldr: Professor Forcing aligns recurrent-network dynamics during training and generation, empirically improving likelihood and sample quality.

title: Professor Forcing: A New Algorithm for Training Recurrent Networks

abstract: In recent years, a rapidly increasing number of applications in practice requires solving non-convex objectives, like training neural networks, learning graphical models, maximum likelihood estimation etc. Though simple heuristics such as gradient descent with very few modifications tend to work well, theoretical understanding is very weak. We consider possibly the most natural class of non-convex functions where one could hope to obtain provable guarantees: functions that are ``approximately convex'', i.e. functions $\tf: \Real^d \to \Real$ for which there exists a \emph{convex function} $f$ such that for all $x$, $|\tf(x) - f(x)| \le \errnoise$ for a fixed value $\errnoise$. We then want to minimize $\tf$, i.e. output a point $\tx$ such that $\tf(\tx) \le \min_{x} \tf(x) + \err$. It is quite natural to conjecture that for fixed $\err$, the problem gets harder for larger $\errnoise$, however, the exact dependency of $\err$ and $\errnoise$ is not known. In this paper, we strengthen the known \emph{information theoretic} lower bounds on the trade-off between $\err$ and $\errnoise$ substantially, and exhibit an algorithm that matches these lower bounds for a large class of convex bodies.

paragraphs: The paper studies a restricted form of nonconvex optimization: the objective may be irregular, but its value stays within a fixed error tolerance of some convex function at every point. This uniform closeness defines the approximately convex class under consideration. The goal is to find a point whose objective value is within a requested accuracy of the true minimum.

Two different errors therefore matter. One measures how far the objective can deviate from convexity; the other measures the optimization accuracy being requested. The central question is how these quantities interact. Being close to a convex function gives useful structure, but the allowable deviations can still obstruct accurate optimization.

The authors substantially strengthen information-theoretic lower bounds describing this tradeoff. They also provide an algorithm that matches those bounds for a large class of convex bodies. Matching upper and lower bounds identifies what can be achieved within that setting and what the available information cannot support, rather than extending guarantees to arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens limits on approximately convex optimization and gives an algorithm matching them for a broad class of convex domains.

title: Algorithms and matching lower bounds for approximately-convex optimization

abstract: n this paper, we propose and study an Asynchronous parallel Greedy Coordinate Descent (Asy-GCD) algorithm for minimizing a smooth function with bounded constraints. At each iteration, workers asynchronously conduct greedy coordinate descent updates on a block of variables. In the first part of the paper, we analyze the theoretical behavior of Asy-GCD and prove a linear convergence rate. In the second part, we develop an efficient kernel SVM solver based on Asy-GCD in the shared memory multi-core setting. Since our algorithm is fully asynchronous---each core does not need to idle and wait for the other cores---the resulting algorithm enjoys good speedup and outperforms existing multi-core kernel SVM solvers including asynchronous stochastic coordinate descent and multi-core LIBSVM.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent optimizes a function by updating selected variables rather than changing every variable at once. This paper proposes an asynchronous parallel version with greedy updates, called Asy-GCD, for smooth optimization with bounded constraints. Multiple workers operate on blocks of variables, making the update process suitable for execution across processor cores.

The asynchronous design lets workers continue without waiting for all other workers to finish their updates. This matters because synchronization can leave computing resources idle. The authors analyze the algorithm and prove a linear convergence rate, providing a theoretical account of its progress in the setting studied. That rate describes how optimization error decreases, rather than merely stating that the procedure eventually converges.

The paper also turns the method into a kernel support vector machine solver for shared-memory multicore systems. The resulting solver achieves good parallel speedup and is reported to outperform existing multicore alternatives, including asynchronous stochastic coordinate descent and multicore LIBSVM. The contribution therefore combines an optimization analysis with evidence that greedy asynchronous updates can be useful in a concrete learning application.
summary.tldr: Asy-GCD combines greedy coordinate updates with asynchronous parallel execution, yielding convergence guarantees and a faster reported multicore kernel SVM solver.

title: Asynchronous Parallel Greedy Coordinate Descent

abstract: Exemplar learning is a powerful paradigm for discovering visual similarities in an unsupervised manner. In this context, however, the recent breakthrough in deep learning could not yet unfold its full potential. With only a single positive sample, a great imbalance between one positive and many negatives, and unreliable relationships between most samples, training of convolutional neural networks is impaired. Given weak estimates of local distance we propose a single optimization problem to extract batches of samples with mutually consistent relations. Conflicting relations are distributed over different batches and similar samples are grouped into compact cliques. Learning exemplar similarities is framed as a sequence of clique categorization tasks. The CNN then consolidates transitivity relations within and between cliques and learns a single representation for all samples without the need for labels. The proposed unsupervised approach has shown competitive performance on detailed posture analysis and object classification.

paragraphs: Learning visual similarity without labels is difficult when each example supplies only one positive training instance against many negatives. Relationships between examples can also be unreliable, making it hard to train a convolutional network consistently. CliqueCNN addresses this problem by organizing the relationships used for training before asking the network to learn a shared representation.

Starting from weak estimates of local distance, the method solves an optimization problem that constructs batches with mutually consistent relationships. Similar examples form compact groups called cliques, while conflicting relationships are placed in different batches. Training then becomes a sequence of tasks in which the network categorizes examples by their clique membership.

Through these tasks, the network consolidates transitive relationships within and between cliques into one representation covering all samples. The method requires no labels, although it does begin with weak local similarity information. The reported results are competitive on detailed posture analysis and object classification. These findings support the usefulness of arranging imperfect similarity evidence into coherent training tasks for unsupervised visual learning.
summary.tldr: CliqueCNN learns visual representations without labels by grouping similar examples into cliques and separating conflicting relationships across training batches.

title: CliqueCNN: Deep Unsupervised Exemplar Learning

abstract: Linkages are essentially determined by similarity measures that may be derived from multiple perspectives. For example, spatial linkages are usually generated based on localities of heterogeneous data, whereas semantic linkages can come from various properties, such as different physical meanings behind social relations. Many existing metric learning models focus on spatial linkages, but leave the rich semantic factors unconsidered. Similarities based on these models are usually overdetermined on linkages. We propose a Unified Multi-Metric Learning (UM2L) framework to exploit multiple types of metrics. In UM2L, a type of combination operator is introduced for distance characterization from multiple perspectives, and thus can introduce flexibilities for representing and utilizing both spatial and semantic linkages. Besides, we propose a uniform solver for UM2L which is guaranteed to converge. Extensive experiments on diverse applications exhibit the superior classification performance and comprehensibility of UM2L. Visualization results also validate its ability on physical meanings discovery.

paragraphs: Objects can be related through several notions of similarity. Spatial links reflect locality, while semantic links can reflect different meanings or properties of a relationship. This paper argues that metric learning methods focused mainly on spatial links leave useful semantic information unrepresented, constraining how their learned similarities describe observed relationships.

The proposed Unified Multi-Metric Learning framework, or UM2L, incorporates multiple types of metrics. A combination operator characterizes distance from multiple perspectives, providing flexibility to represent and use both spatial and semantic links. The authors also introduce a uniform solver for the framework and establish a convergence guarantee for it.

Experiments across diverse applications report superior classification performance and comprehensibility, while visualizations support the framework's ability to discover physical meanings. These findings connect the use of multiple similarity perspectives to both prediction and interpretation in the evaluated applications. The solver's convergence guarantee is a separate algorithmic result; the classification and interpretability advantages are supported by the reported experiments rather than asserted universally.
summary.tldr: UM2L combines multiple metrics to represent spatial and semantic relationships, with a convergent solver and encouraging classification and interpretability results.

title: What Makes Objects Similar: A Unified Multi-Metric Learning Approach

abstract: Few prior works study deep learning on point sets. PointNet is a pioneer in this direction. However, by design PointNet does not capture local structures induced by the metric space points live in, limiting its ability to recognize fine-grained patterns and generalizability to complex scenes. In this work, we introduce a hierarchical neural network that applies PointNet recursively on a nested partitioning of the input point set. By exploiting metric space distances, our network is able to learn local features with increasing contextual scales. With further observation that point sets are usually sampled with varying densities, which results in greatly decreased performance for networks trained on uniform densities, we propose novel set learning layers to adaptively combine features from multiple scales. Experiments show that our network called PointNet++ is able to learn deep point set features efficiently and robustly. In particular, results significantly better than state-of-the-art have been obtained on challenging benchmarks of 3D point clouds.

paragraphs: PointNet processes point sets, but its design does not capture the local structure defined by distances between points. That limits its ability to recognize fine detail and handle complex scenes. PointNet++ addresses this by organizing point processing into a hierarchy that learns local patterns and then combines them at progressively broader scales.

The network repeatedly applies PointNet within nested partitions of the input set. Distances in the underlying metric space determine the local context used for learning. Because real point sets can have uneven sampling density, the paper also introduces layers that adaptively combine features from multiple scales, addressing the performance loss associated with training on uniformly sampled data.

Experiments show efficient and robust learning of deep point-set features, with significantly better results than the compared state-of-the-art methods on challenging 3D point-cloud benchmarks. The findings support two linked architectural choices: explicitly representing local geometry and combining information across scales. Together, they let the model capture fine patterns while also incorporating the wider context around them.
summary.tldr: PointNet++ learns hierarchical local features and adaptively combines scales to handle point clouds with varying sampling density.

title: PointNet++: Deep Hierarchical Feature Learning on Point Sets in a Metric Space

abstract: Processing sequential data of variable length is a major challenge in a wide range of applications, such as speech recognition, language modeling, generative image modeling and machine translation. Here, we address this challenge by proposing a novel recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, the Fast-Slow RNN (FS-RNN). The FS-RNN incorporates the strengths of both multiscale RNNs and deep transition RNNs as it processes sequential data on different timescales and learns complex transition functions from one time step to the next. We evaluate the FS-RNN on two character based language modeling data sets, Penn Treebank and Hutter Prize Wikipedia, where we improve state of the art results to 1.19 and 1.25 bits-per-character (BPC), respectively. In addition, an ensemble of two FS-RNNs achieves 1.20 BPC on Hutter Prize Wikipedia outperforming the best known compression algorithm with respect to the BPC measure. We also present an empirical investigation of the learning and network dynamics of the FS-RNN, which explains the improved performance compared to other RNN architectures. Our approach is general as any kind of RNN cell is a possible building block for the FS-RNN architecture, and thus can be flexibly applied to different tasks.

paragraphs: Sequential data require models to process information across time while learning how one step leads to the next. The Fast-Slow RNN combines two architectural ideas: processing at different timescales and using complex transition functions between successive steps. It brings together strengths associated with multiscale RNNs and deep transition RNNs.

The authors evaluate the architecture on character-level language modeling. They report 1.19 bits per character on Penn Treebank and 1.25 on Hutter Prize Wikipedia, improving the state of the art described in the paper. An ensemble of two models reaches 1.20 on Hutter Prize Wikipedia, outperforming the best known compression algorithm according to that measure.
