Its design permits any kind of RNN cell as a building block, giving it flexibility beyond a single cell choice. The language-modeling results establish the reported performance gains, while the broader architectural flexibility supports potential application to other sequential tasks.
summary.tldr: Fast-Slow RNNs combine multiple timescales with complex transitions to improve character-level language modeling.

title: Fast-Slow Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Data representations that contain all the information about target variables but are invariant to nuisance factors benefit supervised learning algorithms by preventing them from learning associations between these factors and the targets, thus reducing overfitting. We present a novel unsupervised invariance induction framework for neural networks that learns a split representation of data through competitive training between the prediction task and a reconstruction task coupled with disentanglement, without needing any labeled information about nuisance factors or domain knowledge. We describe an adversarial instantiation of this framework and provide analysis of its working. Our unsupervised model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, which are supervised, at inducing invariance to inherent nuisance factors, effectively using synthetic data augmentation to learn invariance, and domain adaptation. Our method can be applied to any prediction task, eg., binary/multi-class classification or regression, without loss of generality.

paragraphs: A useful predictive representation should retain information about the target while avoiding nuisance factors that can encourage overfitting. Learning this separation is difficult when nuisance factors have no labels or known description. The paper introduces a framework for inducing invariance without requiring those labels or domain knowledge.

The framework learns a split representation through competition between prediction and reconstruction tasks, coupled with disentanglement. Prediction emphasizes target-relevant information, while reconstruction and disentanglement participate in organizing the representation. The authors present an adversarial implementation and analyze how it works. Here, unsupervised invariance refers to learning without labeled nuisance information within a framework intended to benefit prediction tasks.

The reported model outperforms supervised state-of-the-art methods in inducing invariance to inherent nuisances, learning invariance from synthetic data augmentation, and domain adaptation. The framework is stated to apply generally to prediction tasks, including binary classification, multiclass classification, and regression. Its contribution is a way to learn nuisance-resistant representations without first specifying or labeling the unwanted factors, supported by the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: Competitive prediction and reconstruction learn nuisance-invariant representations without nuisance labels, outperforming supervised alternatives in the reported evaluations.

title: Unsupervised Adversarial Invariance

abstract: Strongly Rayleigh (SR) measures are discrete probability distributions over the subsets of a ground set. They enjoy strong negative dependence properties, as a result of which they assign higher probability to subsets of diverse elements. We introduce in this paper Exponentiated Strongly Rayleigh (ESR) measures, which sharpen (or smoothen) the negative dependence property of SR measures via a single parameter (the exponent) that can intuitively understood as an inverse temperature. We develop efficient MCMC procedures for approximate sampling from ESRs, and obtain explicit mixing time bounds for two concrete instances: exponentiated versions of Determinantal Point Processes and Dual Volume Sampling. We illustrate some of the potential of ESRs, by applying them to a few machine learning tasks; empirical results confirm that beyond their theoretical appeal, ESR-based models hold significant promise for these tasks.

We introduce in this paper Exponentiated Strongly Rayleigh (ESR) measures, which sharpen (or smoothen) the negative dependence property of SR measures via a single parameter (the exponent) that can intuitively understood as an inverse temperature. paragraphs: Strongly Rayleigh distributions assign probabilities to subsets of a larger collection. Their strong negative dependence properties favor subsets containing diverse elements. The paper introduces an exponentiated version of this family, providing a way to adjust the strength of that behavior through one parameter rather than using a fixed degree of preference.

The exponent can be understood as an inverse temperature: it sharpens or smooths the distribution's negative dependence behavior. To make the resulting models usable, the authors develop efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo procedures for approximate sampling. They also derive explicit mixing-time bounds for exponentiated determinantal point processes and exponentiated dual volume sampling, describing how quickly those sampling procedures approach their target distributions.

The paper applies the models to several machine learning tasks and reports promising empirical results. The contribution combines a controllable family of distributions over subsets with algorithms for drawing approximate samples from them. Its theoretical sampling guarantees are given for two concrete instances, while the experiments illustrate the potential value of adjusting diversity-related behavior in applications.
summary.tldr: Exponentiated strongly Rayleigh distributions add a tunable diversity-related parameter and come with approximate sampling algorithms.

title: Exponentiated Strongly Rayleigh Distributions

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide state-of-the-art performance in processing sequential data but are memory intensive to train, limiting the flexibility of RNN models which can be trained. Reversible RNNs---RNNs for which the hidden-to-hidden transition can be reversed---offer a path to reduce the memory requirements of training, as hidden states need not be stored and instead can be recomputed during backpropagation. We first show that perfectly reversible RNNs, which require no storage of the hidden activations, are fundamentally limited because they cannot forget information from their hidden state. We then provide a scheme for storing a small number of bits in order to allow perfect reversal with forgetting. Our method achieves comparable performance to traditional models while reducing the activation memory cost by a factor of 10--15. We extend our technique to attention-based sequence-to-sequence models, where it maintains performance while reducing activation memory cost by a factor of 5--10 in the encoder, and a factor of 10--15 in the decoder.

paragraphs: Training recurrent neural networks consumes substantial memory because hidden activations must be available during backpropagation. This paper investigates reversible hidden-state transitions, which allow earlier states to be reconstructed during the backward pass. Recomputing those states offers a way to reduce the activation storage that restricts which recurrent models can be trained.

The authors first establish a fundamental problem with completely storage-free reversal: a perfectly reversible recurrent network cannot forget information in its hidden state. They then introduce a scheme that stores a small number of bits, allowing forgetting while retaining exact reversal. This addresses the tension between recovering earlier states and letting the recurrent computation discard information.

The method achieves performance comparable to traditional models while reducing activation memory by a factor of 10–15. Applied to attention-based sequence-to-sequence models, it maintains performance with reductions of 5–10 times in the encoder and 10–15 times in the decoder. These figures concern activation memory, demonstrating substantial savings in that component of training.
summary.tldr: Storing a small amount of information lets reversible RNNs forget while reconstructing activations, substantially reducing training activation memory.

title: Reversible Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce the Sublevel Set (SS) method, a generic method to obtain sufficient guarantees of near-optimality and uniqueness (up to small perturbations) for a clustering. This method can be instantiated for a variety of clustering loss functions for which convex relaxations exist. Obtaining the guarantees in practice amounts to solving a convex optimization. We demonstrate the applicability of this method by obtaining distribution free guarantees for K-means clustering on realistic data sets.
originalAbstract: We introduce the Sublevel Set (SS) method, a generic method to obtain sufficient guarantees of near-optimality and uniqueness (up to small perturbations) for a clustering. This method can be instantiated for a variety of clustering loss functions for which convex relaxations exist. Obtaining the guarantees in practice amounts to solving a convex optimization. We demonstrate the applicability of this method by obtaining distribution free guarantees for K-means clustering on realistic data sets.

paragraphs: After producing a clustering, a separate question remains: how confidently can its quality be assessed? This paper introduces the Sublevel Set method to obtain sufficient guarantees that a clustering is close to optimal and essentially unique. Here, uniqueness allows small perturbations, so the guarantee concerns approximate agreement rather than absolute identity.

The method applies to clustering loss functions that admit convex relaxations. To obtain its guarantees in practice, one solves a convex optimization problem. This creates a way to assess a proposed clustering through a related optimization problem with convex structure. Because the conditions are sufficient, they establish quality when satisfied without claiming that every good clustering must satisfy them.

The authors demonstrate the approach for K-means on realistic datasets, obtaining guarantees that do not depend on a specified data distribution. The contribution is a general framework for certifying clustering quality relative to a chosen objective. It addresses both how far the objective value might be from the optimum and whether substantially different solutions remain plausible under the method’s guarantee.
summary.tldr: The Sublevel Set method uses convex optimization to provide sufficient guarantees of clustering near-optimality and approximate uniqueness.

title: How to tell when a clustering is (approximately) correct using convex relaxations

abstract: Despite the efficacy on a variety of computer vision tasks, deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, limiting their applications in security-critical systems. Recent works have shown the possibility of generating imperceptibly perturbed image inputs (a.k.a., adversarial examples) to fool well-trained DNN classifiers into making arbitrary predictions. To address this problem, we propose a training recipe named "deep defense". Our core idea is to integrate an adversarial perturbation-based regularizer into the classification objective, such that the obtained models learn to resist potential attacks, directly and precisely. The whole optimization problem is solved just like training a recursive network. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms training with adversarial/Parseval regularizations by large margins on various datasets (including MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet) and different DNN architectures. Code and models for reproducing our results are available at https://github.com/ZiangYan/deepdefense.pytorch.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks can classify images effectively while remaining vulnerable to tiny, visually imperceptible changes that cause incorrect predictions. The paper introduces a training method called deep defense to improve resistance to such adversarial inputs. It makes robustness part of the objective used to learn the classifier.

The central addition is a regularizer based on adversarial perturbations. This term is incorporated into the classification objective so that training directly accounts for the model's response to potential attacks. The authors formulate optimization of the complete objective in a manner similar to training a recursive network. This connects the calculation used to characterize adversarial vulnerability with the process that updates the classifier.

Experiments cover multiple neural architectures and datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. The reported results outperform training with adversarial or Parseval regularization by large margins. These findings support the effectiveness of the proposed regularizer across the evaluated settings. The practical contribution is a training recipe that explicitly incorporates adversarial resistance and demonstrates improved robustness in those comparisons.
summary.tldr: Deep defense adds an adversarial-perturbation regularizer to classifier training and reports improved robustness across multiple datasets and architectures.

title: Deep Defense: Training DNNs with Improved Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Parameterizing the approximate posterior of a generative model with neural networks has become a common theme in recent machine learning research. While providing appealing flexibility, this approach makes it difficult to impose or assess structural constraints such as conditional independence. We propose a framework for learning representations that relies on Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes and whose search space is constrained via kernel-based measures of independence. In particular, our method employs the $d$-variable Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (dHSIC) to enforce independence between the latent representations and arbitrary nuisance factors. We show how to apply this method to a range of problems, including the problems of learning invariant representations and the learning of interpretable representations. We also present a full-fledged application to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). In this setting the biological signal in mixed in complex ways with sequencing errors and sampling effects. We show that our method out-performs the state-of-the-art in this domain.

We show how to apply this method to a range of problems, including the problems of learning invariant representations and the learning of interpretable representations. We show that our method out-performs the state-of-the-art in this domain.

paragraphs: Neural networks make approximate posterior distributions flexible, but that flexibility complicates controlling which information a learned representation contains. In particular, structural requirements such as independence can be difficult to impose or assess. This paper adds information constraints to representation learning based on Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.

The framework uses kernel-based independence measures to constrain the space of representations considered during learning. Its specific tool is the d-variable Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, or dHSIC, which is used to enforce independence between latent representations and nuisance factors. This connects a desired statistical property of the representation directly to the learning process, rather than relying only on the neural network's expressive capacity.

The authors apply the framework to learning invariant and interpretable representations. They also present an application to single-cell RNA sequencing, where biological information is entangled with sequencing errors and sampling effects. Their method outperforms the state of the art in that domain. The application illustrates why controlling dependence on nuisance factors can matter when the useful signal and measurement-related effects are mixed together.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based independence constraints help variational models learn representations separated from nuisance factors, with strong results in single-cell RNA sequencing.

title: Information Constraints on Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

abstract: In this paper, we formalize the idea behind capsule nets of using a capsule vector rather than a neuron activation to predict the label of samples. To this end, we propose to learn a group of capsule subspaces onto which an input feature vector is projected. Then the lengths of resultant capsules are used to score the probability of belonging to different classes. We train such a Capsule Projection Network (CapProNet) by learning an orthogonal projection matrix for each capsule subspace, and show that each capsule subspace is updated until it contains input feature vectors corresponding to the associated class. With low dimensionality of capsule subspace as well as an iterative method to estimate the matrix inverse, only a small negligible computing overhead is incurred to train the network. Experiment results on image datasets show the presented network can greatly improve the performance of state-of-the-art Resnet backbones by $10-20\%$ with almost the same computing cost.

It learns a separate subspace associated with each class and projects an input feature vector onto these subspaces. The length of each resulting capsule supplies a score for the probability that the input belongs to the corresponding class.

Training learns an orthogonal projection matrix for every capsule subspace. The authors show that these subspaces are updated until they contain feature vectors associated with their classes. This gives the classifier a geometric interpretation: learning changes the spaces onto which features are projected, and the resulting vector lengths express class membership evidence.

The computational design uses low-dimensional capsule subspaces and an iterative approximation for a matrix inverse. The authors report that these choices add negligible training overhead. On image datasets, they report a 10–20% performance improvement for state-of-the-art ResNet backbones at almost the same computing cost. The abstract describes this as a performance improvement without identifying a more specific interpretation of that percentage.
summary.tldr: CapProNet scores classes using feature projections onto learned capsule subspaces, improving reported ResNet performance with little added computation.

title: CapProNet: Deep Feature Learning via Orthogonal Projections onto Capsule Subspaces

abstract: Designing codes that combat the noise in a communication medium has remained a significant area of research in information theory as well as wireless communications. Asymptotically optimal channel codes have been developed by mathematicians for communicating under canonical models after over 60 years of research. On the other hand, in many non-canonical channel settings, optimal codes do not exist and the codes designed for canonical models are adapted via heuristics to these channels and are thus not guaranteed to be optimal. In this work, we make significant progress on this problem by designing a fully end-to-end jointly trained neural encoder and decoder, namely, Turbo Autoencoder (TurboAE), with the following contributions: (a) under moderate block lengths, TurboAE approaches state-of-the-art performance under canonical channels; (b) moreover, TurboAE outperforms the state-of-the-art codes under non-canonical settings in terms of reliability. TurboAE shows that the development of channel coding design can be automated via deep learning, with near-optimal performance.

paragraphs: Channel codes help messages survive noise during communication. Codes developed for standard channel models can perform extremely well, but adapting them to nonstandard channels often relies on heuristics without optimality guarantees. This paper investigates whether learning the encoder and decoder together can automate code design for different communication conditions.

Turbo Autoencoder, or TurboAE, is a neural encoder–decoder system trained jointly from end to end. Instead of treating message encoding and recovery as separately designed components, it learns them as one communication system. The approach targets both canonical channel models and non-canonical settings where codes adapted from standard models may be less well suited.

At moderate block lengths, TurboAE approaches state-of-the-art performance on canonical channels. In the non-canonical settings studied, it exceeds the reliability of the state-of-the-art codes used for comparison. These findings support deep learning as a way to automate channel-code design with near-optimal performance in the reported settings, while preserving the distinction between approaching established performance and demonstrating an improvement.
summary.tldr: TurboAE jointly learns communication encoders and decoders, approaching leading codes on standard channels and surpassing them in the tested nonstandard settings.

title: Turbo Autoencoder: Deep learning based channel codes for point-to-point communication channels

abstract: A temporal point process is a mathematical model for a time series of discrete events, which covers various applications. Recently, recurrent neural network (RNN) based models have been developed for point processes and have been found effective. RNN based models usually assume a specific functional form for the time course of the intensity function of a point process (e.g., exponentially decreasing or increasing with the time since the most recent event). However, such an assumption can restrict the expressive power of the model. We herein propose a novel RNN based model in which the time course of the intensity function is represented in a general manner. In our approach, we first model the integral of the intensity function using a feedforward neural network and then obtain the intensity function as its derivative. This approach enables us to both obtain a flexible model of the intensity function and exactly evaluate the log-likelihood function, which contains the integral of the intensity function, without any numerical approximations. Our model achieves competitive or superior performances compared to the previous state-of-the-art methods for both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model sequences of discrete events through an intensity function describing how event occurrence varies over time. Existing recurrent neural network models often restrict this function to a particular shape, such as exponential growth or decay since the latest event. Those assumptions can limit the event patterns the model can express.

The paper changes which quantity the neural network represents directly. A feedforward network models the integral of the intensity function, and differentiation then produces the intensity itself. This construction allows a more general time dependence while keeping the integral readily available for evaluating the model's likelihood.

That combination matters because the log-likelihood requires the integrated intensity as well as the intensity. The proposed approach evaluates it exactly without numerical approximations, while retaining a flexible intensity model within an RNN-based framework. On both synthetic and real datasets, the authors report performance competitive with or superior to previous state-of-the-art methods. The findings support modeling the integral as a way to combine expressive event dynamics with tractable likelihood evaluation.
summary.tldr: Modeling integrated event intensity with a neural network enables flexible temporal point processes and exact log-likelihood evaluation.

title: Fully Neural Network based Model for General Temporal Point Processes

abstract: Recently, there has been a growing interest in developing saliency methods that provide visual explanations of network predictions. Still, the usability of existing methods is limited to image classification models. To overcome this limitation, we extend the existing approaches to generate grid saliencies, which provide spatially coherent visual explanations for (pixel-level) dense prediction networks. As the proposed grid saliency allows to spatially disentangle the object and its context, we specifically explore its potential to produce context explanations for semantic segmentation networks, discovering which context most influences the class predictions inside a target object area. We investigate the effectiveness of grid saliency on a synthetic dataset with an artificially induced bias between objects and their context as well as on the real-world Cityscapes dataset using state-of-the-art segmentation networks. Our results show that grid saliency can be successfully used to provide easily interpretable context explanations and, moreover, can be employed for detecting and localizing contextual biases present in the data.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns classes at the pixel level, so explaining its predictions requires more spatial detail than explaining a single image label. This paper extends saliency approaches to produce grid saliencies: spatially coherent visual explanations for networks that make dense predictions. The aim is to show which image information influences a particular prediction area.

The method distinguishes a target object's area from its surrounding context. This allows the authors to ask which contextual regions most affect the class predictions inside the object. That distinction matters because an explanation can reveal dependence on surrounding content even when the predictions being examined lie within the target itself.

The authors evaluate grid saliency on synthetic data with an intentionally introduced relationship between objects and context, and on Cityscapes using contemporary segmentation networks. The results show interpretable context explanations and demonstrate detection and localization of contextual biases in the data. The contribution is thus both an explanation method for dense prediction and a way to examine contextual dependence.
summary.tldr: Grid saliency explains how surrounding image regions influence segmentation predictions and can localize contextual biases.

title: Grid Saliency for Context Explanations of Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We propose a neural architecture search (NAS) algorithm, Petridish, to iteratively add shortcut connections to existing network layers. The added shortcut connections effectively perform gradient boosting on the augmented layers. The proposed algorithm is motivated by the feature selection algorithm forward stage-wise linear regression, since we consider NAS as a generalization of feature selection for regression, where NAS selects shortcuts among layers instead of selecting features. In order to reduce the number of trials of possible connection combinations, we train jointly all possible connections at each stage of growth while leveraging feature selection techniques to choose a subset of them. We experimentally show this process to be an efficient forward architecture search algorithm that can find competitive models using few GPU days in both the search space of repeatable network modules (cell-search) and the space of general networks (macro-search). Petridish is particularly well-suited for warm-starting from existing models crucial for lifelong-learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Petridish searches for neural network architectures by progressively adding shortcut connections to existing layers. The paper views architecture search as a generalization of feature selection: the choices are connections between layers rather than input features in a regression model. Forward stage-wise linear regression provides the motivation for this incremental process.

At each growth stage, the algorithm jointly trains all candidate connections and uses feature-selection techniques to retain a subset. This reduces the number of separate trials needed to explore connection combinations. The added shortcuts effectively perform gradient boosting on the layers they augment, connecting architectural growth to a way of improving the current model step by step.

Experiments show that Petridish finds competitive models using a few GPU days in both cell search, which searches for repeatable network modules, and macro search, which searches general network structures. Because growth starts from an existing network, the approach is particularly suitable for warm starts. That property makes it relevant to lifelong-learning scenarios where an existing model is a useful starting point for further development.
summary.tldr: Petridish efficiently grows neural architectures by jointly training candidate shortcuts and selecting which connections to add.

title: Efficient Forward Architecture Search

abstract: We show that for the problem of $\ell_p$ rank-$k$ approximation of any given matrix over $R^{n\times m}$ and $C^{n\times m}$, the algorithm of column subset selection enjoys approximation ratio $(k+1)^{1/p}$ for $1\le p\le 2$ and $(k+1)^{1-1/p}$ for $p\ge 2$. This improves upon the previous $O(k+1)$ bound (Chierichetti et al.,2017) for $p\ge 1$. We complement our analysis with lower bounds; these bounds match our upper bounds up to constant 1 when $p\geq 2$. At the core of our techniques is an application of Riesz-Thorin interpolation theorem from harmonic analysis, which might be of independent interest to other algorithmic designs and analysis more broadly. Our analysis results in improvements on approximation guarantees of several other algorithms with various time complexity. For example, to make the algorithm of column subset selection computationally efficient, we analyze a polynomial time bi-criteria algorithm which selects $O(k\log m)$ number of columns. We show that this algorithm has an approximation ratio of $O((k+1)^{1/p})$ for $1\le p\le 2$ and $O((k+1)^{1-1/p})$ for $p\ge 2$. This improves over the bound in (Chierichetti et al.,2017) with an $O(k+1)$ approximation ratio. Our bi-criteria algorithm also implies an exact-rank method in polynomial time with a slightly larger approximation ratio.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation seeks a simpler representation of a matrix while controlling reconstruction error. This paper analyzes methods based on selecting original matrix columns when error is measured using an ℓp objective. The results apply to both real and complex matrices and sharpen how approximation quality depends on the desired rank k.

For column subset selection, the approximation ratio is (k + 1)^(1/p) when 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, and (k + 1)^(1 − 1/p) when p ≥ 2. These improve the previous O(k + 1) bound. Matching lower bounds establish tightness, including the constant, for p ≥ 2. The analysis draws on the Riesz–Thorin interpolation theorem from harmonic analysis.

The authors also analyze a polynomial-time method that selects O(k log m) columns, allowing extra columns in exchange for computational efficiency. It achieves the same rank dependence up to big-O factors. This bicriteria result further yields a polynomial-time exact-rank method with a slightly larger approximation ratio, connecting the sharper analysis to multiple computational tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: Sharper, partly tight approximation bounds improve the theory of column-selection methods for ℓp low-rank matrix approximation.

title: Optimal Analysis of Subset-Selection Based L_p Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: Modern machine learning methods including deep learning have achieved great success in predictive accuracy for supervised learning tasks, but may still fall short in giving useful estimates of their predictive uncertainty. Quantifying uncertainty is especially critical in real-world settings, which often involve input distributions that are shifted from the training distribution due to a variety of factors including sample bias and non-stationarity. In such settings, well calibrated uncertainty estimates convey information about when a model's output should (or should not) be trusted. Many probabilistic deep learning methods, including Bayesian-and non-Bayesian methods, have been proposed in the literature for quantifying predictive uncertainty, but to our knowledge there has not previously been a rigorous large-scale empirical comparison of these methods under dataset shift. We present a large-scale benchmark of existing state-of-the-art methods on classification problems and investigate the effect of dataset shift on accuracy and calibration. We find that traditional post-hoc calibration does indeed fall short, as do several other previous methods. However, some methods that marginalize over models give surprisingly strong results across a broad spectrum of tasks.

paragraphs: A classifier can make accurate predictions yet provide unreliable estimates of how certain those predictions are. This distinction matters when deployment inputs differ from training inputs, for example because of sampling bias or changes over time. Useful uncertainty estimates should help indicate when a prediction deserves trust under these changed conditions.

The paper introduces a large-scale empirical benchmark of predictive uncertainty methods for classification under dataset shift. It covers Bayesian and non-Bayesian approaches and examines both prediction accuracy and calibration. Evaluating these together addresses two separate questions: whether predictions remain correct and whether the confidence attached to them remains informative as the data distribution changes.

The study finds that traditional calibration applied after training falls short under the shifts examined, along with several other existing methods. Some methods that average over models instead deliver surprisingly strong results across a broad range of tasks. These are comparative empirical findings: they identify promising uncertainty strategies while showing why strong predictive accuracy alone does not establish trustworthy confidence.
summary.tldr: A large classification benchmark finds that dataset shift undermines several uncertainty methods, while some model-averaging approaches perform strongly.

title: Can you trust your model's uncertainty? Evaluating predictive uncertainty under dataset shift

abstract: Deep neural networks achieve stellar generalisation even when they have enough parameters to easily fit all their training data. We study this phenomenon by analysing the dynamics and the performance of over-parameterised two-layer neural networks in the teacher-student setup, where one network, the student, is trained on data generated by another network, called the teacher. We show how the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is captured by a set of differential equations and prove that this description is asymptotically exact in the limit of large inputs. Using this framework, we calculate the final generalisation error of student networks that have more parameters than their teachers. We find that the final generalisation error of the student increases with network size when training only the first layer, but stays constant or even decreases with size when training both layers. We show that these different behaviours have their root in the different solutions SGD finds for different activation functions. Our results indicate that achieving good generalisation in neural networks goes beyond the properties of SGD alone and depends on the interplay of at least the algorithm, the model architecture, and the data set.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why a neural network can generalize well despite having more parameters than needed to fit its training data. It uses a teacher-student setup: one network generates the data, and a two-layer student network learns from it. This controlled setting lets the authors study students with more parameters than their teachers.

They describe stochastic gradient descent through a system of differential equations and prove that this description becomes exact asymptotically as input size grows. Using that framework, they calculate the student’s final generalization error. This connects the trajectory of training to the eventual performance of an overparameterized network.

The outcome depends on which layers are trained. When only the first layer changes, final generalization error increases with student size; when both layers are trained, it remains constant or can decrease. The authors connect these differences to the solutions found under different activation functions. Their findings indicate that generalization depends on interactions among the optimization algorithm, architecture, and dataset, rather than on properties of stochastic gradient descent alone.
summary.tldr: A teacher-student analysis shows that the generalization effect of network size depends on which layers are trained and which activations are used.

title: Dynamics of stochastic gradient descent for two-layer neural networks in the teacher-student setup

abstract: Neural machine translation models usually use the encoder-decoder framework and generate translation from left to right (or right to left) without fully utilizing the target-side global information. A few recent approaches seek to exploit the global information through two-pass decoding, yet have limitations in translation quality and model efficiency. In this work, we propose a new framework that introduces a soft prototype into the encoder-decoder architecture, which allows the decoder to have indirect access to both past and future information, such that each target word can be generated based on the better global understanding. We further provide an efficient and effective method to generate the prototype. Empirical studies on various neural machine translation tasks show that our approach brings significant improvement in generation quality over the baseline model, with little extra cost in storage and inference time, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Specially, we achieve state-of-the-art results on WMT2014, 2015 and 2017 English to German translation.

paragraphs: Neural translation systems commonly generate a sentence in one direction, which limits their use of global information about the target sentence. Earlier two-pass approaches try to supply that information but face quality and efficiency limitations. This paper introduces a soft prototype into the encoder-decoder framework to give generation a broader view of the translation.

The prototype gives the decoder indirect access to information about both earlier and later target content. Each word can therefore be generated with more global context than one-directional decoding alone provides. The authors also develop an efficient method for producing the prototype, addressing the practical cost of adding this source of information.

Experiments across translation tasks show significant generation-quality improvements over the baseline with little additional storage or inference time. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on the WMT2014, WMT2015, and WMT2017 English-to-German tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the prototype as a way to improve target-side context while keeping its added computational cost small in the evaluated systems.
summary.tldr: A soft target-sentence prototype gives translation decoders indirect past and future context, improving quality with little additional storage or inference time.

title: Neural Machine Translation with Soft Prototype

abstract: The robustness of a neural network to adversarial examples can be provably certified by solving a convex relaxation. If the relaxation is loose, however, then the resulting certificate can be too conservative to be practically useful. Recently, a less conservative robustness certificate was proposed, based on a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation of the ReLU activation function. In this paper, we describe a geometric technique that determines whether this SDP certificate is exact, meaning whether it provides both a lower-bound on the size of the smallest adversarial perturbation, as well as a globally optimal perturbation that attains the lower-bound. Concretely, we show, for a least-squares restriction of the usual adversarial attack problem, that the SDP relaxation amounts to the nonconvex projection of a point onto a hyperbola. The resulting SDP certificate is exact if and only if the projection of the point lies on the major axis of the hyperbola. Using this geometric technique, we prove that the certificate is exact over a single hidden layer under mild assumptions, and explain why it is usually conservative for several hidden layers. We experimentally confirm our theoretical insights using a general-purpose interior-point method and a custom rank-2 Burer-Monteiro algorithm.

paragraphs: A robustness certificate can guarantee that adversarial changes below a certain size will not defeat a neural network. Convex relaxations make such certification possible, but a loose relaxation can give an overly conservative bound. This paper studies when a semidefinite relaxation of ReLU networks provides an exact certificate.

Exactness here means obtaining both a lower bound on the smallest adversarial perturbation and a globally optimal perturbation that reaches it. For a least-squares restriction of the attack problem, the authors develop a geometric description involving projection onto a hyperbola. The certificate is exact precisely when that projection lies on the hyperbola’s major axis.

This geometric criterion supports a proof of exactness for a single hidden layer under mild assumptions and an explanation of why certificates are usually conservative with several hidden layers. Experiments using a general-purpose interior-point solver and a custom rank-2 Burer-Monteiro algorithm confirm the theoretical insights. The result helps distinguish conservatism caused by the relaxation from the actual robustness question being studied.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis identifies when semidefinite robustness certificates are exact and explains their usual conservatism in deeper networks.

title: On the Tightness of Semidefinite Relaxations for Certifying Robustness to Adversarial Examples

abstract: A common challenge faced in practical supervised learning, such as medical image processing and robotic interactions, is that there are plenty of tasks but each task cannot afford to collect enough labeled examples to be learned in isolation. However, by exploiting the similarities across those tasks, one can hope to overcome such data scarcity. Under a canonical scenario where each task is drawn from a mixture of $k$ linear regressions, we study a fundamental question: can abundant small-data tasks compensate for the lack of big-data tasks? Existing second moment based approaches of \cite{2020arXiv200208936K} show that such a trade-off is efficiently achievable, with the help of medium-sized tasks with $\Omega(k^{1/2})$ examples each. However, this algorithm is brittle in two important scenarios. The predictions can be arbitrarily bad $(i)$ even with only a few outliers in the dataset; or $(ii)$ even if the medium-sized tasks are slightly smaller with $o(k^{1/2})$ examples each. We introduce a spectral approach that is simultaneously robust under both scenarios. To this end, we first design a novel outlier-robust principal component analysis algorithm that achieves an optimal accuracy. This is followed by a sum-of-squares algorithm to exploit the information from higher order moments. Together, this approach is robust against outliers and achieves a graceful statistical trade-off; the lack of $\Omega(k^{1/2})$-size tasks can be compensated for with smaller tasks, which can now be as small as ${\cal O}(\log k)$.
originalAbstract: A common challenge faced in practical supervised learning, such as medical image processing and robotic interactions, is that there are plenty of tasks but each task cannot afford to collect enough labeled examples to be learned in isolation. However, by exploiting the similarities across those tasks, one can hope to overcome such data scarcity. Under a canonical scenario where each task is drawn from a mixture of $k$ linear regressions, we study a fundamental question: can abundant small-data tasks compensate for the lack of big-data tasks? Existing second moment based approaches of \cite{2020arXiv200208936K} show that such a trade-off is efficiently achievable, with the help of medium-sized tasks with $\Omega(k^{1/2})$ examples each. However, this algorithm is brittle in two important scenarios. The predictions can be arbitrarily bad $(i)$ even with only a few outliers in the dataset; or $(ii)$ even if the medium-sized tasks are slightly smaller with $o(k^{1/2})$ examples each. We introduce a spectral approach that is simultaneously robust under both scenarios. To this end, we first design a novel outlier-robust principal component analysis algorithm that achieves an optimal accuracy. This is followed by a sum-of-squares algorithm to exploit the information from higher order moments. Together, this approach is robust against outliers and achieves a graceful statistical trade-off; the lack of $\Omega(k^{1/2})$-size tasks can be compensated for with smaller tasks, which can now be as small as ${\cal O}(\log k)$.

paragraphs: Many learning tasks have too few labeled examples to be solved individually, yet related tasks may collectively contain enough information. This paper asks whether numerous small-data tasks can compensate for missing larger tasks. It studies a setting where each task comes from a mixture of k linear regressions.

Earlier second-moment approaches described in the abstract rely on medium-sized tasks with roughly square-root-of-k examples and can fail badly with outliers or somewhat smaller tasks. The authors develop a spectral approach robust to both problems. It starts with a new outlier-robust principal component analysis algorithm that achieves optimal accuracy, then uses a sum-of-squares algorithm to extract information from higher-order moments.

Together, these components provide a gradual statistical trade-off between task size and the availability of tasks. Within the studied mixture setting, the method can compensate for the missing medium-sized tasks with smaller ones, potentially containing only logarithmically many examples in k. The result strengthens the case for pooling information across scarce-data tasks while explicitly addressing contamination by outliers.
summary.tldr: A robust spectral and higher-moment method lets smaller tasks compensate for missing larger tasks in mixed linear-regression meta-learning.

title: Robust Meta-learning for Mixed Linear Regression with Small Batches

abstract: Value function approximation has demonstrated phenomenal empirical success in reinforcement learning (RL). Nevertheless, despite a handful of recent progress on developing theory for RL with linear function approximation, the understanding of \emph{general} function approximation schemes largely remains missing. In this paper, we establish the first provably efficient RL algorithm with general value function approximation. We show that if the value functions admit an approximation with a function class $\mathcal{F}$, our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(dH)\sqrt{T})$ where $d$ is a complexity measure of $\mathcal{F}$ that depends on the eluder dimension~[Russo and Van Roy, 2013] and log-covering numbers, $H$ is the planning horizon, and $T$ is the number interactions with the environment. Our theory generalizes the linear MDP assumption to general function classes. Moreover, our algorithm is model-free and provides a framework to justify the effectiveness of algorithms used in practice.

paragraphs: Value function approximation is widely successful in reinforcement learning, but theoretical understanding has been stronger for linear approximations than for general function classes. This paper establishes a provably efficient algorithm for general value function approximation, extending the theory beyond the linear setting. Its guarantee depends on whether the value functions admit approximation within a specified function class.

The regret bound grows roughly with the square root of the number of environment interactions, multiplied by a polynomial in the planning horizon and a function-class complexity measure, with logarithmic factors suppressed. That complexity measure depends on eluder dimension and log-covering numbers. Consequently, the guarantee makes the approximation class’s complexity an explicit part of how difficult learning is.

The theory generalizes the linear Markov decision process assumption to broader function classes. The algorithm is also model-free, addressing learning through value approximation without requiring a learned environment model. The result supplies a framework for understanding the effectiveness of practical algorithms, while keeping its efficiency claim tied to the stated approximation and complexity conditions.
summary.tldr: A model-free algorithm obtains regret guarantees for general value-function classes under approximation and bounded-complexity conditions.

title: Reinforcement Learning with General Value Function Approximation: Provably Efficient Approach via Bounded Eluder Dimension

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning includes a broad family of algorithms that parameterise an internal representation, such as a value function or policy, by a deep neural network. Each algorithm optimises its parameters with respect to an objective, such as Q-learning or policy gradient, that defines its semantics. In this work, we propose an algorithm based on meta-gradient descent that discovers its own objective, flexibly parameterised by a deep neural network, solely from interactive experience with its environment. Over time, this allows the agent to learn how to learn increasingly effectively. Furthermore, because the objective is discovered online, it can adapt to changes over time. We demonstrate that the algorithm discovers how to address several important issues in RL, such as bootstrapping, non-stationarity, and off-policy learning. On the Atari Learning Environment, the meta-gradient algorithm adapts over time to learn with greater efficiency, eventually outperforming the median score of a strong actor-critic baseline.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning algorithm normally updates its policy or value function using a predefined objective. This paper instead lets an agent discover that learning objective through interaction with its environment. The objective is represented by a deep neural network, giving the agent flexibility in how it learns from experience.

The proposed algorithm uses meta-gradient descent to learn the objective while the agent is also learning its behavior. Because discovery happens online, the objective can change over time. The authors demonstrate that this process discovers ways to handle bootstrapping, changing conditions, and off-policy learning, all of which affect how experience should guide an update.

Experiments in the Atari Learning Environment show increasingly efficient learning as the objective adapts. Eventually, the method exceeds the median score of a strong actor-critic baseline. That finding concerns the reported median comparison, rather than superiority on every task. The paper’s contribution is evidence that an agent can improve its own learning procedure during interaction, using a learned objective that remains responsive to its ongoing experience.
summary.tldr: An agent learns and adapts its own neural training objective online, eventually exceeding a strong actor-critic baseline’s median Atari score.

title: Meta-Gradient Reinforcement Learning with an Objective Discovered Online

abstract: Score-based diffusion models synthesize samples by reversing a stochastic process that diffuses data to noise, and are trained by minimizing a weighted combination of score matching losses. The log-likelihood of score-based diffusion models can be tractably computed through a connection to continuous normalizing flows, but log-likelihood is not directly optimized by the weighted combination of score matching losses. We show that for a specific weighting scheme, the objective upper bounds the negative log-likelihood, thus enabling approximate maximum likelihood training of score-based diffusion models. We empirically observe that maximum likelihood training consistently improves the likelihood of score-based diffusion models across multiple datasets, stochastic processes, and model architectures. Our best models achieve negative log-likelihoods of 2.83 and 3.76 bits/dim on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet $32\times 32$ without any data augmentation, on a par with state-of-the-art autoregressive models on these tasks.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models generate data by reversing a stochastic process that gradually turns data into noise. Their usual training objective combines score-matching losses with chosen weights. Although a connection to continuous normalizing flows makes likelihood computation tractable, that does not mean the usual training loss directly optimizes likelihood. This paper addresses that mismatch.

The authors identify a weighting scheme for which the training objective upper-bounds negative log-likelihood. Minimizing this bound enables approximate maximum-likelihood training within the score-based diffusion framework. The distinction matters: the result supplies a mathematically justified objective connected to likelihood, while retaining the qualification that optimization proceeds through a bound rather than directly minimizing the exact negative log-likelihood.

Across multiple datasets, stochastic processes, and architectures, the authors empirically observe consistent likelihood improvements. Their best models obtain 2.83 bits per dimension on CIFAR-10 and 3.76 on ImageNet at 32 by 32 resolution, without data augmentation. These results are comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive models on those tasks, showing that the revised weighting can make diffusion models competitive on this likelihood-based evaluation.
summary.tldr: A particular score-matching weighting enables approximate maximum-likelihood training and consistently improves diffusion-model likelihoods in the reported experiments.

title: Maximum Likelihood Training of Score-Based Diffusion Models

abstract: Spatial verification is a crucial technique for particular object retrieval. It utilizes spatial information for the accurate detection of true positive images. However, existing query expansion and diffusion methods cannot efficiently propagate the spatial information in an ordinary graph with scalar edge weights, resulting in low recall or precision. To tackle these problems, we propose a novel hypergraph-based framework that efficiently propagates spatial information in query time and retrieves an object in the database accurately. Additionally, we propose using the image graph's structure information through community selection technique, to measure the accuracy of the initial search result and to provide correct starting points for hypergraph propagation without heavy spatial verification computations. Experiment results on ROxford and RParis show that our method significantly outperforms the existing query expansion and diffusion methods.

paragraphs: Retrieving images of a particular object requires distinguishing genuine matches from images that merely look similar. Spatial verification helps by checking spatial information, but existing query expansion and diffusion methods struggle to propagate that information efficiently through ordinary graphs with scalar edge weights. This can reduce either the completeness or the accuracy of retrieval results.

The paper introduces a hypergraph framework that propagates spatial information during a query. It also uses community selection based on the structure of an image graph to assess the initial search results. This step supplies suitable starting points for propagation without requiring heavy spatial verification computations to establish those starting points.

The two components address complementary parts of retrieval: selecting reliable initial matches and spreading spatial evidence through the database. Experiments on ROxford and RParis show significant improvements over existing query expansion and diffusion methods. The reported findings support using richer relationships and graph structure to improve object retrieval in these evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Hypergraph propagation and graph-based community selection improve object retrieval by spreading spatial evidence from better starting points.

title: Hypergraph Propagation and Community Selection for Objects Retrieval

abstract: Most prior approaches to offline reinforcement learning (RL) have taken an iterative actor-critic approach involving off-policy evaluation. In this paper we show that simply doing one step of constrained/regularized policy improvement using an on-policy Q estimate of the behavior policy performs surprisingly well. This one-step algorithm beats the previously reported results of iterative algorithms on a large portion of the D4RL benchmark. The one-step baseline achieves this strong performance while being notably simpler and more robust to hyperparameters than previously proposed iterative algorithms. We argue that the relatively poor performance of iterative approaches is a result of the high variance inherent in doing off-policy evaluation and magnified by the repeated optimization of policies against those estimates. In addition, we hypothesize that the strong performance of the one-step algorithm is due to a combination of favorable structure in the environment and behavior policy.
originalAbstract: Most prior approaches to offline reinforcement learning (RL) have taken an iterative actor-critic approach involving off-policy evaluation. In this paper we show that simply doing one step of constrained/regularized policy improvement using an on-policy Q estimate of the behavior policy performs surprisingly well. This one-step algorithm beats the previously reported results of iterative algorithms on a large portion of the D4RL benchmark. The one-step baseline achieves this strong performance while being notably simpler and more robust to hyperparameters than previously proposed iterative algorithms. We argue that the relatively poor performance of iterative approaches is a result of the high variance inherent in doing off-policy evaluation and magnified by the repeated optimization of policies against those estimates. In addition, we hypothesize that the strong performance of the one-step algorithm is due to a combination of favorable structure in the environment and behavior policy.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from previously collected experience. Many approaches repeatedly evaluate and improve a policy, including evaluating policies different from the one that produced the data. This paper studies a simpler alternative: estimate the action values of the behavior policy, then perform a single constrained or regularized policy-improvement step.

That one-step method outperforms previously reported iterative-algorithm results on a large portion of D4RL. The authors also report greater robustness to hyperparameter choices and a simpler procedure. The finding establishes a strong baseline: repeated policy-improvement cycles are not required to achieve the reported performance across those benchmark settings.

The paper argues that off-policy evaluation introduces high variance, which repeated optimization against those estimates can amplify. It separately hypothesizes that favorable structure in the environment and behavior policy helps explain the one-step method's success. These proposed explanations have different status from the benchmark results: they motivate why the simpler approach works without establishing universal superiority over iterative learning.
summary.tldr: A single regularized improvement of the behavior policy outperforms reported iterative methods on much of D4RL while simplifying offline learning.

title: Offline RL Without Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: In computer vision and natural language processing, innovations in model architecture that increase model capacity have reliably translated into gains in performance. In stark contrast with this trend, state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms often use small MLPs, and gains in performance typically originate from algorithmic innovations. It is natural to hypothesize that small datasets in RL necessitate simple models to avoid overfitting; however, this hypothesis is untested. In this paper we investigate how RL agents are affected by exchanging the small MLPs with larger modern networks with skip connections and normalization, focusing specifically on actor-critic algorithms. We empirically verify that naively adopting such architectures leads to instabilities and poor performance, likely contributing to the popularity of simple models in practice. However, we show that dataset size is not the limiting factor, and instead argue that instability from taking gradients through the critic is the culprit. We demonstrate that spectral normalization (SN) can mitigate this issue and enable stable training with large modern architectures. After smoothing with SN, larger models yield significant performance improvements --- suggesting that more ``easy'' gains may be had by focusing on model architectures in addition to algorithmic innovations.

paragraphs: Larger neural architectures have helped vision and language systems, yet reinforcement learning commonly uses small multilayer perceptrons. This paper investigates that mismatch in actor-critic methods by replacing small networks with larger architectures containing skip connections and normalization. It tests whether limited data explains the apparent preference for simpler models.

The experiments show that directly substituting larger modern networks can cause unstable training and poor performance. The authors find that dataset size is not the limiting factor in their investigation. Instead, they argue that instability associated with taking gradients through the critic is responsible, directing attention toward the learning dynamics rather than model capacity alone.

Spectral normalization mitigates this instability and enables stable training with larger architectures. Once the networks are smoothed this way, larger models yield significant performance improvements in the reported experiments. The results suggest that architectural improvements offer additional opportunities in reinforcement learning alongside algorithmic changes. They support addressing critic-related instability before concluding that increased network capacity is unhelpful.
summary.tldr: Spectral normalization stabilizes larger actor-critic networks, allowing increased model capacity to improve reinforcement learning performance.

title: Towards Deeper Deep Reinforcement Learning with Spectral Normalization

abstract: Haze, a common kind of bad weather caused by atmospheric scattering, decreases the visibility of scenes and degenerates the performance of computer vision algorithms. Single-image dehazing methods have shown their effectiveness in a large variety of scenes, however, they are based on handcrafted priors or learned features, which do not generalize well to real-world images. Polarization information can be used to relieve its ill-posedness, however, real-world images are still challenging since existing polarization-based methods usually assume that the transmitted light is not significantly polarized, and they require specific clues to estimate necessary physical parameters. In this paper, we propose a generalized physical formation model of hazy images and a robust polarization-based dehazing pipeline without the above assumption or requirement, along with a neural network tailored to the pipeline. Experimental results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic data and real-world hazy images.

paragraphs: Haze results from atmospheric scattering and makes scenes harder to see and process computationally. Recovering a clear image from a single hazy image is ambiguous, and methods based on handcrafted assumptions or learned features can struggle to generalize to real photographs. This paper uses polarization information to help resolve that ambiguity.

Existing polarization-based approaches have their own restrictions: they commonly assume that transmitted light has little polarization and need particular clues to estimate physical parameters. The authors introduce a more general physical model of hazy image formation and a dehazing pipeline that does not require either restriction. They also design a neural network specifically for this pipeline, connecting the physical formulation with learned image recovery.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on synthetic data and real-world hazy images. The contribution therefore combines a broader model of how haze affects measured light with a corresponding computational method. Its stated advantage is particularly relevant to real imagery, where the assumptions and parameter-estimation clues required by earlier polarization methods can be difficult to satisfy.
summary.tldr: A generalized physical model and tailored neural pipeline use polarization to remove haze without two restrictions of earlier methods.

title: Learning to dehaze with polarization

abstract: We develop scalable methods for producing conformal Bayesian predictive intervals with finite sample calibration guarantees. Bayesian posterior predictive distributions, $p(y \mid x)$, characterize subjective beliefs on outcomes of interest, $y$, conditional on predictors, $x$. Bayesian prediction is well-calibrated when the model is true, but the predictive intervals may exhibit poor empirical coverage when the model is misspecified, under the so called ${\cal{M}}$-open perspective. In contrast, conformal inference provides finite sample frequentist guarantees on predictive confidence intervals without the requirement of model fidelity. Using 'add-one-in' importance sampling, we show that conformal Bayesian predictive intervals are efficiently obtained from re-weighted posterior samples of model parameters. Our approach contrasts with existing conformal methods that require expensive refitting of models or data-splitting to achieve computational efficiency. We demonstrate the utility on a range of examples including extensions to partially exchangeable settings such as hierarchical models.

paragraphs: Bayesian prediction describes uncertainty about future outcomes through a posterior predictive distribution. When the assumed model is correct, its predictions are well calibrated. When that model does not accurately describe the data, however, its predictive intervals can contain the observed outcomes less reliably than their stated uncertainty suggests.

This paper develops computational methods for combining Bayesian prediction with conformal inference. Conformal methods provide finite-sample coverage guarantees without requiring the predictive model to be correct. The authors use an approach called add-one-in importance sampling, which constructs conformal Bayesian predictive intervals by assigning new weights to existing posterior samples of model parameters.

Reusing posterior samples addresses a practical computational obstacle: existing conformal approaches can require expensive model refitting or split the data to make computation manageable. The proposed method offers a scalable route to calibrated intervals while retaining Bayesian predictions as its starting point. Examples demonstrate its utility across several settings, including extensions to partially exchangeable data in hierarchical models. The contribution connects a coverage guarantee with a computational procedure for obtaining the corresponding intervals.
summary.tldr: Reweighting posterior samples makes conformal Bayesian predictive intervals computationally practical while providing finite-sample calibration guarantees.

title: Conformal Bayesian Computation

abstract: The recently proposed FixMatch achieved state-of-the-art results on most semi-supervised learning (SSL) benchmarks. However, like other modern SSL algorithms, FixMatch uses a pre-defined constant threshold for all classes to select unlabeled data that contribute to the training, thus failing to consider different learning status and learning difficulties of different classes. To address this issue, we propose Curriculum Pseudo Labeling (CPL), a curriculum learning approach to leverage unlabeled data according to the model's learning status. The core of CPL is to flexibly adjust thresholds for different classes at each time step to let pass informative unlabeled data and their pseudo labels. CPL does not introduce additional parameters or computations (forward or backward propagation). We apply CPL to FixMatch and call our improved algorithm FlexMatch. FlexMatch achieves state-of-the-art performance on a variety of SSL benchmarks, with especially strong performances when the labeled data are extremely limited or when the task is challenging. For example, FlexMatch achieves 13.96% and 18.96% error rate reduction over FixMatch on CIFAR-100 and STL-10 datasets respectively, when there are only 4 labels per class. CPL also significantly boosts the convergence speed, e.g., FlexMatch can use only 1/5 training time of FixMatch to achieve even better performance. Furthermore, we show that CPL can be easily adapted to other SSL algorithms and remarkably improve their performances. We open-source our code at https://github.com/TorchSSL/TorchSSL.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses a small labeled dataset together with unlabeled examples. Methods such as FixMatch select predicted labels for training using a fixed confidence threshold shared across classes. This paper argues that a shared threshold overlooks differences in how difficult classes are and how far the model has progressed in learning each one.

Curriculum Pseudo Labeling, or CPL, adjusts the threshold for each class throughout training according to the model’s learning status. This changes which unlabeled examples and predicted labels contribute to learning as training progresses. Incorporating CPL into FixMatch produces FlexMatch, without adding model parameters or extra forward or backward propagation.

FlexMatch achieves state-of-the-art results across the evaluated benchmarks, particularly with very few labels or challenging tasks. Improvements when CPL is applied to other methods suggest that adaptive selection is useful beyond this particular combination.
summary.tldr: FlexMatch adapts pseudo-label confidence thresholds by class and learning progress, improving semi-supervised accuracy and convergence without extra forward or backward passes.

title: FlexMatch: Boosting Semi-Supervised Learning with Curriculum Pseudo Labeling

abstract: Few-shot learning is a central problem in meta-learning, where learners must quickly adapt to new tasks given limited training data. Recently, feature pre-training has become a ubiquitous component in state-of-the-art meta-learning methods and is shown to provide significant performance improvement. However, there is limited theoretical understanding of the connection between pre-training and meta-learning. Further, pre-training requires global labels shared across tasks, which may be unavailable in practice. In this paper, we show why exploiting pre-training is theoretically advantageous for meta-learning, and in particular the critical role of global labels. This motivates us to propose Meta Label Learning (MeLa), a novel meta-learning framework that automatically infers global labels to obtains robust few-shot models. Empirically, we demonstrate that MeLa is competitive with existing methods and provide extensive ablation experiments to highlight its key properties.
