Recently, feature pre-training has become a ubiquitous component in state-of-the-art meta-learning methods and is shown to provide significant performance improvement. However, there is limited theoretical understanding of the connection between pre-training and meta-learning. Further, pre-training requires global labels shared across tasks, which may be unavailable in practice. In this paper, we show why exploiting pre-training is theoretically advantageous for meta-learning, and in particular the critical role of global labels. This motivates us to propose Meta Label Learning (MeLa), a novel meta-learning framework that automatically infers global labels to obtains robust few-shot models. Empirically, we demonstrate that MeLa is competitive with existing methods and provide extensive ablation experiments to highlight its key properties.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to adapt to a new task using only a small amount of labeled data. Pretraining features has become an important part of successful approaches, but its connection to meta-learning has lacked theoretical explanation. This paper investigates that connection, emphasizing the role of global labels shared across tasks.

The authors show theoretically why pretraining can benefit meta-learning and why shared label information matters to that benefit. This also exposes a practical obstacle: global labels may be unavailable even when individual training tasks have their own labels. The proposed Meta Label Learning framework, MeLa, addresses this by automatically inferring global labels.

MeLa uses this inferred information to obtain robust few-shot models. Empirical evaluations find it competitive with existing methods, and ablation experiments examine its key properties. The contribution joins an explanation of pretraining’s value with a method aimed at supplying the shared label structure that pretraining needs, extending the approach to situations where that structure is not directly provided.
summary.tldr: MeLa infers labels shared across tasks, motivated by a theoretical account of why global labels make pretraining useful for few-shot learning.

title: The Role of Global Labels in Few-Shot Classification and How to Infer Them

abstract: We propose a new learning framework that captures the tiered structure of many real-world user-interaction applications, where the users can be divided into two groups based on their different tolerance on exploration risks and should be treated separately. In this setting, we simultaneously maintain two policies $\pi^{\text{O}}$ and $\pi^{\text{E}}$: $\pi^{\text{O}}$ (``O'' for ``online'') interacts with more risk-tolerant users from the first tier and minimizes regret by balancing exploration and exploitation as usual, while $\pi^{\text{E}}$ (``E'' for ``exploit'') exclusively focuses on exploitation for risk-averse users from the second tier utilizing the data collected so far. An important question is whether such a separation yields advantages over the standard online setting (i.e., $\pi^{\text{E}}=\pi^{\text{O}}$) for the risk-averse users. We individually consider the gap-independent vs.~gap-dependent settings. For the former, we prove that the separation is indeed not beneficial from a minimax perspective. For the latter, we show that if choosing Pessimistic Value Iteration as the exploitation algorithm to produce $\pi^{\text{E}}$, we can achieve a constant regret for risk-averse users independent of the number of episodes $K$, which is in sharp contrast to the $\Omega(\log K)$ regret for any online RL algorithms in the same setting, while the regret of $\pi^{\text{O}}$ (almost) maintains its online regret optimality and does not need to compromise for the success of $\pi^{\text{E}}$.
originalAbstract: We propose a new learning framework that captures the tiered structure of many real-world user-interaction applications, where the users can be divided into two groups based on their different tolerance on exploration risks and should be treated separately. In this setting, we simultaneously maintain two policies $\pi^{\text{O}}$ and $\pi^{\text{E}}$: $\pi^{\text{O}}$ (``O'' for ``online'') interacts with more risk-tolerant users from the first tier and minimizes regret by balancing exploration and exploitation as usual, while $\pi^{\text{E}}$ (``E'' for ``exploit'') exclusively focuses on exploitation for risk-averse users from the second tier utilizing the data collected so far. An important question is whether such a separation yields advantages over the standard online setting (i.e., $\pi^{\text{E}}=\pi^{\text{O}}$) for the risk-averse users. We individually consider the gap-independent vs.~gap-dependent settings. For the former, we prove that the separation is indeed not beneficial from a minimax perspective. For the latter, we show that if choosing Pessimistic Value Iteration as the exploitation algorithm to produce $\pi^{\text{E}}$, we can achieve a constant regret for risk-averse users independent of the number of episodes $K$, which is in sharp contrast to the $\Omega(\log K)$ regret for any online RL algorithms in the same setting, while the regret of $\pi^{\text{O}}$ (almost) maintains its online regret optimality and does not need to compromise for the success of $\pi^{\text{E}}$.

paragraphs: Users of a learning system may differ in their tolerance for exploratory decisions. This paper formalizes that distinction with two policies. One interacts with more risk-tolerant users and balances exploration with exploitation. The other serves risk-averse users by exploiting the information collected so far, without taking on the same exploration role.

The authors ask whether separating these roles improves the experience of risk-averse users. In the gap-independent setting, the separation provides no minimax advantage. In the gap-dependent setting, however, using Pessimistic Value Iteration for the exploitation policy yields regret bounded independently of the number of episodes.

That constant-regret result contrasts with the logarithmic regret lower bound for online reinforcement-learning algorithms in the same setting. Meanwhile, the exploratory policy almost retains optimal online regret, so the improvement does not require sacrificing its performance guarantee. The result identifies a conditional benefit of sharing data across distinct interaction policies: the advantage emerges in the gap-dependent analysis, rather than as a universal consequence of separating users into tiers.
summary.tldr: Separating exploration from exploitation yields constant regret for risk-averse users in the gap-dependent setting with pessimistic value iteration.

title: Tiered Reinforcement Learning: Pessimism in the Face of Uncertainty and Constant Regret

abstract: We tackle the problem of novel class discovery and localization (NCDL). In this setting, we assume a source dataset with supervision for only some object classes. Instances of other classes need to be discovered, classified, and localized automatically based on visual similarity without any human supervision. To tackle NCDL, we propose a two-stage object detection network Region-based NCDL (RNCDL) that uses a region proposal network to localize regions of interest (RoIs). We then train our network to learn to classify each RoI, either as one of the known classes, seen in the source dataset, or one of the novel classes, with a long-tail distribution constraint on the class assignments, reflecting the natural frequency of classes in the real world. By training our detection network with this objective in an end-to-end manner, it learns to classify all region proposals for a large variety of classes, including those not part of the labeled object class vocabulary. Our experiments conducted using COCO and LVIS datasets reveal that our method is significantly more effective than multi-stage pipelines that rely on traditional clustering algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generality of our approach by applying our method to a large-scale Visual Genome dataset, where our network successfully learns to detect various semantic classes without direct supervision.

paragraphs: This paper considers object detection when only some classes have human-provided supervision. Objects from other classes must be discovered, grouped by visual similarity, and localized automatically. The task therefore extends beyond recognizing an existing label vocabulary: the detector must also organize and locate previously unlabeled categories.

The proposed RNCDL network first uses region proposals to locate candidate objects. It then learns to assign each region to either a known class or a newly discovered class. A long-tail constraint on these assignments reflects the unequal frequencies of classes in the real world. Training the detection network end to end connects localization with this broader classification objective.

On COCO and LVIS, the authors report substantially better results than multistage pipelines based on traditional clustering. They also apply the method to Visual Genome, where it learns to detect semantic classes without direct supervision for those classes. The findings support jointly learning discovery and detection under the stated assumption that supervision is available for some source classes.
summary.tldr: RNCDL learns to locate objects and discover novel categories while using supervision only for a subset of classes.

title: Learning to Discover and Detect Objects

abstract: Weak supervision (WS) is a powerful method to build labeled datasets for training supervised models in the face of little-to-no labeled data. It replaces hand-labeling data with aggregating multiple noisy-but-cheap label estimates expressed by labeling functions (LFs). While it has been used successfully in many domains, weak supervision's application scope is limited by the difficulty of constructing labeling functions for domains with complex or high-dimensional features. To address this, a handful of methods have proposed automating the LF design process using a small set of ground truth labels. In this work, we introduce AutoWS-Bench-101: a framework for evaluating automated WS (AutoWS) techniques in challenging WS settings---a set of diverse application domains on which it has been previously difficult or impossible to apply traditional WS techniques. While AutoWS is a promising direction toward expanding the application-scope of WS, the emergence of powerful methods such as zero-shot foundation models reveal the need to understand how AutoWS techniques compare or cooperate with modern zero-shot or few-shot learners. This informs the central question of AutoWS-Bench-101: given an initial set of 100 labels for each task, we ask whether a practitioner should use an AutoWS method to generate additional labels or use some simpler baseline, such as zero-shot predictions from a foundation model or supervised learning. We observe that it is necessary for AutoWS methods to incorporate signal from foundation models if they are to outperform simple few-shot baselines, and AutoWS-Bench-101 promotes future research in this direction. We conclude with a thorough ablation study of AutoWS methods.

AutoWS-Bench-101 evaluates this strategy across diverse, challenging application domains. Its central comparison starts each task with 100 labels and asks how practitioners should use them. This identifies an empirical requirement in the evaluated settings, rather than a universal rule for every application. The framework and accompanying ablation study help examine whether automated labeling adds value and how it can cooperate with modern foundation-model capabilities.
summary.tldr: AutoWS-Bench-101 tests how best to use 100 labels and finds foundation-model signals necessary for AutoWS to beat simple few-shot baselines in its evaluations.

title: AutoWS-Bench-101: Benchmarking Automated Weak Supervision with 100 Labels

abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD), a technique for constructing new programs which compute the derivative of an original program, has become ubiquitous throughout scientific computing and deep learning due to the improved performance afforded by gradient-based optimization. However, AD systems have been restricted to the subset of programs that have a continuous dependence on parameters. Programs that have discrete stochastic behaviors governed by distribution parameters, such as flipping a coin with probability $p$ of being heads, pose a challenge to these systems because the connection between the result (heads vs tails) and the parameters ($p$) is fundamentally discrete. In this paper we develop a new reparameterization-based methodology that allows for generating programs whose expectation is the derivative of the expectation of the original program. We showcase how this method gives an unbiased and low-variance estimator which is as automated as traditional AD mechanisms. We demonstrate unbiased forward-mode AD of discrete-time Markov chains, agent-based models such as Conway's Game of Life, and unbiased reverse-mode AD of a particle filter. Our code package is available at https://github.com/gaurav-arya/StochasticAD.jl.

paragraphs: Automatic differentiation constructs a program that computes derivatives of another program. Discrete randomness creates a difficulty: changing a coin's probability of heads does not produce a smoothly changing individual outcome. Yet the expected output of a program using that coin can change with the probability, making its derivative useful for optimization.

The paper develops a reparameterization-based method that generates programs whose expected output equals the derivative of the original program's expected output. The distinction matters: the method targets sensitivity of an expectation, rather than treating an individual discrete outcome as a continuously varying value. The authors present the resulting estimator as unbiased, low variance, and as automated as traditional automatic differentiation.

Demonstrations cover forward-mode differentiation of discrete-time Markov chains and agent-based models, including Conway's Game of Life, alongside reverse-mode differentiation of a particle filter. These examples show the method operating across several kinds of stochastic computation. The contribution extends automated derivative estimation to programs whose behavior includes parameter-dependent discrete random choices.
summary.tldr: A reparameterization-based method automatically estimates derivatives of expected program outputs despite discrete random choices.

title: Automatic Differentiation of Programs with Discrete Randomness

abstract: Structural pruning can simplify network architecture and improve inference speed. We propose Hardware-Aware Latency Pruning (HALP) that formulates structural pruning as a global resource allocation optimization problem, aiming at maximizing the accuracy while constraining latency under a predefined budget on targeting device. For filter importance ranking, HALP leverages latency lookup table to track latency reduction potential and global saliency score to gauge accuracy drop. Both metrics can be evaluated very efficiently during pruning, allowing us to reformulate global structural pruning under a reward maximization problem given target constraint. This makes the problem solvable via our augmented knapsack solver, enabling HALP to surpass prior work in pruning efficacy and accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We examine HALP on both classification and detection tasks, over varying networks, on ImageNet and VOC datasets, on different platforms. In particular, for ResNet-50/-101 pruning on ImageNet, HALP improves network throughput by $1.60\times$/$1.90\times$ with $+0.3\%$/$-0.2\%$ top-1 accuracy changes, respectively. For SSD pruning on VOC, HALP improves throughput by $1.94\times$ with only a $0.56$ mAP drop. HALP consistently outperforms prior art, sometimes by large margins. Project page at \url{https://halp-neurips.github.io/}.

paragraphs: Structural pruning simplifies a network by removing components, with the goal of making inference faster while preserving accuracy. Hardware-Aware Latency Pruning, or HALP, frames this as a global allocation problem: choose a pruned architecture that maximizes accuracy while meeting a specified latency budget on the target device.

HALP combines two signals when ranking filters. A latency lookup table estimates potential speed gains, and a global saliency score estimates the accuracy consequences of removal. Both are inexpensive to evaluate during pruning. An augmented knapsack solver then uses this information to make coordinated choices across the network under the latency constraint.

Experiments span classification and detection, multiple networks, and different platforms. On ImageNet, pruned ResNet-50 and ResNet-101 improve throughput by 1.60 and 1.90 times, with top-1 accuracy changes of +0.3% and −0.2%, respectively. For SSD on VOC, throughput improves 1.94 times with a 0.56 mAP decrease. The authors report consistently stronger tradeoffs than prior methods. These results support treating device latency and accuracy impact jointly when allocating a network’s remaining structure.
summary.tldr: HALP uses a knapsack formulation to prune networks globally according to accuracy impact and target-device latency.

title: Structural Pruning via Latency-Saliency Knapsack

abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) has shown a lot of promise in providing robustness in learning as well as sample-based optimization problems. We endeavor to provide DRO solutions for a class of sum of fractionals, non-convex optimization which is used for decision making in prominent areas such as facility location and security games. In contrast to previous work, we find it more tractable to optimize the equivalent variance regularized form of DRO rather than the minimax form. We transform the variance regularized form to a mixed-integer second-order cone program (MISOCP), which, while guaranteeing global optimality, does not scale enough to solve problems with real-world datasets. We further propose two abstraction approaches based on clustering and stratified sampling to increase scalability, which we then use for real-world datasets. Importantly, we provide global optimality guarantees for our approach and show experimentally that our solution quality is better than the locally optimal ones achieved by state-of-the-art gradient-based methods. We experimentally compare our different approaches and baselines and reveal nuanced properties of a DRO solution.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization seeks decisions that account for uncertainty in the distribution underlying observed samples. This paper develops methods for a nonconvex class of objectives formed from sums of fractional terms. Such problems arise in applications including facility location and security games, where obtaining globally good decisions can be computationally difficult.

The authors work with an equivalent variance-regularized formulation, which they find more tractable than the minimax form. They transform it into a mixed-integer second-order cone program. This formulation guarantees global optimality, but its computational demands prevent it from scaling adequately to the real-world datasets considered.

To improve scalability, the paper introduces two abstraction approaches based on clustering and stratified sampling and applies them to real-world data. The authors provide global optimality guarantees for their approach and experimentally obtain better solution quality than the local optima found by state-of-the-art gradient methods. Comparisons among the proposed approaches and baselines also reveal nuanced behavior of robust solutions. The contribution combines a globally grounded formulation with mechanisms intended to make it computationally usable.
summary.tldr: A variance-regularized formulation and data abstractions make globally grounded distributionally robust optimization more scalable for fractional objectives.

title: Scalable Distributional Robustness in a Class of Non-Convex Optimization with Guarantees

abstract: Graph contrastive learning (GCL), leveraging graph augmentations to convert graphs into different views and further train graph neural networks (GNNs), has achieved considerable success on graph benchmark datasets. Yet, there are still some gaps in directly applying existing GCL methods to real-world data. First, handcrafted graph augmentations require trials and errors, but still can not yield consistent performance on multiple tasks. Second, most real-world graph data present class-imbalanced distribution but existing GCL methods are not immune to data imbalance. Therefore, this work proposes to explicitly tackle these challenges, via a principled framework called \textit{\textbf{C}o-\textbf{M}odality \textbf{G}raph \textbf{C}ontrastive \textbf{L}earning} (\textbf{CM-GCL}) to automatically generate contrastive pairs and further learn balanced representation over unlabeled data. Specifically, we design inter-modality GCL to automatically generate contrastive pairs (e.g., node-text) based on rich node content. Inspired by the fact that minority samples can be ``forgotten'' by pruning deep neural networks, we naturally extend network pruning to our GCL framework for mining minority nodes. Based on this, we co-train two pruned encoders (e.g., GNN and text encoder) in different modalities by pushing the corresponding node-text pairs together and the irrelevant node-text pairs away. Meanwhile, we propose intra-modality GCL by co-training non-pruned GNN and pruned GNN, to ensure node embeddings with similar attribute features stay closed. Last, we fine-tune the GNN encoder on downstream class-imbalanced node classification tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models and learns more balanced representations on real-world graphs. Our source code is available at https://github.com/graphprojects/CM-GCL.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning trains representations by comparing related and unrelated views of graph data. The paper addresses two obstacles: manually designed graph transformations can require extensive trial and error, and existing methods can struggle when some node classes are much rarer than others. CM-GCL uses node content to construct comparisons automatically while seeking more balanced representations from unlabeled data.

For comparisons across modalities, the method pairs a node with content such as its text. It trains graph and content encoders to bring matching pairs closer and separate unrelated pairs. Network pruning helps identify minority nodes, motivated by the observation that pruning can cause minority examples to be forgotten. Two pruned encoders then learn together across the modalities.

Within the graph modality, a pruned and an unpruned graph encoder are co-trained to keep nodes with similar attributes close in representation space. The graph encoder is subsequently fine-tuned for imbalanced node classification. Experiments on real-world graphs report stronger performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods and more balanced representations.
summary.tldr: CM-GCL combines graph-content comparisons and network pruning to learn more balanced representations for imbalanced node classification.

title: Co-Modality Graph Contrastive Learning for Imbalanced Node Classification

abstract: Modern deep learning systems require huge data sets to achieve impressive performance, but there is little guidance on how much or what kind of data to collect. Over-collecting data incurs unnecessary present costs, while under-collecting may incur future costs and delay workflows. We propose a new paradigm for modeling the data collection workflow as a formal optimal data collection problem that allows designers to specify performance targets, collection costs, a time horizon, and penalties for failing to meet the targets. Additionally, this formulation generalizes to tasks requiring multiple data sources, such as labeled and unlabeled data used in semi-supervised learning. To solve our problem, we develop Learn-Optimize-Collect (LOC), which minimizes expected future collection costs. Finally, we numerically compare our framework to the conventional baseline of estimating data requirements by extrapolating from neural scaling laws. We significantly reduce the risks of failing to meet desired performance targets on several classification, segmentation, and detection tasks, while maintaining low total collection costs.

paragraphs: Collecting too much training data wastes resources, while collecting too little can delay a project and create additional costs later. This paper treats data collection as an optimization problem with explicit performance targets, collection costs, a planning horizon, and penalties for missing the targets. The formulation makes the consequences of collection decisions part of the learning workflow.

It also accommodates tasks that draw on several data sources, including the combination of labeled and unlabeled examples in semi-supervised learning. The proposed Learn-Optimize-Collect method minimizes expected future collection costs. This shifts the decision from simply estimating a final dataset size to optimizing collection under the specified costs and performance requirements.

The authors compare their framework numerically with the conventional approach of extrapolating data needs from neural scaling laws. Across several classification, segmentation, and detection tasks, it substantially reduces the risk of missing desired performance targets while maintaining low total collection costs. The findings support planning data acquisition around both achievement risk and expenditure, making explicit the trade-off between collecting now and potentially paying more later.
summary.tldr: Learn-Optimize-Collect plans data acquisition around costs and performance targets, reducing target-miss risk while keeping collection costs low in experiments.

title: Optimizing Data Collection for Machine Learning

abstract: In this work we demonstrate a novel separation between symmetric neural network architectures. Specifically, we consider the Relational Network~\parencite{santoro2017simple} architecture as a natural generalization of the DeepSets~\parencite{zaheer2017deep} architecture, and study their representational gap. Under the restriction to analytic activation functions, we construct a symmetric function acting on sets of size $N$ with elements in dimension $D$, which can be efficiently approximated by the former architecture, but provably requires width exponential in $N$ and $D$ for the latter.
originalAbstract: In this work we demonstrate a novel separation between symmetric neural network architectures. Specifically, we consider the Relational Network~\parencite{santoro2017simple} architecture as a natural generalization of the DeepSets~\parencite{zaheer2017deep} architecture, and study their representational gap. Under the restriction to analytic activation functions, we construct a symmetric function acting on sets of size $N$ with elements in dimension $D$, which can be efficiently approximated by the former architecture, but provably requires width exponential in $N$ and $D$ for the latter.

paragraphs: A symmetric function on a set produces the same result regardless of the order in which the elements are presented. Neural architectures can build this symmetry into their design, but sharing that property does not mean they represent functions equally efficiently. This paper compares the expressive efficiency of Relational Networks and DeepSets.

The authors treat the Relational Network architecture as a natural generalization of DeepSets and construct a function that separates their capabilities. The function acts on sets containing N elements, each with D dimensions. Under a restriction to analytic activation functions, a Relational Network can approximate it efficiently.

For DeepSets, approximating the constructed function provably requires width exponential in N and D. This establishes a potentially enormous representation-cost difference between the architectures even though both handle symmetric functions. The result is an existence statement with a stated activation restriction: it identifies a function exposing a strong architectural gap, rather than claiming that every set-processing task needs exponentially larger DeepSets models.
summary.tldr: With analytic activations, a constructed symmetric function is efficiently approximated by Relational Networks but requires exponentially wide DeepSets.

title: Exponential Separations in Symmetric Neural Networks

abstract: Equilibrium systems are a powerful way to express neural computations. As special cases, they include models of great current interest in both neuroscience and machine learning, such as deep neural networks, equilibrium recurrent neural networks, deep equilibrium models, or meta-learning. Here, we present a new principle for learning such systems with a temporally- and spatially-local rule. Our principle casts learning as a \emph{least-control} problem, where we first introduce an optimal controller to lead the system towards a solution state, and then define learning as reducing the amount of control needed to reach such a state. We show that incorporating learning signals within a dynamics as an optimal control enables transmitting activity-dependent credit assignment information, avoids storing intermediate states in memory, and does not rely on infinitesimal learning signals. In practice, our principle leads to strong performance matching that of leading gradient-based learning methods when applied to an array of problems involving recurrent neural networks and meta-learning. Our results shed light on how the brain might learn and offer new ways of approaching a broad class of machine learning problems.

paragraphs: Equilibrium systems describe neural computation through states reached by a system's dynamics. The paper proposes a learning principle for these systems using information local in both space and time. Its central move is to connect learning with the amount of external control needed to bring the system to a solution state.

The method first introduces an optimal controller that guides the system toward a solution. Learning then reduces the control required to reach that state. Incorporating learning signals into the dynamics this way transmits activity-dependent credit-assignment information. The authors show that the approach avoids storing intermediate states and does not require learning signals to be infinitesimally small.

Experiments involving recurrent neural networks and meta-learning report performance matching leading gradient-based methods. This supports least-control learning as a practical approach for the tested problems as well as a theoretical principle. Its local learning rules also offer a possible perspective on biological learning, while the paper presents that connection as insight into how the brain might learn rather than an established account.
summary.tldr: The least-control principle trains equilibrium systems by reducing the external control needed to reach a solution, enabling local learning rules.

title: The least-control principle for local learning at equilibrium

abstract: In machine learning, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is widely deployed to train models using highly non-convex objectives with equally complex noise models. Unfortunately, SGD theory often makes restrictive assumptions that fail to capture the non-convexity of real problems, and almost entirely ignore the complex noise models that exist in practice. In this work, we demonstrate the restrictiveness of these assumptions using three canonical models in machine learning. Then, we develop novel theory to address this shortcoming in two ways. First, we establish that SGD's iterates will either globally converge to a stationary point or diverge under nearly arbitrary nonconvexity and noise models. Under a slightly more restrictive assumption on the joint behavior of the non-convexity and noise model that generalizes current assumptions in the literature, we show that the objective function cannot diverge, even if the iterates diverge. As a consequence of our results, SGD can be applied to a greater range of stochastic optimization problems with confidence about its global convergence behavior and stability.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is used with complicated nonconvex objectives and noisy updates, but its theoretical guarantees often rely on more restrictive settings. The authors illustrate this mismatch using three canonical machine-learning models. They then develop results that accommodate much broader combinations of objective geometry and noise.

The first result establishes an either-or outcome: under nearly arbitrary nonconvexity and noise models, the sequence of SGD iterates globally converges to a stationary point or diverges. This characterizes possible long-run behavior without asserting that convergence always occurs. A stationary point is also not necessarily a globally optimal solution, so global convergence here should not be read as global optimality.

A second result imposes a somewhat stronger condition on how the objective and noise behave jointly. Under that condition, the objective function cannot diverge even if the parameter iterates do. This separates stability of objective values from stability of the parameters themselves. Together, the results extend the range of stochastic optimization problems for which SGD's long-run behavior can be characterized.
summary.tldr: Broader SGD theory characterizes convergence or divergence and gives conditions keeping objective values stable even when iterates diverge.

title: Global Convergence and Stability of Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Kernel density estimation (KDE) is integral to a range of generative and discriminative tasks in machine learning. Drawing upon tools from the multidimensional calculus of variations, we derive an optimal weight function that reduces bias in standard kernel density estimates for density ratios, leading to improved estimates of prediction posteriors and information-theoretic measures. In the process, we shed light on some fundamental aspects of density estimation, particularly from the perspective of algorithms that employ KDEs as their main building blocks.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation is used as a building block in both generative and discriminative machine learning. This paper focuses on estimating density ratios, where the quantity of interest compares densities. Its concern is bias in the standard kernel estimates used for that task and how weighting can reduce it.

The authors use multidimensional calculus of variations to derive an optimal weight function. The weighting is designed to reduce bias in kernel-based density-ratio estimation. This treats the choice of weights as a mathematical optimization problem, producing a principled correction to the estimation procedure rather than simply accepting the bias of the standard estimates.

The stated benefits extend to estimates of prediction posteriors and information-theoretic measures, both of which the paper connects to density-ratio estimation. The work also examines fundamental aspects of density estimation from the perspective of algorithms built around kernel estimates. Its significance lies in improving a statistical component that other methods depend on: reducing bias at that component can improve the downstream quantities identified in the paper.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an optimal weighting function that reduces bias in kernel density-ratio estimates and improves related posterior and information-theoretic estimates.

title: Variational Weighting for Kernel Density Ratios

abstract: Current state-of-the-art object-centric models use slots and attention-based routing for binding. However, this class of models has several conceptual limitations: the number of slots is hardwired; all slots have equal capacity; training has high computational cost; there are no object-level relational factors within slots. Synchrony-based models in principle can address these limitations by using complex-valued activations which store binding information in their phase components. However, working examples of such synchrony-based models have been developed only very recently, and are still limited to toy grayscale datasets and simultaneous storage of less than three objects in practice. Here we introduce architectural modifications and a novel contrastive learning method that greatly improve the state-of-the-art synchrony-based model. For the first time, we obtain a class of synchrony-based models capable of discovering objects in an unsupervised manner in multi-object color datasets and simultaneously representing more than three objects.

paragraphs: Object-centric models try to organize a scene into representations of individual objects. Many leading approaches allocate a fixed collection of slots and use attention to assign information to them. The paper highlights restrictions of this design, including a predetermined slot count, equal capacity across slots, expensive training, and a lack of object-level relational factors within slots.

An alternative uses complex-valued activations, storing information about which features belong together in their phase components. Such synchrony-based models could, in principle, address the slot-based limitations. Existing working examples, however, had been confined to simple grayscale datasets and had practically represented fewer than three objects simultaneously.

The authors introduce architectural changes and a new contrastive training method that substantially improve the existing synchrony-based approach. Their models discover objects without supervision in color datasets containing multiple objects and can represent more than three objects at once. This expands the demonstrated capabilities of phase-based object representations; it does not establish that every conceptual limitation of slot-based models has been resolved.
summary.tldr: Architectural changes and contrastive learning extend synchrony-based object discovery to multi-object color datasets and more than three simultaneous objects.

title: Contrastive Training of Complex-Valued Autoencoders for Object Discovery

abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust framework for hybrid query (HQ) processing, which combines approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) with attribute constraint. HQ aims to find objects that are similar to a feature vector and match some structured attributes. Existing methods handle ANNS and attribute filtering separately, leading to inefficiency and inaccuracy. Our framework, called native hybrid query (NHQ), builds a composite index based on proximity graph (PG) and applies joint pruning for HQ. We can easily adapt existing PGs to this framework for efficient HQ processing. We also propose two new navigable PGs (NPGs) with optimized edge selection and routing, which improve the overall ANNS performance. We implement five HQ methods based on the proposed NPGs and existing PGs in NHQ, and show that they outperform the state-of-the-art methods on 10 real-world datasets (up to 315$\times$ faster with the same accuracy).

paragraphs: A hybrid search query asks for objects that are close to a feature vector and also satisfy structured attribute requirements. Both conditions matter to the answer. The paper identifies a problem with handling them as separate operations: separating similarity search from attribute filtering can make the overall search inefficient and inaccurate.

The proposed native hybrid query framework, NHQ, combines the requirements within a composite index built on a proximity graph. Such a graph organizes objects through connections based on proximity. NHQ uses joint pruning to narrow the search while considering the combined query. Existing proximity graphs can be adapted to this framework, so the approach is not restricted to a single new graph design.

The authors also introduce two navigable proximity graphs with improved edge selection and routing. They implement five hybrid-query methods using both new and existing graphs. Across ten real-world datasets, these methods outperform the compared state-of-the-art approaches, with speedups reaching 315 times at the same accuracy. That maximum is an experimental result, rather than a speedup promised for every query or dataset.
summary.tldr: NHQ integrates similarity search and attribute constraints within a graph index, achieving substantial speedups at matched accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: An Efficient and Robust Framework for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with Attribute Constraint

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has emerged as a popular unsupervised graph representation learning method. However, it has been shown that GCL is vulnerable to adversarial attacks on both the graph structure and node attributes. Although empirical approaches have been proposed to enhance the robustness of GCL, the certifiable robustness of GCL is still remain unexplored. In this paper, we develop the first certifiably robust framework in GCL. Specifically, we first propose a unified criteria to evaluate and certify the robustness of GCL. We then introduce a novel technique, RES (Randomized Edgedrop Smoothing), to ensure certifiable robustness for any GCL model, and this certified robustness can be provably preserved in downstream tasks. Furthermore, an effective training method is proposed for robust GCL. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in providing effective certifiable robustness and enhancing the robustness of any GCL model. The source code of RES is available at https://github.com/ventr1c/RES-GCL.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations without supervised labels, but changes to graph connections or node attributes can undermine those representations. Earlier robustness approaches relied on empirical improvements. This paper investigates certification: establishing a formal basis for assessing robustness alongside measuring how a model performs in experiments.

The authors first introduce a unified criterion for evaluating and certifying graph contrastive learning robustness. They then propose Randomized Edgedrop Smoothing, or RES, as a technique for providing certifiable robustness to any graph contrastive learning model. The framework also establishes that its certified robustness can be preserved in downstream tasks, connecting representation-level guarantees to later uses of those representations.

An additional training method is designed to improve robust graph contrastive learning. Experiments on real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the approach for certification and robustness enhancement. The contribution therefore spans a criterion, a smoothing procedure, and a training method. Its significance lies in giving formal robustness support to a learning setting previously addressed empirically, without treating certification as an unrestricted guarantee against every possible attack.
summary.tldr: Randomized Edgedrop Smoothing provides graph contrastive learning with robustness certificates that can carry through to downstream tasks.

title: Certifiably Robust Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Kernelized bandits, also known as Bayesian optimization (BO), has been a prevalent method for optimizing complicated black-box reward functions. Various BO algorithms have been theoretically shown to enjoy upper bounds on their cumulative regret which are sub-linear in the number $T$ of iterations, and a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ has been derived which represents the unavoidable regrets for any classical BO algorithm. Recent works on quantum bandits have shown that with the aid of quantum computing, it is possible to achieve tighter regret upper bounds better than their corresponding classical lower bounds. However, these works are restricted to either multi-armed or linear bandits, and are hence not able to solve sophisticated real-world problems with non-linear reward functions. To this end, we introduce the quantum-Gaussian process-upper confidence bound (Q-GP-UCB) algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, our Q-GP-UCB is the first BO algorithm able to achieve a regret upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(\text{poly}\log T)$, which is significantly smaller than its regret lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ in the classical setting. Moreover, thanks to our novel analysis of the confidence ellipsoid, our Q-GP-UCB with the linear kernel achieves a smaller regret than the quantum linear UCB algorithm from the previous work. We use simulations, as well as an experiment using a real quantum computer, to verify that the theoretical quantum speedup achieved by our Q-GP-UCB is also potentially relevant in practice.

Classical algorithms face a stated lower bound growing with the square root of the number of iterations. A new confidence-ellipsoid analysis also gives its linear-kernel version a smaller regret bound than the previous quantum linear UCB algorithm.

Simulations and an experiment on a real quantum computer examine whether the theoretical advantage could matter in practice. The abstract describes the evidence as showing potential practical relevance. The main contribution is therefore a stronger theoretical regret guarantee for quantum Bayesian optimization, accompanied by empirical exploration of that advantage rather than a universal practical speedup claim.
summary.tldr: Q-GP-UCB achieves a polylogarithmic quantum Bayesian optimization regret bound, with experiments suggesting potential practical relevance.

title: Quantum Bayesian Optimization

abstract: We present Masked Audio-Video Learners (MAViL) to learn audio-visual representations with three complementary forms of self-supervision: (1) reconstructing masked raw audio and video inputs, (2) intra-modal and inter-modal contrastive learning with masking, and (3) self-training to predict aligned and contextualized audio-video representations learned from the first two objectives. Empirically, MAViL achieves state-of-the-art audio-video classification performance on AudioSet (53.3 mAP) and VGGSound (67.1\% accuracy), surpassing recent self-supervised models and supervised models that utilize external labeled data. Notably, pre-training with MAViL not only enhances performance in multimodal classification and retrieval tasks, but it also improves the representations of each modality in isolation, without relying on information from the other modality during uni-modal fine-tuning or inference. The code and models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/MAViL.

Empirically, MAViL achieves state-of-the-art audio-video classification performance on AudioSet (53.3 mAP) and VGGSound (67.1\% accuracy), surpassing recent self-supervised models and supervised models that utilize external labeled data. Notably, pre-training with MAViL not only enhances performance in multimodal classification and retrieval tasks, but it also improves the representations of each modality in isolation, without relying on information from the other modality during uni-modal fine-tuning or inference. The code and models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/MAViL.

paragraphs: MAViL learns representations from paired audio and video through three complementary self-supervised tasks. The first reconstructs hidden portions of the raw sound and visual inputs. The second uses contrastive learning, with masking, both within each modality and between them. Together, these tasks train the model to recover information and connect related audio-visual representations.

The third task is self-training: the model predicts aligned, contextualized representations learned through the first two objectives. This adds a target built from learned audio-video structure alongside reconstruction of raw inputs. The approach therefore combines learning from missing content, relationships within and across modalities, and representations produced by the training process itself.

The authors report state-of-the-art classification results of 53.3 mAP on AudioSet and 67.1% accuracy on VGGSound, surpassing the compared self-supervised and externally supervised models. Pre-training also improves multimodal retrieval and the representations of audio and video individually. Those individual gains remain when fine-tuning and inference use only one modality, showing that joint training can benefit later single-modality tasks.
summary.tldr: MAViL combines masked reconstruction, contrastive learning, and self-training to improve joint audio-video representations and each modality used alone.

title: MAViL: Masked Audio-Video Learners

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities in learning complex hierarchical data representations, but the nature of these representations remains largely unknown. Existing global explainability methods, such as Network Dissection, face limitations such as reliance on segmentation masks, lack of statistical significance testing, and high computational demands. We propose Inverse Recognition (INVERT), a scalable approach for connecting learned representations with human-understandable concepts by leveraging their capacity to discriminate between these concepts. In contrast to prior work, INVERT is capable of handling diverse types of neurons, exhibits less computational complexity, and does not rely on the availability of segmentation masks. Moreover, INVERT provides an interpretable metric assessing the alignment between the representation and its corresponding explanation and delivering a measure of statistical significance. We demonstrate the applicability of INVERT in various scenarios, including the identification of representations affected by spurious correlations, and the interpretation of the hierarchical structure of decision-making within the models.

paragraphs: Neural networks learn layered internal representations, but explaining what those representations mean remains difficult. INVERT connects them to human-understandable concepts by examining their ability to distinguish between concepts. The idea is to use a representation's discriminative behavior as evidence for assigning it an explanation.

The method addresses several practical obstacles in earlier global explanation approaches. It supports diverse neuron types, reduces computational complexity, and does not require segmentation masks. It also supplies an interpretable score for how well a representation aligns with its proposed explanation, together with a measure of statistical significance. These outputs make the quality of a concept assignment part of the explanation itself.

The paper demonstrates uses that include locating representations influenced by spurious correlations and interpreting the hierarchical organization of model decisions. These applications show how concept labeling can help investigate both what a model has learned and how that knowledge is organized. The contribution is a scalable explanation method with explicit measures for assessing the correspondence between internal representations and their labels.
summary.tldr: INVERT labels neural representations through their ability to distinguish concepts, with alignment scores and statistical significance measures.

title: Labeling Neural Representations with Inverse Recognition

abstract: Understanding model’s sensitivity to its training data is crucial but can also be challenging and costly, especially during training. To simplify such issues, we present the Memory-Perturbation Equation (MPE) which relates model's sensitivity to perturbation in its training data. Derived using Bayesian principles, the MPE unifies existing sensitivity measures, generalizes them to a wide-variety of models and algorithms, and unravels useful properties regarding sensitivities. Our empirical results show that sensitivity estimates obtained during training can be used to faithfully predict generalization on unseen test data. The proposed equation is expected to be useful for future research on robust and adaptive learning.

paragraphs: Understanding how a model responds to changes in its training data can reveal useful information about its behavior. Measuring that sensitivity can be difficult and expensive, especially while training is still underway. This paper introduces the Memory-Perturbation Equation, or MPE, to express the relationship between data perturbations and model sensitivity.

The equation is derived from Bayesian principles. The authors use it to unify existing sensitivity measures, extend them across a wide variety of models and algorithms, and expose useful properties of sensitivity. This common formulation provides a framework for studying measures that might otherwise be treated separately for different learning procedures.

Empirically, the authors find that sensitivity estimates collected during training can faithfully predict generalization to unseen test data. This connects a quantity observed during optimization to performance beyond the training set. The finding is an experimental result, while applications to robust and adaptive learning are presented as an expectation for future research. The contribution combines that demonstrated predictive use with a broader mathematical framework.
summary.tldr: The Memory-Perturbation Equation unifies data-sensitivity measures, with experiments showing that training-time estimates can predict test generalization.

title: The Memory-Perturbation Equation: Understanding Model's Sensitivity to Data

abstract: People are relying on AI agents to assist them with various tasks. The human must know when to rely on the agent, collaborate with the agent, or ignore its suggestions. In this work, we propose to learn rules grounded in data regions and described in natural language that illustrate how the human should collaborate with the AI. Our novel region discovery algorithm finds local regions in the data as neighborhoods in an embedding space that corrects the human prior. Each region is then described using an iterative and contrastive procedure where a large language model describes the region. We then teach these rules to the human via an onboarding stage. Through user studies on object detection and question-answering tasks, we show that our method can lead to more accurate human-AI teams. We also evaluate our region discovery and description algorithms separately.

paragraphs: An AI assistant can improve a person's decisions only if the person knows how to use its suggestions. Depending on the situation, useful behavior might involve relying on the system, collaborating with it, or ignoring its advice. This paper proposes learning plain-language rules that teach people how to make those choices for particular kinds of inputs.

The method first discovers local regions of the data, represented as neighborhoods in an embedding space. These regions are selected to correct the human's prior understanding of collaboration. A large language model then describes each region through an iterative, contrastive procedure. This connects the resulting advice to identified data regions rather than leaving it as general guidance about AI use.

The rules are taught through an onboarding stage before people work with the system. User studies involving object detection and question answering show that the method can produce more accurate human-AI teams. The authors also evaluate region discovery and description separately. The stated result supports onboarding as a way to improve collaboration by teaching when different patterns of reliance are appropriate.
summary.tldr: Data-grounded language rules taught during onboarding can help people collaborate with AI more accurately.

title: Effective Human-AI Teams via Learned Natural Language Rules and Onboarding

abstract: Recently, diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have achieved promising results in diverse generative tasks. A typical DPM framework includes a forward process that gradually diffuses the data distribution and a reverse process that recovers the data distribution from time-dependent data scores. In this work, we observe that the stochastic reverse process of data scores is a martingale, from which concentration bounds and the optional stopping theorem for data scores can be derived. Then, we discover a simple way for calibrating an arbitrary pretrained DPM, with which the score matching loss can be reduced and the lower bounds of model likelihood can consequently be increased. We provide general calibration guidelines under various model parametrizations. Our calibration method is performed only once and the resulting models can be used repeatedly for sampling. We conduct experiments on multiple datasets to empirically validate our proposal. Our code is available at https://github.com/thudzj/Calibrated-DPMs.

paragraphs: Diffusion probabilistic models generate data through a reverse process that counteracts a forward corruption process. The reverse process relies on time-dependent data scores describing the evolving distribution. This paper examines a mathematical property of those scores and uses it to develop a calibration method for pretrained diffusion models.

The authors observe that the stochastic reverse process of data scores is a martingale. This property enables concentration bounds and an optional stopping theorem for the scores. From that analysis, they derive a simple calibration procedure that can reduce the score matching loss and consequently increase lower bounds on model likelihood.

The paper provides calibration guidance for different model parameterizations and describes the method as applicable to an arbitrary pretrained diffusion probabilistic model. Calibration is performed once, after which the resulting model can be reused for sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets empirically validate the proposal, connecting the theoretical score behavior to a practical adjustment of an already trained generator.
summary.tldr: A martingale property of diffusion scores motivates a one-time calibration that can lower score matching loss and improve likelihood lower bounds.

title: On Calibrating Diffusion Probabilistic Models

abstract: Animals have a developed ability to explore that aids them in important tasks such as locating food, exploring for shelter, and finding misplaced items. These exploration skills necessarily track where they have been so that they can plan for finding items with relative efficiency. Contemporary exploration algorithms often learn a less efficient exploration strategy because they either condition only on the current state or simply rely on making random open-loop exploratory moves. In this work, we propose $\eta\psi$-Learning, a method to learn efficient exploratory policies by conditioning on past episodic experience to make the next exploratory move. Specifically, $\eta\psi$-Learning learns an exploration policy that maximizes the entropy of the state visitation distribution of a single trajectory. Furthermore, we demonstrate how variants of the predecessor representation and successor representations can be combined to predict the state visitation entropy. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of $\eta\psi$-Learning to strategically explore the environment and maximize the state coverage with limited samples.

This paper introduces ηψ-Learning, which uses experience from the current episode when choosing the next exploratory action.

The method learns a policy that maximizes the entropy of the state-visitation distribution along a single trajectory. This objective favors spreading visits across states rather than concentrating them narrowly. Its focus on one trajectory makes the agent’s history within that trajectory directly relevant to deciding where to go next.

The authors combine variants of predecessor and successor representations to predict state-visitation entropy. These representations connect information about past and future visitation so that the exploration policy can be guided by its entropy objective. Experiments demonstrate strategic exploration and broad state coverage with limited samples. The contribution is an exploration method whose decisions account for accumulated episodic experience and whose objective explicitly rewards diversity of visited states.
summary.tldr: ηψ-Learning uses episodic history and predecessor–successor representations to learn exploration policies that spread visits across states.

title: Maximum State Entropy Exploration using Predecessor and Successor Representations

abstract: The striking ability of unsupervised word translation has been demonstrated recently with the help of low-dimensional word vectors / pretraining, which is used by all successful methods and assumed to be necessary. We test and challenge this assumption by developing a method that can also make use of high dimensional signal. Freed from the limits of low dimensions, we show that relying on low-dimensional vectors and their incidental properties miss out on better denoising methods and signals in high dimensions, thus stunting the potential of the data. Our results show that unsupervised translation can be achieved more easily and robustly than previously thought -- less than 80MB and minutes of CPU time is required to achieve over 50\% accuracy for English to Finnish, Hungarian, and Chinese translations when trained in the same domain; even under domain mismatch, the method still works fully unsupervised on English NewsCrawl to Chinese Wikipedia and English Europarl to Spanish Wikipedia, among others. These results challenge prevailing assumptions on the necessity and superiority of low-dimensional vectors and show that the higher dimension signal can be used rather than thrown away.

paragraphs: Unsupervised word translation seeks to connect words across languages without supervised translation examples. Successful approaches had relied on low-dimensional word vectors or pretraining, encouraging the assumption that such representations were necessary. This paper challenges that assumption by developing a method that can retain and use information in higher dimensions.

The authors argue that reducing information to low-dimensional vectors can discard useful translation signals and restrict the available denoising methods. Their approach explores those higher-dimensional signals instead. The underlying question is whether the representation choices of existing systems reflect a true requirement of unsupervised translation or merely one successful way of approaching it.

For training data from the same domain, the method exceeds 50% accuracy on English-to-Finnish, English-to-Hungarian, and English-to-Chinese translation using less than 80 MB and minutes of CPU time. It also works fully unsupervised on reported mismatched-domain pairs, including English NewsCrawl with Chinese Wikipedia. These results challenge the necessity and presumed superiority of low-dimensional vectors without establishing that higher-dimensional representations always perform better.
summary.tldr: Higher-dimensional signals enable efficient unsupervised word translation, challenging the assumption that low-dimensional word vectors are necessary.

title: Accessing Higher Dimensions for Unsupervised Word Translation

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have recently gained attention with state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image synthesis. Abiding by the tradition in deep learning, DMs are trained and evaluated on the images with fixed sizes. However, users are demanding for various images with specific sizes and various aspect ratio. This paper focuses on adapting text-to-image diffusion models to handle such variety while maintaining visual fidelity. First we observe that, during the synthesis, lower resolution images suffer from incomplete object portrayal, while higher resolution images exhibit repetitively disordered presentation. Next, we establish a statistical relationship indicating that attention entropy changes with token quantity, suggesting that models aggregate spatial information in proportion to image resolution. The subsequent interpretation on our observations is that objects are incompletely depicted due to limited spatial information for low resolutions, while repetitively disorganized presentation arises from redundant spatial information for high resolutions. From this perspective, we propose a scaling factor to alleviate the change of attention entropy and mitigate the defective pattern observed. Extensive experimental results validate the efficacy of the proposed scaling factor, enabling models to achieve better visual effects, image quality, and text alignment. Notably, these improvements are achieved without additional training or fine-tuning techniques.

This paper examines the defects that appear when models are used at other sizes. The authors observe incomplete objects at lower resolutions and repetitive, disorganized content at higher resolutions.

They establish a statistical relationship between the number of tokens and attention entropy, a property of how attention is distributed. This suggests that the amount of spatial information aggregated changes with image resolution. The contribution connects a measurable change in attention behavior to a practical adaptation method, while the proposed explanation for the observed image defects remains an interpretation of that relationship.
summary.tldr: An attention-scaling adjustment improves diffusion-generated images at varied sizes without additional training or fine-tuning.

title: Training-free Diffusion Model Adaptation for Variable-Sized Text-to-Image Synthesis

abstract: Causal effect identification and estimation are two crucial tasks in causal inference. Although causal effect identification has been theoretically resolved, many existing estimators only address a subset of scenarios, known as the sequential back-door adjustment (SBD) (Pearl and Robins, 1995) or g-formula (Robins, 1986). Recent efforts for developing general-purpose estimators with broader coverage, incorporating the front-door adjustment (FD) (Pearl, 2000) and more, lack scalability due to the high computational cost of summing over high-dimensional variables. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that achieves broad coverage of causal estimands beyond the SBD, incorporating various sum-product functionals like the FD, while maintaining scalability -- estimated in polynomial time relative to the number of variables and samples. Specifically, we present the class of UCA for which a scalable and doubly robust estimator is developed. In particular, we illustrate the expressiveness of UCA for a wide spectrum of causal estimands (e.g., SBD, FD, and more) in causal inference. We then develop an estimator that exhibits computational efficiency and doubly robustness. The scalability and robustness of the proposed framework are verified through simulations.

This paper targets the estimation step. Many existing estimators cover sequential back-door adjustment, while broader approaches can become expensive because they require summation over high-dimensional variables.

The authors introduce Unified Covariate Adjustment, or UCA, a class covering a wide range of causal estimands. It includes sequential back-door and front-door adjustment, along with additional expressions involving sums and products. For this class, they develop an estimator whose computation scales polynomially with the number of variables and samples.

The estimator also has a double-robustness property, and simulations verify the framework’s reported scalability and robustness. The contribution is to bring broader causal coverage together with an efficient estimation procedure. This matters because having an identifiable causal quantity alone does not supply a practical method for estimating it: UCA addresses the computational difficulty for the broad class of expressions it represents.
summary.tldr: UCA provides a scalable, doubly robust estimator for a broad class of causal quantities, including back-door and front-door adjustments.

title: Unified Covariate Adjustment for Causal Inference

abstract: Previous work on Universal Transformers (UTs) has demonstrated the importance of parameter sharing across layers. By allowing recurrence in depth, UTs have advantages over standard Transformers in learning compositional generalizations, but layer-sharing comes with a practical limitation of parameter-compute ratio: it drastically reduces the parameter count compared to the non-shared model with the same dimensionality. Naively scaling up the layer size to compensate for the loss of parameters makes its computational resource requirements prohibitive. In practice, no previous work has succeeded in proposing a shared-layer Transformer design that is competitive in parameter count-dominated tasks such as language modeling. Here we propose MoEUT (pronounced "moot"), an effective mixture-of-experts (MoE)-based shared-layer Transformer architecture, which combines several recent advances in MoEs for both feedforward and attention layers of standard Transformers together with novel layer-normalization and grouping schemes that are specific and crucial to UTs. The resulting UT model, for the first time, slightly outperforms standard Transformers on language modeling tasks such as BLiMP and PIQA, while using significantly less compute and memory.

Simply widening shared layers to restore capacity can make computation prohibitively expensive, creating a practical obstacle for language modeling.

MoEUT addresses this parameter-to-compute tradeoff with a mixture-of-experts architecture for shared-layer transformers. It combines expert-based developments in both feedforward and attention layers with new normalization and grouping schemes designed specifically for Universal Transformers. The abstract identifies these additional schemes as crucial, making the contribution a coordinated architecture rather than only the addition of experts.

In the reported evaluations, including BLiMP and PIQA, MoEUT slightly outperforms standard transformers while using substantially less computation and memory. The performance improvement is modest, but it comes alongside meaningful resource savings. These findings demonstrate that shared-layer models can be competitive in tasks where parameter capacity matters, addressing a practical weakness that had limited earlier Universal Transformer designs.
summary.tldr: MoEUT combines expert layers with specialized sharing schemes to slightly outperform standard transformers in reported evaluations while reducing compute and memory.

title: MoEUT: Mixture-of-Experts Universal Transformers

abstract: Augmented Lagrangian Methods (ALMs) are widely employed in solving constrained optimizations, and some efficient solvers are developed based on this framework. Under the quadratic growth assumption, it is known that the dual iterates and the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) residuals of ALMs applied to conic programs converge linearly. In contrast, the convergence rate of the primal iterates has remained elusive. In this paper, we resolve this challenge by establishing new $\textit{quadratic growth}$ and $\textit{error bound}$ properties for primal and dual conic programs under the standard strict complementarity condition. Our main results reveal that both primal and dual iterates of the ALMs converge linearly contingent solely upon the assumption of strict complementarity and a bounded solution set. This finding provides a positive answer to an open question regarding the asymptotically linear convergence of the primal iterates of ALMs applied to conic optimization.

paragraphs: Augmented Lagrangian methods are widely used to solve constrained optimization problems. For conic programs, previous theory established linear convergence of dual iterates and optimality residuals under a quadratic growth assumption. The remaining question concerned the primal iterates: the actual sequence of candidate solutions to the original optimization problem.

This paper develops new quadratic growth and error bound properties for both primal and dual conic programs under strict complementarity. These properties connect the geometry of the optimization problem with how closely an iterate approaches a solution. They provide the theoretical ingredients needed to analyze primal convergence alongside the already studied dual behavior.

The main result establishes linear convergence of both primal and dual iterates under strict complementarity and a bounded solution set. Linear convergence describes an eventual geometric rate of improvement, making the result more informative than convergence alone. The conclusion resolves the stated open question about asymptotic primal convergence, with the guarantee explicitly tied to those problem assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under strict complementarity and a bounded solution set, augmented Lagrangian methods have linear convergence of both primal and dual iterates.

title: Inexact Augmented Lagrangian Methods for Conic Optimization: Quadratic Growth and Linear Convergence

abstract: While synthetic data hold great promise for privacy protection, their statistical analysis poses significant challenges that necessitate innovative solutions. The use of deep generative models (DGMs) for synthetic data generation is known to induce considerable bias and imprecision into synthetic data analyses, compromising their inferential utility as opposed to original data analyses. This bias and uncertainty can be substantial enough to impede statistical convergence rates, even in seemingly straightforward analyses like mean calculation. The standard errors of such estimators then exhibit slower shrinkage with sample size than the typical 1 over root-$n$ rate. This complicates fundamental calculations like p-values and confidence intervals, with no straightforward remedy currently available. In response to these challenges, we propose a new strategy that targets synthetic data created by DGMs for specific data analyses. Drawing insights from debiased and targeted machine learning, our approach accounts for biases, enhances convergence rates, and facilitates the calculation of estimators with easily approximated large sample variances. We exemplify our proposal through a simulation study on toy data and two case studies on real-world data, highlighting the importance of tailoring DGMs for targeted data analysis. This debiasing strategy contributes to advancing the reliability and applicability of synthetic data in statistical inference.

This paper studies bias and uncertainty introduced by deep generative models. The issue can affect even simple quantities such as means, making uncertainty shrink more slowly than the familiar inverse-square-root sample-size rate.

That slower convergence matters because confidence intervals and p-values depend on understanding an estimator's uncertainty. The authors propose tailoring synthetic-data generation to a specific intended analysis. Drawing on debiased and targeted machine learning, their strategy accounts for bias, improves convergence rates, and produces estimators whose large-sample variances can be approximated readily.

The paper illustrates the approach with a toy-data simulation and two real-world case studies. Its central contribution is to connect how synthetic data are generated with the statistical question those data will answer. The findings support analysis-specific tailoring as a way to improve inferential reliability, rather than treating the usefulness of synthetic data as independent of their eventual analytical purpose.
summary.tldr: Tailoring deep generative models to specific statistical analyses can reduce synthetic-data bias and improve uncertainty estimation.

title: Debiasing Synthetic Data Generated by Deep Generative Models

abstract: The recent emergence of diffusion models has significantly advanced the precision of learnable priors, presenting innovative avenues for addressing inverse problems. Previous works have endeavored to integrate diffusion priors into the maximum a posteriori estimation (MAP) framework and design optimization methods to solve the inverse problem. However, prevailing optimization-based rithms primarily exploit the prior information within the diffusion models while neglecting their denoising capability. To bridge this gap, this work leverages the diffusion process to reframe noisy inverse problems as a two-variable constrained optimization task by introducing an auxiliary optimization variable that represents a 'noisy' sample at an equivalent denoising step. The projection gradient descent method is efficiently utilized to solve the corresponding optimization problem by truncating the gradient through the $\mu$-predictor. The proposed algorithm, termed ProjDiff, effectively harnesses the prior information and the denoising capability of a pre-trained diffusion model within the optimization framework. Extensive experiments on the image restoration tasks and source separation and partial generation tasks demonstrate that ProjDiff exhibits superior performance across various linear and nonlinear inverse problems, highlighting its potential for practical applications. Code is available at https://github.com/weigerzan/ProjDiff/.
