The paper argues that existing optimization-based approaches mainly use those priors while leaving the models' denoising capability underused. ProjDiff aims to bring both capabilities into the same optimization procedure for noisy inverse problems.

The method introduces an auxiliary variable representing a noisy sample at an equivalent step in the diffusion process. This reformulates the inverse problem as constrained optimization over two variables. It then uses projected gradient descent, truncating the gradient through the diffusion model's μ-predictor to solve the resulting problem efficiently.

This construction gives the pretrained model's denoising behavior an explicit role in the optimization, alongside its prior information. Experiments span image restoration, source separation, and partial generation, covering both linear and nonlinear inverse problems. The authors report superior performance across the evaluated problems. These findings support the reformulation as a way to make fuller use of an existing diffusion model when solving reconstruction and generation tasks.
summary.tldr: ProjDiff reformulates inverse problems to use both the learned prior and denoising capability of a pretrained diffusion model.

title: Unleashing the Denoising Capability of Diffusion Prior for Solving Inverse Problems

abstract: Video language continual learning involves continuously adapting to information from video and text inputs, enhancing a model’s ability to handle new tasks while retaining prior knowledge. This field is a relatively under-explored area, and establishing appropriate datasets is crucial for facilitating communication and research in this field. In this study, we present the first dedicated benchmark, ViLCo-Bench, designed to evaluate continual learning models across a range of video-text tasks. The dataset comprises ten-minute-long videos and corresponding language queries collected from publicly available datasets. Additionally, we introduce a novel memory-efficient framework that incorporates self-supervised learning and mimics long-term and short-term memory effects. This framework addresses challenges including memory complexity from long video clips, natural language complexity from open queries, and text-video misalignment. We posit that ViLCo-Bench, with greater complexity compared to existing continual learning benchmarks, would serve as a critical tool for exploring the video-language domain, extending beyond conventional class-incremental tasks, and addressing complex and limited annotation issues. The curated data, evaluations, and our novel method are available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/ViLCo.

paragraphs: Video-language continual learning asks models to keep learning from video and text while retaining earlier knowledge. ViLCo-Bench provides a dedicated benchmark for this relatively underexplored setting. It combines ten-minute videos with corresponding language queries drawn from publicly available datasets, supporting evaluation across a range of video-text tasks.

The benchmark brings together several challenges: long videos create memory demands, open language queries introduce linguistic complexity, and text may not align cleanly with video. The authors also propose a memory-efficient framework that uses self-supervised learning and mechanisms inspired by short-term and long-term memory effects to address these difficulties.

The intended contribution is to broaden continual learning evaluation beyond conventional tasks that add new classes over time. The authors argue that the benchmark's greater complexity can support research into video-language learning with difficult or limited annotations. The supplied abstract presents the benchmark and accompanying method as research infrastructure, with curated data and evaluations available to support further investigation of how models adapt without losing prior knowledge.
summary.tldr: ViLCo-Bench introduces long-video and language-query tasks for continual learning, alongside a memory-efficient learning framework.

title: ViLCo-Bench: VIdeo Language COntinual learning Benchmark

abstract: We study the differentially private top-$k$ selection problem, aiming to identify a sequence of $k$ items with approximately the highest scores from $d$ items. Recent work by Gillenwater et al. (2022) employs a direct sampling approach from the vast collection of $O(d^k)$ possible length-$k$ sequences, showing superior empirical accuracy compared to previous pure or approximate differentially private methods. Their algorithm has a time and space complexity of $\tilde{O}(dk)$. In this paper, we present an improved algorithm that achieves time and space complexity of $\tilde{O}(d + k^2)$.Experimental results show that our algorithm runs orders of magnitude faster than their approach, while achieving similar empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select an ordered list of approximately the highest-scoring items while preserving differential privacy. There are d candidate items and k positions to fill, so the collection of possible output sequences grows on the order of d to the power k. Working with this enormous collection creates a computational challenge.

Prior work handles the problem through direct sampling and achieves strong empirical accuracy compared with earlier private selection methods. Its time and memory costs scale approximately as d times k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The new algorithm improves both costs to approximately d plus k squared. This changes how the candidate-set size and requested list length contribute to computational expense.

Experiments show speed improvements of orders of magnitude over that direct-sampling approach while retaining similar empirical accuracy. The result makes the accuracy achieved by joint sequence selection more computationally accessible in the tested settings. Its main contribution is an efficiency improvement in private top-k selection, with observed accuracy preservation rather than a claim of universally better selected outputs.
summary.tldr: The proposed private top-k algorithm substantially reduces time and memory costs while maintaining similar empirical selection accuracy.

title: Faster Differentially Private Top-$k$ Selection: A Joint Exponential Mechanism with Pruning

abstract: Widely adopted in modern Vision Transformer designs, Softmax attention can effectively capture long-range visual information; however, it incurs excessive computational cost when dealing with high-resolution inputs. In contrast, linear attention naturally enjoys linear complexity and has great potential to scale up to higher-resolution images. Nonetheless, the unsatisfactory performance of linear attention greatly limits its practical application in various scenarios. In this paper, we take a step forward to close the gap between the linear and Softmax attention with novel theoretical analyses, which demystify the core factors behind the performance deviations. Specifically, we present two key perspectives to understand and alleviate the limitations of linear attention: the injective property and the local modeling ability. Firstly, we prove that linear attention is not injective, which is prone to assign identical attention weights to different query vectors, thus adding to severe semantic confusion since different queries correspond to the same outputs. Secondly, we confirm that effective local modeling is essential for the success of Softmax attention, in which linear attention falls short. The aforementioned two fundamental differences significantly contribute to the disparities between these two attention paradigms, which is demonstrated by our substantial empirical validation in the paper. In addition, more experiment results indicate that linear attention, as long as endowed with these two properties, can outperform Softmax attention across various tasks while maintaining lower computation complexity. Code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/InLine.

paragraphs: Softmax attention captures relationships across an image but becomes computationally expensive at high resolution. Linear attention offers more favorable computational scaling, yet its weaker performance has limited adoption. This paper investigates the reasons for that gap and identifies two properties that help explain why the approaches behave differently.

The first is injectivity: whether different query vectors can be distinguished by the attention operation. The authors prove that linear attention is not injective, meaning distinct queries can receive identical attention weights and produce the same outputs. This can confuse different semantic requests. The second property is local modeling, or effectively representing nearby visual information, which the authors identify as essential to Softmax attention’s success and weaker in linear attention.

Extensive experiments support the importance of both properties. Further results show that linear attention equipped with them can outperform Softmax attention across various tasks while retaining lower computational complexity. The findings connect an efficiency–performance tradeoff to specific representational weaknesses and show empirically that addressing those weaknesses can improve the tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Preserving query distinctions and strengthening local modeling can help linear attention outperform Softmax attention while retaining lower computational complexity.

title: Bridging the Divide: Reconsidering Softmax and Linear Attention

abstract: Standard Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with handling dialogues with long contexts due to efficiency and consistency issues. According to our observation, dialogue contexts are highly structured, and the special token of End-of-Utterance (EoU) in dialogues has the potential to aggregate information. We refer to the EoU tokens as ``conversational attention sinks'' (conv-attn sinks). Accordingly, we introduce StreamingDialogue, which compresses long dialogue history into conv-attn sinks with minimal losses, and thus reduces computational complexity quadratically with the number of sinks (i.e., the number of utterances). Current LLMs already demonstrate the ability to handle long context window, e.g., a window size of 200K or more. To this end, by compressing utterances into EoUs, our method has the potential to handle more than 200K of utterances, resulting in a prolonged dialogue learning. In order to minimize information losses from reconstruction after compression, we design two learning strategies of short-memory reconstruction (SMR) and long-memory reactivation (LMR). title: StreamingDialogue: Prolonged Dialogue Learning via Long Context Compression with Minimal Losses

abstract: Cross-Validation (CV) is the default choice for estimate the out-of-sample performance of machine learning models. Despite its wide usage, their statistical benefits have remained half-understood, especially in challenging nonparametric regimes. In this paper we fill in this gap and show that, in terms of estimating the out-of-sample performances, for a wide spectrum of models, CV does not statistically outperform the simple ``plug-in'' approach where one reuses training data for testing evaluation. Specifically, in terms of both the asymptotic bias and coverage accuracy of the associated interval for out-of-sample evaluation, $K$-fold CV provably cannot outperform plug-in regardless of the rate at which the parametric or nonparametric models converge. Leave-one-out CV can have a smaller bias as compared to plug-in; however, this bias improvement is negligible compared to the variability of the evaluation, and in some important cases leave-one-out again does not outperform plug-in once this variability is taken into account. We obtain our theoretical comparisons via a novel higher-order Taylor analysis that dissects the limit theorems of testing evaluations, which applies to model classes that are not amenable to previously known sufficient conditions. Our numerical results demonstrate that plug-in performs indeed no worse than CV in estimating model performance across a wide range of examples.

This paper studies its statistical advantages relative to plug-in evaluation, which reuses the training data for assessment. The comparison concerns estimating out-of-sample performance across a broad range of model classes, including challenging nonparametric settings. It examines both evaluation bias and the accuracy of uncertainty-interval coverage.

For the models covered by the analysis, K-fold cross-validation cannot improve on plug-in evaluation in asymptotic bias or interval coverage accuracy, regardless of the model's convergence rate. Leave-one-out cross-validation can reduce bias, but that reduction is small compared with evaluation variability. In some important cases, accounting for variability again removes its advantage over plug-in evaluation.

The authors derive these comparisons through higher-order Taylor analysis, extending the theory to model classes beyond earlier sufficient conditions. Numerical results also show plug-in evaluation performing no worse across many examples. The findings challenge a general preference for cross-validation in this estimation problem, while retaining the paper's specific statistical scope and its distinctions between K-fold and leave-one-out evaluation.
summary.tldr: Across the analyzed model classes, cross-validation offers limited or no statistical advantage over training-data plug-in estimates of out-of-sample performance.

title: Is Cross-validation the Gold Standard to Estimate Out-of-sample Model Performance?

abstract: Designing computationally efficient network architectures remains an ongoing necessity in computer vision. In this paper, we adapt Mamba, a state-space language model, into VMamba, a vision backbone with linear time complexity. At the core of VMamba is a stack of Visual State-Space (VSS) blocks with the 2D Selective Scan (SS2D) module. By traversing along four scanning routes, SS2D bridges the gap between the ordered nature of 1D selective scan and the non-sequential structure of 2D vision data, which facilitates the collection of contextual information from various sources and perspectives. Based on the VSS blocks, we develop a family of VMamba architectures and accelerate them through a succession of architectural and implementation enhancements. Extensive experiments demonstrate VMamba’s promising performance across diverse visual perception tasks, highlighting its superior input scaling efficiency compared to existing benchmark models. Source code is available at https://github.com/MzeroMiko/VMamba

paragraphs: VMamba adapts the Mamba state-space language model into a backbone for visual perception with linear time complexity. The central challenge is structural: language is naturally ordered as a sequence, while an image contains two-dimensional spatial relationships. A vision architecture must gather context without relying on a single natural sequence through the image.

The proposed backbone stacks Visual State-Space blocks built around a 2D Selective Scan module. This module traverses visual data along four scanning routes, collecting contextual information from different directions and perspectives. The routes connect one-dimensional selective scanning with the spatial organization of images, allowing the state-space approach to serve as a visual feature processor.

The authors develop a family of architectures and accelerate them through architectural and implementation improvements. Experiments report promising performance across diverse visual perception tasks and better input-scaling efficiency than benchmark models. These findings support the approach as a computationally efficient vision backbone, particularly when considering how processing demands grow with input size.
summary.tldr: VMamba adapts state-space modeling to vision using four-directional selective scans, achieving linear complexity and strong reported input-scaling efficiency.

title: VMamba: Visual State Space Model

abstract: Over the past years, YOLOs have emerged as the predominant paradigm in the field of real-time object detection owing to their effective balance between computational cost and detection performance. Researchers have explored the architectural designs, optimization objectives, data augmentation strategies, and others for YOLOs, achieving notable progress. However, the reliance on the non-maximum suppression (NMS) for post-processing hampers the end-to-end deployment of YOLOs and adversely impacts the inference latency. Besides, the design of various components in YOLOs lacks the comprehensive and thorough inspection, resulting in noticeable computational redundancy and limiting the model's capability. It renders the suboptimal efficiency, along with considerable potential for performance improvements. In this work, we aim to further advance the performance-efficiency boundary of YOLOs from both the post-processing and the model architecture. To this end, we first present the consistent dual assignments for NMS-free training of YOLOs, which brings the competitive performance and low inference latency simultaneously. Moreover, we introduce the holistic efficiency-accuracy driven model design strategy for YOLOs. We comprehensively optimize various components of YOLOs from both the efficiency and accuracy perspectives, which greatly reduces the computational overhead and enhances the capability. The outcome of our effort is a new generation of YOLO series for real-time end-to-end object detection, dubbed YOLOv10. Extensive experiments show that YOLOv10 achieves the state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across various model scales. For example, our YOLOv10-S is 1.8$\times$ faster than RT-DETR-R18 under the similar AP on COCO, meanwhile enjoying 2.8$\times$ smaller number of parameters and FLOPs. Compared with YOLOv9-C, YOLOv10-B has 46\% less latency and 25\% fewer parameters for the same performance. Code and models are available at https://github.com/THU-MIG/yolov10.

title: YOLOv10: Real-Time End-to-End Object Detection

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in large or infinite state spaces is notoriously challenging, both theoretically (where worst-case sample and computational complexities must scale with state space cardinality) and experimentally (where function approximation and policy gradient techniques often scale poorly and suffer from instability and high variance). One line of research attempting to address these difficultiesmakes the natural assumption that we are given a collection of base or *constituent* policies (possibly heuristic) upon which we would like to improve in a scalable manner. In this work we aim to compete with the *max-following policy*, which at each state follows the action of whichever constituent policy has the highest value. The max-following policy is always at least as good as the best constituent policy, and may be considerably better. Our main result is an efficient algorithm that learns to compete with the max-following policy, given only access to the constituent policies (but not their value functions). In contrast to prior work in similar settings, our theoretical results require only the minimal assumption of an ERM oracle for value function approximation for the constituent policies (and not the global optimal policy or the max-following policy itself) on samplable distributions. We illustrate our algorithm's experimental effectiveness and behavior on several robotic simulation testbeds.

paragraphs: When reinforcement learning starts with several available policies, a useful goal is to combine their strengths. This paper targets the max-following policy, which chooses, at each state, the action of the constituent policy with the highest value there. That policy is at least as good as the best constituent and can be substantially better.

The challenge is that the learner has access to the constituent policies but not their value functions. The authors give an efficient algorithm that learns to compete with the max-following policy under an empirical-risk-minimization oracle assumption. The oracle supports value-function approximation for constituent policies on distributions that can be sampled, rather than requiring approximation of the globally optimal or max-following policy.

This distinction matters because the learning assumption is tied to the supplied collection of policies. It offers a scalable route to improvement without directly assuming that the more ambitious target policy's value function can be learned. Experiments on several robotic simulation testbeds illustrate the algorithm's effectiveness and behavior alongside the theoretical result.
summary.tldr: An oracle-efficient RL algorithm learns to compete with a statewise combination of existing policies without receiving their value functions.

title: Oracle-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Max Value Ensembles

abstract: Many applications today provide users with multiple auto-complete drafts as they type, including GitHub's code completion, Gmail's smart compose, and Apple's messaging auto-suggestions. Under the hood, language models support this by running an autoregressive inference pass to provide a draft. Consequently, providing $k$ drafts to the user requires running an expensive language model $k$ times. To alleviate the computation cost of running $k$ inference passes, we propose Superposed Decoding, a new decoding algorithm that generates $k$ drafts at the computation cost of one autoregressive inference pass. We achieve this by feeding a superposition of the most recent token embeddings from the $k$ drafts as input to the next decoding step of the language model. At every inference step we combine the $k$ drafts with the top-$k$ tokens to get $k^2$ new drafts and cache the $k$ most likely options, using an n-gram interpolation with minimal compute overhead to filter out incoherent generations. Our experiments show that $k$ drafts from Superposed Decoding are at least as coherent and factual as Nucleus Sampling and Greedy Decoding respectively, while being at least $2.44\times$ faster for $k\ge3$. In a compute-normalized setting, user evaluations demonstrably favor text generated by Superposed Decoding over Nucleus Sampling. Superposed Decoding can also be combined with other decoding strategies, resulting in universal coverage gains when scaling inference time compute. Code and more examples open-sourced at https://github.com/RAIVNLab/SuperposedDecoding.

paragraphs: Producing several text-completion drafts ordinarily requires repeatedly running a language model. Superposed Decoding aims to generate k drafts at the computational cost of one autoregressive inference pass. Its key idea is to combine the latest token embeddings from the different drafts into a superposition that becomes the input to the next decoding step.

At each step, the algorithm combines the k current drafts with the top k tokens, forming k squared candidate continuations. It then retains the k most likely candidates. An n-gram interpolation procedure helps filter incoherent generations with little computational overhead. This maintains several draft candidates while sharing the expensive language-model computation across them.

In the reported experiments, the drafts are at least as coherent as nucleus sampling outputs and as factual as greedy decoding outputs, with at least a 2.44-fold speedup for k of three or more. Users also prefer its outputs over nucleus sampling under matched compute. The authors report further coverage gains when combining the method with other decoding strategies as inference compute increases.
summary.tldr: Superposed Decoding shares a language-model inference pass across multiple drafts, reducing computation while preserving quality in the reported comparisons.

title: Superposed Decoding: Multiple Generations from a Single Autoregressive Inference Pass

abstract: Obtaining effective representations of DNA sequences is crucial for genome analysis. Metagenomic binning, for instance, relies on genome representations to cluster complex mixtures of DNA fragments from biological samples with the aim of determining their microbial compositions. In this paper, we revisit k-mer-based representations of genomes and provide a theoretical analysis of their use in representation learning. Based on the analysis, we propose a lightweight and scalable model for performing metagenomic binning at the genome read level, relying only on the k-mer compositions of the DNA fragments. We compare the model to recent genome foundation models and demonstrate that while the models are comparable in performance, the proposed model is significantly more effective in terms of scalability, a crucial aspect for performing metagenomic binning of real-world data sets.

paragraphs: Metagenomic binning groups DNA fragments from a biological sample to help determine which microbes are present. Its effectiveness depends on representations that make relevant similarities between fragments accessible to a clustering method. This paper revisits k-mer composition as the basis for those representations and analyzes its role in genome representation learning.

Using that theoretical analysis, the authors develop a lightweight model for binning at the genome-read level. The model relies only on the fragments’ k-mer compositions. This concentrates the representation on a restricted input description and makes scalability a central part of the method’s design, alongside its ability to support useful grouping.

Comparisons with recent genome foundation models show comparable performance while the proposed model scales substantially better. This matters because practical metagenomic binning requires processing real-world collections of DNA fragments, where the amount of data is a major consideration. The findings support revisiting a relatively simple representation when it offers a favorable combination of task performance and capacity to handle larger datasets.
summary.tldr: A lightweight model using only k-mer composition matches recent genome foundation models in reported binning performance while scaling substantially better.

title: Revisiting K-mer Profile for Effective and Scalable Genome Representation Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are becoming a prominent generative AI tool, where the user enters a query and the LLM generates an answer. To reduce harm and misuse, efforts have been made to align these LLMs to human values using advanced training techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). However, recent studies have highlighted the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial jailbreak attempts aiming at subverting the embedded safety guardrails. To address this challenge, this paper defines and investigates the **Refusal Loss** of LLMs and then proposes a method called **Gradient Cuff** to detect jailbreak attempts. Gradient Cuff exploits the unique properties observed in the refusal loss landscape, including functional values and its smoothness, to design an effective two-step detection strategy. Experimental results on two aligned LLMs (LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B-V1.5) and six types of jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, TAP, Base64, and LRL) show that Gradient Cuff can significantly improve the LLM's rejection capability for malicious jailbreak queries, while maintaining the model's performance for benign user queries by adjusting the detection threshold.

paragraphs: Safety training does not eliminate attempts to make language models bypass their guardrails. This paper studies how to detect such jailbreak queries through a model's refusal behavior. It defines a refusal loss and examines the surrounding loss landscape, using that analysis as the foundation for a detector called Gradient Cuff.

The detector combines two kinds of information in a two-step strategy: the value of the refusal loss and the smoothness of its landscape. This makes the shape of the refusal-related response part of the detection signal. The method is motivated by distinctive properties observed in that landscape when investigating jailbreak attempts.

Experiments cover LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B-V1.5 against six attack types: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, TAP, Base64, and LRL. The authors report significantly improved rejection of malicious jailbreak queries while maintaining performance on benign queries through adjustment of the detection threshold. That threshold is part of the stated result, linking the detector's operating choice to its treatment of ordinary user requests.
summary.tldr: Gradient Cuff uses refusal-loss values and landscape smoothness to improve jailbreak detection while preserving benign-query performance through threshold adjustment.

title: Gradient Cuff: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models by Exploring Refusal Loss Landscapes

abstract: Graph incremental learning has gained widespread attention for its ability to mitigate catastrophic forgetting for graph neural networks (GNN). Conventional methods typically require numerous labels for node classification. However, obtaining abundant labels is often challenging in practice, which makes graph few-shot incremental learning necessary. Current approaches rely on large number of samples from meta-learning to construct memories, and heavy fine-tuning of the GNN parameters that lead to the loss of past knowledge. These result in significant memory consumption and loss of past knowledge information, respectively. To tackle these issues, We introduce Mecoin to efficient construct and Preserve memory. For efficient storage and update of class prototypes, Mecoin use Structured Memory Unit (SMU) to cache prototypes of the seen classes and update new class prototypes through interaction between nodes and the cached prototypes by Memory Construction module(MeCo). Besides, to avoid extensive parameter fine-tuning and forgetting, we introduce a Memory Representation Adaptive Module called MRaM to separate the learning of prototypes and class representations and use Graph Knowledge Interchange Module (GKIM) to injects past knowledge information into GNN. We analyze the effectiveness of our paradigm from the perspectives of generalization error, and discuss the impact of different distillation methods on model performance through experiments and VC-dimension. By comparison with other related methods, we validate that Mecoin achieves higher accuracy and lower forgetting rate.

paragraphs: Graph classifiers may need to learn new classes from only a few labeled nodes while retaining knowledge of earlier classes. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: constructing memories can require many samples, and extensive adjustment of the graph neural network can erase past knowledge. Mecoin addresses memory construction and knowledge preservation together.

A Structured Memory Unit stores class prototypes, which act as compact representations of previously seen classes. The Memory Construction module updates new prototypes through interactions between nodes and the stored prototypes. A separate adaptive module distinguishes prototype learning from class-representation learning, while a knowledge interchange module feeds past knowledge back into the graph neural network.

This separation aims to reduce reliance on heavy parameter fine-tuning while keeping old class information available. The authors analyze generalization error and examine how different distillation methods affect performance, including discussion through VC-dimension. Their comparisons report higher classification accuracy and lower forgetting rates than related methods, supporting the proposed memory organization for incremental graph learning with scarce labels.
summary.tldr: Mecoin organizes class prototypes and transfers stored knowledge to improve few-shot graph learning while reducing forgetting.

title: An Efficient Memory Module for Graph Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: A critical approach for efficiently deploying computationally demanding large language models (LLMs) is Key-Value (KV) caching. The KV cache stores key-value states of previously generated tokens, significantly reducing the need for repetitive computations and thereby lowering latency in autoregressive generation. However, the size of the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, posing challenges for applications requiring long context input and extensive sequence generation. In this paper, we present a simple yet effective approach, called MiniCache, to compress the KV cache across layers from a novel depth perspective, significantly reducing the memory footprint for LLM inference. Our approach is based on the observation that KV cache states exhibit high similarity between the adjacent layers in the middle-to-deep portion of LLMs. To facilitate merging, we propose disentangling the states into the magnitude and direction components, interpolating the directions of the state vectors while preserving their lengths unchanged. Furthermore, we introduce a token retention strategy to keep highly distinct state pairs unmerged, thus preserving the information with minimal additional storage overhead. Our MiniCache is training-free and general, complementing existing KV cache compression strategies, such as quantization and sparsity. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of MiniCache utilizing various models including LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, Phi-3, Mistral, and Mixtral across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating its exceptional performance in achieving superior compression ratios and high throughput. On the ShareGPT dataset, LLaMA-2-7B with cross-layer merging achieves a compression ratio of $1.53\times$. Additionally, since MiniCache is orthogonal to existing quantization techniques, it can achieve a compression ratio of up to $5.02\times$ when combined with the 4-bit quantization technique, enhancing inference throughput by approximately $5\times$ and reducing the memory footprint by $41\%$ compared to the FP16 full cache baseline, all while maintaining near-lossless performance. Project is available at https://minicache.vmv.re .

However, the size of the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, posing challenges for applications requiring long context input and extensive sequence generation. Our approach is based on the observation that KV cache states exhibit high similarity between the adjacent layers in the middle-to-deep portion of LLMs. To facilitate merging, we propose disentangling the states into the magnitude and direction components, interpolating the directions of the state vectors while preserving their lengths unchanged. Furthermore, we introduce a token retention strategy to keep highly distinct state pairs unmerged, thus preserving the information with minimal additional storage overhead. Our MiniCache is training-free and general, complementing existing KV cache compression strategies, such as quantization and sparsity. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of MiniCache utilizing various models including LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, Phi-3, Mistral, and Mixtral across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating its exceptional performance in achieving superior compression ratios and high throughput. On the ShareGPT dataset, LLaMA-2-7B with cross-layer merging achieves a compression ratio of $1.53\times$. Additionally, since MiniCache is orthogonal to existing quantization techniques, it can achieve a compression ratio of up to $5.02\times$ when combined with the 4-bit quantization technique, enhancing inference throughput by approximately $5\times$ and reducing the memory footprint by $41\%$ compared to the FP16 full cache baseline, all while maintaining near-lossless performance. Project is available at https://minicache.vmv.re .

paragraphs: A language model’s key-value cache saves computations by retaining states for earlier tokens, but its memory use grows with sequence length. MiniCache compresses this cache across network layers. Its starting observation is that neighboring layers in the middle-to-deep portion of a model often have highly similar cached states.

To merge states, MiniCache separates vector magnitude from direction, interpolates directions, and preserves the original lengths. A retention mechanism leaves highly distinct state pairs unmerged, protecting information that is less redundant. The method requires no training and can complement other compression approaches, including quantization and sparsity.

Evaluations span several language-model families and benchmarks. For LLaMA-2-7B on ShareGPT, cross-layer merging achieves a 1.53-fold compression ratio. Combined with four-bit quantization, the reported ratio reaches up to 5.02-fold, with approximately fivefold throughput and a 41% smaller memory footprint than the full FP16 cache baseline, while maintaining near-lossless performance. These are reported evaluation outcomes, showing how reducing redundancy across depth can complement compression within cached states.
summary.tldr: MiniCache reduces language-model cache memory by merging similar states across layers while retaining distinctive states and complementing quantization.

title: MiniCache: KV Cache Compression in Depth Dimension for Large Language Models

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin technological advancements, the privacy of their training data emerges as a critical concern. Differential Privacy (DP) serves as a rigorous mechanism to protect this data, yet its integration via Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) introduces substantial challenges, primarily due to the complexities of per-sample gradient clipping. Current explicit methods, such as Opacus, necessitate extensive storage for per-sample gradients, significantly inflating memory requirements. Conversely, implicit methods like GhostClip reduce storage needs by recalculating gradients multiple times, which leads to inefficiencies due to redundant computations. This paper introduces FlashDP, an innovative cache-friendly per-layer DP-SGD that consolidates necessary operations into a single task, calculating gradients only once in a fused manner. This approach not only diminishes memory movement by up to 50\% but also cuts down redundant computations by 20\%, compared to previous methods. Consequently, FlashDP does not increase memory demands and achieves a 90\% throughput compared to the Non-DP method on a four-A100 system during the pre-training of the Llama-13B model, while maintaining parity with standard per-layer clipped DP-SGD in terms of accuracy. These advancements establish FlashDP as a pivotal development for efficient and privacy-preserving training of LLMs. FlashDP's code has been open-sourced in https://github.com/kaustpradalab/flashdp.

Explicit methods store these individual gradients and consume substantial memory, while implicit methods reduce storage by recomputing gradients, creating additional computational work.

The proposed system implements per-layer private stochastic gradient descent with a cache-friendly fused operation. It consolidates the necessary work so gradients are calculated once, reducing both repeated computation and movement of data through memory. Compared with previous methods, the paper reports up to 50% less memory movement and 20% less redundant computation.

During Llama-13B pretraining on four A100 GPUs, FlashDP reaches 90% of the throughput of non-private training without increasing memory demands. Its accuracy matches standard per-layer clipped private training. This result concerns a specific reported configuration, but it demonstrates that implementation choices around clipping and gradient handling can substantially narrow the performance gap between private and non-private training while retaining the evaluated private method's accuracy.
summary.tldr: FlashDP fuses per-layer private-training operations, reaching 90% of non-private throughput in the reported Llama-13B setup.

title: Private Training Large-scale Models with Efficient DP-SGD

abstract: Masked generative models (MGMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for image synthesis, combining parallel decoding with strong bidirectional context modeling. However, generating high-quality samples typically requires many iterative decoding steps, resulting in high inference costs. A straightforward way to speed up generation is by decoding more tokens in each step, thereby reducing the total number of steps. However, when many tokens are decoded simultaneously, the model can only estimate the univariate marginal distributions independently, failing to capture the dependency among them. As a result, reducing the number of steps significantly compromises generation fidelity. In this work, we introduce ReCAP (Reused Context-Aware Prediction), a plug-and-play module that accelerates inference in MGMs by constructing low-cost steps via reusing feature embeddings from previously decoded context tokens. ReCAP interleaves standard full evaluations with lightweight steps that cache and reuse context features, substantially reducing computation while preserving the benefits of fine-grained, iterative generation. We demonstrate its effectiveness on top of three representative MGMs (MaskGIT, MAGE, and MAR), including both discrete and continuous token spaces and covering diverse architectural designs. In particular, on ImageNet256 class-conditional generation, ReCAP achieves up to 2.4$\times$ faster inference than the base model with minimal performance drop, and consistently delivers better efficiency–fidelity trade-offs under various generation settings.

Decoding more tokens at once can reduce the number of steps, but it also treats those tokens independently at that step. This misses dependencies and can substantially reduce image fidelity.

ReCAP accelerates generation by making some steps cheaper while preserving fine-grained iteration. It alternates standard full model evaluations with lightweight steps that reuse cached feature embeddings from previously decoded context tokens. The approach reduces repeated computation while retaining the opportunity to incorporate context across successive generation steps.

The authors evaluate ReCAP with MaskGIT, MAGE, and MAR, covering different architectures and both discrete and continuous token representations. Across generation settings, it delivers better efficiency–fidelity trade-offs. The results support feature reuse as a practical way to accelerate iterative masked generation without relying solely on decoding larger batches of tokens simultaneously.
summary.tldr: ReCAP reuses cached context features between full evaluations to speed up masked image generation with minimal reported fidelity loss.

title: Plug-and-Play Context Feature Reuse for Efficient Masked Generation

abstract: Despite rapid advances in 3D content generation, quality assessment for the generated 3D assets remains challenging.Existing methods mainly rely on image-based metrics and operate solely at the object level, limiting their ability to capture spatial Despite rapid advances in 3D content generation, quality assessment for the generated 3D assets remains challenging.Existing methods mainly rely on image-based metrics and operate solely at the object level, limiting their ability to capture spatial coherence, material authenticity, and high-fidelity local details.1) To address these challenges, we introduce Hi3DEval, a hierarchical evaluation framework tailored for 3D generative content. It combines both object-level and part-level evaluation, enabling holistic assessments across multiple dimensions as well as fine-grained quality analysis. Additionally, we extend texture evaluation beyond aesthetic appearance by explicitly assessing material realism, focusing on attributes such as albedo, saturation, and metallicness. 2) To support this framework, we construct Hi3DBench, a large-scale dataset comprising diverse 3D assets and high-quality annotations, accompanied by a reliable multi-agent annotation pipeline.We further propose a 3D-aware automated scoring system based on hybrid 3D representations. Specifically, we leverage video-based representations for object-level and material-subject evaluations to enhance modeling of spatio-temporal consistency and employ pretrained 3D features for part-level perception.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing image-based metrics in modeling 3D characteristics and achieves superior alignment with human preference, providing a scalable alternative to manual evaluations.

paragraphs: Hi3DEval addresses the difficulty of evaluating generated 3D assets using metrics centered on images and whole objects. Those assessments can overlook spatial coherence, material realism, and local details. The proposed framework evaluates both complete objects and individual parts, providing a broader quality assessment together with a closer examination of specific regions.

Material evaluation extends beyond whether a texture looks attractive. It explicitly considers properties including albedo, saturation, and metallicness. The authors also introduce Hi3DBench, a dataset of diverse 3D assets with annotations supported by a multi-agent annotation pipeline. Together, the framework and dataset provide a structured basis for assessing different aspects of generated content.

The automated scoring system combines representations suited to different levels of evaluation. Video-based representations support object and material assessment, while pretrained 3D features support part-level perception. Experiments report better modeling of 3D characteristics than existing image-based metrics and stronger agreement with human preferences. This supports automated evaluation that attends to both overall appearance and the asset's finer 3D properties.
summary.tldr: Hi3DEval combines object, part, and material assessment to evaluate generated 3D assets with stronger reported alignment to human preferences.

title: Hi3DEval: Advancing 3D Generation Evaluation with Hierarchical Validity

abstract: We introduce *NeuralSurv*, the first deep survival model to incorporate Bayesian uncertainty quantification. Our non‑parametric, architecture‑agnostic framework flexibly captures time‑varying covariate–risk relationships in continuous time via a novel two‑stage data‑augmentation scheme, for which we establish theoretical guarantees. For efficient posterior inference, we introduce a mean‑field variational algorithm with coordinate‑ascent updates that scale linearly in model size. By locally linearizing the Bayesian neural network, we obtain full conjugacy and derive all coordinate updates in closed form. In experiments, *NeuralSurv* delivers superior calibration compared to state-of-the-art deep survival models, while matching or exceeding their discriminative performance across both synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets. Our results demonstrate the value of Bayesian principles in data‑scarce regimes by enhancing model calibration and providing robust, well‑calibrated uncertainty estimates for the survival function.

By locally linearizing the Bayesian neural network, we obtain full conjugacy and derive all coordinate updates in closed form. paragraphs: Survival analysis models how the probability of an event changes over time. NeuralSurv introduces Bayesian uncertainty quantification into a deep survival framework, aiming to provide both flexible predictions and calibrated uncertainty about the survival function. Its nonparametric, architecture-agnostic design captures relationships between covariates and risk that can vary continuously with time.

The method uses a two-stage data-augmentation scheme with theoretical guarantees. For posterior inference, the authors develop a mean-field variational algorithm using coordinate-ascent updates that scale linearly with model size. Locally linearizing the Bayesian neural network creates a conjugate formulation, allowing every coordinate update to be calculated in closed form.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better calibration than state-of-the-art deep survival models while matching or exceeding their ability to discriminate between outcomes. The authors particularly emphasize benefits when data are scarce. The findings suggest that Bayesian modeling can improve the reliability of survival probabilities and their uncertainty estimates without sacrificing the predictive distinctions needed for useful survival analysis.
summary.tldr: NeuralSurv combines flexible deep survival modeling with efficient Bayesian inference to improve calibration and quantify uncertainty.

title: NeuralSurv: Deep Survival Analysis with Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: Connectomics—the mapping of neural connections in an organism's brain—currently requires extraordinary human effort to proofread the data collected from imaging and machine-learning assisted segmentation. With the growing excitement around using AI agents to automate important scientific tasks, we explore whether current AI systems can perform multiple tasks necessary for data proofreading. We introduce ConnectomeBench, a multimodal benchmark evaluating large language model (LLM) capabilities in three critical proofreading tasks: segment type identification, split error correction, and merge error detection. Using expert annotated data from two large open-source datasets—a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex and the complete Drosophila brain—we evaluate proprietary multimodal LLMs including Claude 3.7/4 Sonnet, o4-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, as well as open source models like InternVL-3 and NVLM. Our results demonstrate that current models achieve surprisingly high performance in segment identification (52-82\% balanced accuracy vs. 20-25\% chance) and binary/multiple choice split error correction (75-85\% accuracy vs. 50\% chance) while generally struggling on merge error identification tasks. Overall, while the best models still lag behind expert performance, they demonstrate promising capabilities that could eventually enable them to augment and potentially replace human proofreading in connectomics.

paragraphs: Mapping neural connections requires extensive human checking of imaging data and machine-assisted segmentation. ConnectomeBench asks whether multimodal language models can perform parts of this proofreading work. Its three tasks test segment identification, correction of split errors, and detection of merge errors, separating capabilities that contribute to the overall checking process.

The benchmark uses expert annotations from two open datasets: a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex and a complete fruit fly brain. Evaluated proprietary and open models achieve 52–82% balanced accuracy on segment identification, against 20–25% chance levels. For binary or multiple-choice split correction, reported accuracy reaches 75–85%, compared with 50% chance.

These results establish useful capabilities without showing that autonomous proofreading is already solved. The benchmark identifies both promising entry points for assistance and a harder error category, supporting the authors’ view that such systems could eventually augment, and potentially replace, human proofreading.
summary.tldr: ConnectomeBench finds promising model performance on segment identification and split correction, but merge detection remains difficult and experts still perform better.

title: ConnectomeBench: Can LLMs proofread the connectome?

abstract: Though safety alignment has been applied to most large language models (LLMs), LLM service providers generally deploy a subsequent moderation as the external safety guardrail in real-world products. Existing moderators mainly practice a conventional full detection, which determines the harmfulness based on the complete LLM output, causing high service latency. Recent works pay more attention to partial detection where moderators oversee the generation midway and early stop the output if harmfulness is detected, but they directly apply moderators trained with the full detection paradigm to incomplete outputs, introducing a training-inference gap that lowers the performance. In this paper, we explore how to form a data-and-model solution that natively supports partial detection. For the data, we construct **FineHarm**, a dataset consisting of 29K prompt-response pairs with fine-grained token-level annotations to provide reasonable supervision for token-level training. Then, we propose the **Streaming Content Monitor (SCM)**, which is trained with dual supervision of response- and token-level labels and can follow the output stream of LLM to make a timely judgment of harmfulness. Experiments show that SCM gains 0.95+ in macro F1 score that is comparable to full-detection, by only seeing the first 18% of tokens in responses on average. Moreover, the SCM can serve as a pseudo-harmfulness annotator for improving safety alignment and lead to a higher harmlessness score than DPO.

paragraphs: This paper develops moderation that can judge a language model’s response while it is still being generated. Waiting for the complete response adds latency, but applying a conventional full-response moderator to unfinished text creates a mismatch between training and use. The authors address that mismatch with data and training designed for partial outputs.

They introduce FineHarm, containing 29,000 prompt-response pairs with token-level annotations. Their Streaming Content Monitor learns from both labels for entire responses and labels attached to individual tokens. This dual supervision supports judgments as the output stream arrives, allowing harmful generation to be stopped before the response is complete.

In the reported experiments, the monitor achieves a macro F1 score above 0.95, comparable to full-response detection, while seeing only the first 18% of response tokens on average. That is an average observation requirement, not a fixed stopping point for every response. The monitor can also supply pseudo-labels for safety alignment; the authors report a higher harmlessness score than DPO when using it in that role.
summary.tldr: Token-level supervision lets a streaming moderator detect harmful responses early with reported accuracy comparable to full-response moderation.

title: From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring

abstract: Recent studies have shown LLMs possess some ability to improve their responses when given external feedback. However, it remains unclear how effectively and thoroughly these models can incorporate extrinsic feedback. In an ideal scenario, if LLMs receive near-perfect and complete feedback, we would expect them to fully integrate the feedback and reach correct solutions. In this paper, we systematically investigate LLMs’ ability to incorporate feedback by designing a controlled experimental environment. For each problem, a solver model attempts a solution, then a feedback generator with access to near-complete ground-truth answers produces targeted feedback, after which the solver tries again. We evaluate this pipeline across a diverse range of tasks, including math reasoning, knowledge reasoning, scientific reasoning, and general multi-domain evaluations with state-of-the-art language models including Claude 3.7 with extended thinking. Surprisingly, even under these near-ideal conditions, solver models consistently show resistance to feedback, a limitation that we term FEEDBACK FRICTION. To mitigate this limitation, we experiment with sampling-based strategies like progressive temperature increases and explicit rejection of previously attempted incorrect answers, which yield improvements but still fail to help models achieve target performance. We analyze FEEDBACK FRICTION and find that models’ confidence on specific questions, measured by semantic entropy, predicts feedback resistance: high-confidence predictions remain resistant to external correction. We hope that highlighting this issue in LLMs will help future research in self-improvement.

paragraphs: Corrective feedback should help a language model repair an incorrect answer, but how completely does the model use that feedback? This paper investigates the question in a controlled setting. A solver attempts a problem, a feedback generator with access to nearly complete ground-truth answers supplies targeted guidance, and the solver then tries again.

The authors call this behavior feedback friction. Their evaluation includes state-of-the-art models such as Claude 3.7 with extended thinking, showing that the observed difficulty also appears in advanced reasoning systems.

The authors test progressively increasing sampling temperature and explicitly rejecting earlier incorrect answers. Both strategies help, but they do not bring models to the target performance. Confidence measured through semantic entropy predicts resistance: highly confident predictions are harder to correct. The findings identify feedback uptake as a distinct obstacle to improvement, since providing strong corrective information does not ensure that the solver will use it successfully.
summary.tldr: Tested language models resist even highly informative corrections, with greater confidence predicting stronger feedback resistance.

title: FEEDBACK FRICTION: LLMs Struggle to Fully Incorporate External Feedback

abstract: Expected information gain (EIG) is a crucial quantity in Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED), quantifying how useful an experiment is by the amount we expect the posterior to differ from the prior. However, evaluating the EIG can be computationally expensive since it generally requires estimating the posterior normalizing constant. In this work, we leverage two idiosyncrasies of BOED to improve efficiency of EIG estimation via sequential Monte Carlo (SMC). First, in BOED we simulate the data and thus know the true underlying parameters. Second, we ultimately care about the EIG, not the individual normalizing constants. Often we observe that the Monte Carlo variance of standard SMC estimators for the normalizing constant of a single dataset are significantly lower than the variance of the normalizing constants across datasets; the latter thus contributes the majority of the variance for EIG estimates. This suggests the potential to slightly increase variance while drastically decreasing computation time by reducing the SMC population size, which leads us to an EIG-specific SMC estimator that starts with a only a single sample from the posterior and tempers \textit{backwards} towards the prior. Using this single-sample estimator, which we call reverse-annealed SMC (RA-SMC), we show that it is possible to estimate EIG with orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations in three models: a four-dimensional spring-mass, a six-dimensional Johnson-Cook model and a four-dimensional source-finding problem.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design ranks candidate experiments by their expected information gain: how much observations are expected to change prior beliefs. Computing this quantity can be expensive because it generally requires estimating posterior normalizing constants. Standard sequential Monte Carlo methods devote computation to estimating these constants for individual simulated datasets.

The paper exploits two features of experimental design. Simulated data come with known generating parameters, and the ultimate target is average information gain across datasets. The authors often find that variation across datasets dominates the sampling error within a dataset. This suggests that spending less computation on each individual estimate can be worthwhile.

Reverse-annealed sequential Monte Carlo starts with a single posterior sample and gradually moves backward toward the prior. It trades some additional sampling variance for much lower computational cost. In spring-mass, Johnson-Cook, and source-finding models, the authors demonstrate information-gain estimation using orders of magnitude fewer likelihood evaluations. The efficiency argument depends on the relative contributions of these sources of variance.
summary.tldr: Reverse-annealed SMC estimates experimental information gain with far fewer likelihood evaluations by starting from one posterior sample and moving toward the prior.

title: Reverse-Annealed Sequential Monte Carlo for Efficient Bayesian Optimal Experiment Design

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become popular in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) emerging as a widely used algorithm in recent systems. Despite GRPO's widespread adoption, we identify a previously unrecognized phenomenon we term Lazy Likelihood Displacement (LLD), wherein the likelihood of correct responses marginally increases or even decreases during training. This behavior mirrors a recently discovered misalignment issue in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), attributed to the influence of negative gradients. We provide a theoretical analysis of GRPO’s learning dynamic, identifying the source of LLD as the naive penalization of all tokens in incorrect responses with the same strength. To address this, we develop a method called NTHR, which downweights penalties on tokens contributing to the LLD. Unlike prior DPO-based approaches, NTHR takes advantage of GRPO’s group-based structure, using correct responses as anchors to identify influential tokens. Experiments on math reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that NTHR effectively mitigates LLD, yielding consistent performance gains across models ranging from 0.5B to 3B parameters.

To address this, we develop a method called NTHR, which downweights penalties on tokens contributing to the LLD. Unlike prior DPO-based approaches, NTHR takes advantage of GRPO’s group-based structure, using correct responses as anchors to identify influential tokens. Experiments on math reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that NTHR effectively mitigates LLD, yielding consistent performance gains across models ranging from 0.5B to 3B parameters.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization is used to improve language-model reasoning through reinforcement learning. This paper identifies a training phenomenon called Lazy Likelihood Displacement: the probability assigned to correct responses may increase only slightly or even decrease. That behavior raises a specific question about how penalties for incorrect responses affect the learning signal for correct ones.

The authors' theoretical analysis attributes the phenomenon to penalizing every token in an incorrect response with the same strength. Their proposed method, NTHR, reduces penalties on tokens that contribute to this displacement. It uses correct responses within GRPO's groups as anchors for identifying influential tokens, taking advantage of information already available in the algorithm's group-based structure.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that NTHR mitigates Lazy Likelihood Displacement and delivers consistent performance gains for models ranging from 0.5 billion to 3 billion parameters. The contribution links an observed training failure to a particular treatment of negative gradients, then changes that treatment through more selective token penalties.
summary.tldr: NTHR improves GRPO reasoning training by selectively reducing token penalties that can suppress the likelihood of correct responses.

title: On the Effect of Negative Gradient in Group Relative Deep Reinforcement Optimization

abstract: Recent progress on Remote Sensing Foundation Models (RSFMs) aims toward universal representations for Earth observation imagery. However, current efforts often scale up in size significantly without addressing efficiency constraints critical for real-world applications (e.g., onboard processing, rapid disaster response) or treat multispectral (MS) data as generic imagery, overlooking valuable physical priors. We introduce PhySwin, a foundation model for MS data that integrates physical priors with computational efficiency. PhySwin combines three innovations: (i) physics-informed pretraining objectives leveraging radiometric constraints to enhance feature learning; (ii) an efficient MixMAE formulation tailored to SwinV2 for low-FLOP, scalable pretraining; and (iii) token-efficient spectral embedding to retain spectral detail without increasing token counts. Pretrained on over 1M Sentinel-2 tiles, PhySwin achieves SOTA results (+1.32\% mIoU segmentation, +0.80\% F1 change detection) while reducing inference latency by up to 14.4$\times$ and computational complexity by up to 43.6$\times$ compared to ViT-based RSFMs.

summary.tldr: PhySwin combines physical constraints and efficient multispectral processing to improve Earth-observation results while substantially reducing reported inference costs.

title: PhySwin: An Efficient and Physically-Informed Foundation Model for Multispectral Earth Observation

abstract: Language models deployed in real-world systems often require post-hoc updates to incorporate new or corrected knowledge. However, editing such models efficiently and reliably—without retraining or forgetting previous information—remains a major challenge. Existing methods for lifelong model editing either compromise generalization, interfere with past edits, or fail to scale to long editing sequences. We propose MEMOIR, a novel scalable framework that injects knowledge through a residual memory, i.e., a dedicated parameter module, while preserving the core capabilities of the pre-trained model. By sparsifying input activations through data-dependent masks, MEMOIR confines each edit to a distinct subset of the memory parameters, minimizing interference among edits. At inference, it identifies relevant edits by comparing the sparse activation patterns of new queries to those stored during editing. This enables generalization to rephrased queries by activating only the relevant knowledge while suppressing unnecessary memory activation for unrelated prompts. Experiments on question answering, hallucination correction, and out-of-distribution generalization benchmarks across LLaMA-3 and Mistral demonstrate that MEMOIR achieves state-of-the-art performance across reliability, generalization, and locality metrics, scaling to thousands of sequential edits with minimal forgetting.

paragraphs: Updating a deployed language model requires adding or correcting knowledge while preserving previous information and core capabilities. Repeated edits make this harder because changes can interfere with one another. MEMOIR addresses long sequences of edits using a dedicated residual memory module.

During editing, data-dependent masks make input activations sparse and confine each change to a distinct subset of memory parameters. This limits overlap among edits. At inference time, the framework compares a query's sparse activation pattern with patterns stored during editing, identifying which changes are relevant. This supports rephrased queries while suppressing unnecessary memory activation for unrelated prompts.

The authors report state-of-the-art reliability, generalization, and locality results, with thousands of sequential edits and minimal forgetting. The contribution combines selective writing with selective retrieval: limiting where an edit is stored helps preserve earlier updates, while identifying when it should activate helps make that knowledge useful without unnecessarily affecting other responses.
summary.tldr: MEMOIR stores edits in sparse residual memory and selectively activates relevant changes, supporting thousands of updates with minimal forgetting.

title: MEMOIR: Lifelong Model Editing with Minimal Overwrite and Informed Retention for LLMs

abstract: Evaluating natural language generation (NLG) systems remains a core challenge, further complicated by the rise of general-purpose large language models (LLMs). Recently, large language models as judges (LLJs) have emerged as a scalable, cost-effective alternative to traditional metrics, but their validity remains underexplored. This position paper argues that the current enthusiasm around LLJs may be premature, as their adoption has outpaced rigorous scrutiny of their reliability and validity as evaluators. Drawing on measurement theory from the social sciences, we identify and critically assess four core assumptions underlying the use of LLJs: their ability to act as proxies for human judgment, their capabilities as evaluators, their scalability, and their cost-effectiveness. We examine how each of these assumptions may be challenged by the inherent limitations of LLMs, LLJs, or current practices in NLG evaluation. To ground our analysis, we explore three applications of LLJs at various stages of the machine learning pipeline: text summarization, data annotation and safety alignment. Finally, we highlight the need for more responsible evaluation practices in LLJs evaluation, to ensure that their growing role in the field supports, rather than undermines, progress in NLG.

paragraphs: Using a language model to judge generated text offers an appealing route to scalable evaluation. This position paper argues that adoption has moved faster than scrutiny of whether those judgments are reliable and valid. Its concern is whether an evaluator measures the intended qualities consistently and meaningfully, rather than whether it can readily produce a score.

Drawing on measurement theory from the social sciences, the authors examine four assumptions: that model judges can substitute for human judgment, that they possess suitable evaluation capabilities, that they scale effectively, and that they are cost-effective. Each assumption is assessed against limitations of language models, model-based judging, and current practices for evaluating generated language.

The discussion is grounded in text summarization, data annotation, and safety alignment, covering several stages of the machine-learning pipeline. As a position paper, its contribution is a critical framework for examining evaluation practices rather than a universal empirical verdict against model judges. It calls for more responsible assessment so that increasingly common automated judgments support dependable progress in language generation.
summary.tldr: This position paper questions four assumptions behind language-model judges and argues for stronger scrutiny of their reliability and validity.

title: Neither Valid nor Reliable? Investigating the Use of LLMs as Judges

abstract: 3D vector graphics play a crucial role in various applications including 3D shape retrieval, conceptual design, and virtual reality interactions due to their ability to capture essential structural information with minimal representation. While recent approaches have shown promise in generating 3D vector graphics, they often suffer from lengthy processing times and struggle to maintain view consistency. To address these limitations, we propose VC3D (**V**iew**C**raft**3D**), an efficient method that leverages 3D priors to generate 3D vector graphics. Specifically, our approach begins with 3D object analysis, employs a geometric extraction algorithm to fit 3D vector graphics to the underlying structure, and applies view-consistent refinement process to enhance visual quality. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that VC3D outperforms previous methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, while significantly reducing computational overhead. The resulting 3D sketches maintain view consistency and effectively capture the essential characteristics of the original objects.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional vector graphics summarize an object's essential structure in a compact representation. This makes them useful for tasks such as shape retrieval, conceptual design, and virtual-reality interaction. However, existing generation approaches can take substantial time and produce sketches whose appearance is inconsistent across viewpoints. ViewCraft3D addresses both processing cost and view consistency.

The method uses 3D priors and begins by analyzing the object. A geometric extraction algorithm then fits vector graphics to the object's underlying structure. A subsequent refinement stage improves visual quality while maintaining consistency between views. The sequence gives structural extraction and visual refinement separate roles, with the three-dimensional object providing the basis for the generated sketch.

The authors report better qualitative and quantitative results than previous methods, together with substantially reduced computational overhead. The generated sketches preserve essential characteristics of the original objects and remain consistent when viewed from different directions. These findings support using 3D structural information throughout generation, so the compact output can represent the object coherently across views while requiring less computation than the compared approaches.
summary.tldr: ViewCraft3D uses object geometry and view-consistent refinement to produce coherent 3D vector sketches with lower reported computational overhead.

title: ViewCraft3D: High-fidelity and View-Consistent 3D Vector Graphics Synthesis

abstract: Recent studies show that LLMs possess different skills and specialize in different tasks. In fact, we observe that their varied performance occur in several levels of granularity. For example, in the code optimization task, code LLMs excel at different optimization categories and no one dominates others. This observation prompts the question of how one leverages multiple LLM agents to solve a coding problem without knowing their complementary strengths a priori. We argue that a team of agents can learn from each other's successes and failures so as to improve their own performance. Thus, a lesson is the knowledge produced by an agent and passed on to other agents in the collective solution process. We propose a lesson-based collaboration framework, design the lesson solicitation--banking--selection mechanism, and demonstrate that a team of small LLMs with lessons learned can outperform a much larger LLM and other multi-LLM collaboration methods.

paragraphs: Coding language models have different strengths, and those differences can appear within a single task. The authors observe that models excel in different categories of code optimization, with no model dominating the others. This raises a coordination problem: how can a team benefit from complementary abilities when those abilities are not known beforehand?

The proposed framework makes lessons the basis of collaboration. A lesson is knowledge generated by an agent and passed to other agents during the collective solution process. Agents can therefore learn from one another's successes and failures. The framework includes mechanisms for soliciting lessons, storing them in a bank, and selecting lessons for use.

The authors demonstrate that a team of small language models using these lessons can outperform a much larger model and other multi-model collaboration methods. This finding supports the value of sharing useful experience across agents during coding work. The contribution centers on how agents communicate and reuse what they discover, allowing complementary strengths to become useful without first requiring a complete map of each model's abilities.
summary.tldr: A lesson-sharing framework lets coding agents reuse one another's successes and failures, enabling small-model teams to outperform larger-model and collaboration alternatives.

title: Lessons Learned: A Multi-Agent Framework for Code LLMs to Learn and Improve

abstract: Retinal vessel segmentation is critical for medical diagnosis, yet existing models often struggle to generalize across domains due to appearance variability, limited annotations, and complex vascular morphology. We propose GraphSeg, a variational Bayesian framework that integrates anatomical graph priors with structure-aware image decomposition to enhance cross-domain segmentation. GraphSeg factorizes retinal images into structure-preserved and structure-degraded components, enabling domain-invariant representation. A deformable graph prior, derived from a statistical retinal atlas, is incorporated via a differentiable alignment and guided by an unsupervised energy function. Experiments on three public benchmarks (CHASE, DRIVE, HRF) show that GraphSeg consistently outperforms existing methods under domain shifts. These results highlight the importance of jointly modeling anatomical topology and image structure for robust generalizable vessel segmentation.

paragraphs: Retinal vessel appearance changes across datasets, and limited annotations make it difficult to learn every variation. GraphSeg uses anatomical structure as a shared constraint, helping segmentation transfer when image appearance differs from training conditions.

The variational Bayesian framework decomposes images into structure-preserved and structure-degraded components. A deformable graph prior from a statistical retinal atlas is aligned differentiably, guided by an unsupervised energy function. This combines a representation of vessel topology with image-specific structural evidence.

On CHASE, DRIVE, and HRF, GraphSeg consistently outperforms existing methods under domain shift. The contribution is the joint treatment of anatomy and visual structure: vessel connectivity offers information that appearance-only models can overlook. The evidence concerns segmentation robustness on these benchmarks, while clinical diagnostic effectiveness would require separate assessment beyond accurate delineation of vessels.
summary.tldr: GraphSeg combines retinal anatomy priors with image decomposition to improve vessel segmentation across domains.

title: Towards Generalizable Retina Vessel Segmentation with Deformable Graph Priors

abstract: Diffusion models have advanced rapidly in recent years, producing high-fidelity images while raising concerns about intellectual property protection and the misuse of generative AI. Image watermarking for diffusion models, particularly Noise-as-Watermark (NaW) methods, encode watermark as specific standard Gaussian noise vector for image generation, embedding the infomation seamlessly while maintaining image quality. For detection, the generation process is inverted to recover the initial noise vector containing the watermark before extraction. However, existing NaW methods struggle to balance watermark robustness with generation diversity. Some methods achieve strong robustness by heavily constraining initial noise sampling, which degrades user experience, while others preserve diversity but prove too fragile for real-world deployment. To address this issue, we propose T2SMark, a two-stage watermarking scheme based on Tail-Truncated Sampling (TTS). Unlike prior methods that simply map bits to positive or negative values, TTS enhances robustness by embedding bits exclusively in the reliable tail regions while randomly sampling the central zone to preserve the latent distribution. Our two-stage framework then ensures sampling diversity by integrating a randomly generated session key into both encryption pipelines. We evaluate T2SMark on diffusion models with both U-Net and DiT backbones. Extensive experiments show that it achieves an optimal balance between robustness and diversity.
