paragraphs: Noise-as-Watermark methods embed identifying information in the initial Gaussian noise used to generate a diffusion image. Detection reverses generation to estimate that noise and recover the watermark. The challenge is that constraining noise strongly can improve watermark recovery while reducing the diversity of generated images.

T2SMark introduces Tail-Truncated Sampling to manage this tradeoff. It embeds bits in reliable tail regions of the noise distribution and samples the central region randomly to preserve the latent distribution. The authors evaluate the method on diffusion models with U-Net and DiT backbones and report an optimal balance between watermark robustness and generation diversity in their experiments. The mechanism matters because it assigns information-bearing and freely sampled portions of the noise different roles. This provides a concrete way to strengthen watermark extraction while retaining variability in the generation process.
summary.tldr: T2SMark embeds watermark bits in reliable noise tails and randomizes other components to balance recovery robustness with image diversity.

title: T2SMark: Balancing Robustness and Diversity in Noise-as-Watermark for Diffusion Models

abstract: We consider the problem of designing models to leverage a recently introduced approximate model averaging technique called dropout. We define a simple new model called maxout (so named because its output is the max of a set of inputs, and because it is a natural companion to dropout) designed to both facilitate optimization by dropout and improve the accuracy of dropout's fast approximate model averaging technique. We empirically verify that the model successfully accomplishes both of these tasks. We use maxout and dropout to demonstrate state of the art classification performance on four benchmark datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.

We empirically verify that the model successfully accomplishes both of these tasks. paragraphs: The paper approaches neural-network design by asking what kind of model works especially well with dropout. Dropout is treated as a fast, approximate way to average models. The authors aim to improve both the optimization carried out with dropout and the accuracy of the approximation used for that averaging.

They introduce maxout, a model whose output is the maximum of a collection of inputs. This simple operation is chosen as a natural companion to dropout. The design connects the model's form to the training and averaging procedure, making compatibility with dropout a central objective of the architecture.

Experiments support both intended benefits: easier optimization with dropout and more accurate approximate model averaging. Combining maxout with dropout also produces reported state-of-the-art classification results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. The significance is that a deliberately matched model and training technique can improve several parts of the learning process together, with the stated gains demonstrated on those four benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Maxout is designed to improve dropout optimization and approximate model averaging, yielding leading reported results on four classification benchmarks.

title: Maxout Networks

abstract: Recent work in method of moments provide consistent estimates for latent-variable models, avoiding local optima issues, but these methods can only be applied to certain types of graphical models. In this work, we show that the method of moments in conjunction with a composite marginal likelihood objective yields consistent parameter estimates for a much broader class of directed and undirected graphical models, including loopy graphs with high treewidth. Specifically, we use tensor factorization to reveal partial information about the hidden variables, rendering the otherwise non-convex negative log-likelihood convex. Our approach gracefully extends to models outside our class by incorporating the partial information via posterior regulraization.
originalAbstract: Recent work in method of moments provide consistent estimates for latent-variable models, avoiding local optima issues, but these methods can only be applied to certain types of graphical models. In this work, we show that the method of moments in conjunction with a composite marginal likelihood objective yields consistent parameter estimates for a much broader class of directed and undirected graphical models, including loopy graphs with high treewidth. Specifically, we use tensor factorization to reveal partial information about the hidden variables, rendering the otherwise non-convex negative log-likelihood convex. Our approach gracefully extends to models outside our class by incorporating the partial information via posterior regulraization.

paragraphs: Learning graphical models with hidden variables can involve difficult optimization landscapes. Method-of-moments approaches offer consistent estimates while avoiding local-optimum problems, but their applicability has been restricted to particular model types. This paper combines moment information with a composite marginal likelihood objective to extend the range of models that can be estimated consistently.

The key step uses tensor factorization to uncover partial information about hidden variables. Within the model class studied, that information makes an otherwise nonconvex negative log-likelihood convex. The recovered information therefore does more than provide an initial guess: it changes the optimization problem in a way that supports the paper's estimation guarantees.

The resulting class includes directed and undirected graphical models, including graphs with loops and high treewidth. For models outside that class, the authors describe an extension that incorporates the partial information through posterior regularization. The consistency result applies to the supported class; the abstract presents the outside-class construction as an extension, without assigning it the same guarantee. The broader contribution is a bridge between moment-based recovery and likelihood-based estimation.
summary.tldr: Combining tensor-derived hidden-variable information with composite likelihood yields consistent estimation for a broader class of graphical models.

title: Estimating Latent-Variable Graphical Models using Moments and Likelihoods

abstract: We study nonconvex finite-sum problems and analyze stochastic variance reduced gradient (SVRG) methods for them. SVRG and related methods have recently surged into prominence for convex optimization given their edge over stochastic gradient descent (SGD); but their theoretical analysis almost exclusively assumes convexity. In contrast, we prove non-asymptotic rates of convergence (to stationary points) of SVRG for nonconvex optimization, and show that it is provably faster than SGD and gradient descent. We also analyze a subclass of nonconvex problems on which SVRG attains linear convergence to the global optimum. We extend our analysis to mini-batch variants of SVRG, showing (theoretical) linear speedup due to minibatching in parallel settings.

SVRG and related methods have recently surged into prominence for convex optimization given their edge over stochastic gradient descent (SGD); but their theoretical analysis almost exclusively assumes convexity. In contrast, we prove non-asymptotic rates of convergence (to stationary points) of SVRG for nonconvex optimization, and show that it is provably faster than SGD and gradient descent. We also analyze a subclass of nonconvex problems on which SVRG attains linear convergence to the global optimum. We extend our analysis to mini-batch variants of SVRG, showing (theoretical) linear speedup due to minibatching in parallel settings.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes stochastic variance reduced gradient methods for nonconvex objectives expressed as finite sums. These methods had become prominent for convex optimization, but their theoretical treatment largely depended on convexity. The authors establish guarantees that apply to the nonconvex setting, where the type of solution being guaranteed becomes especially important.

For the general problem class studied, they prove finite-time convergence rates to stationary points and show provable speed advantages over stochastic gradient descent and gradient descent. A stationary point is a point where the gradient vanishes; the general guarantee does not assert that it is a global optimum. For a particular subclass of nonconvex problems, the authors separately establish linear convergence to the global optimum.

The analysis also covers mini-batch versions of the method. In parallel settings, it yields a theoretical linear speedup from minibatching. The contribution thus extends variance-reduction theory in three directions: general nonconvex stationarity guarantees, stronger optimization results for a specified subclass, and parallel computation through batches.
summary.tldr: SVRG receives finite-time nonconvex convergence guarantees, with stronger global convergence for a subclass and theoretical parallel minibatch speedups.

title: Stochastic Variance Reduction for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Scaling Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to estimate posterior distributions from large datasets has been made possible as a result of advances in stochastic gradient techniques. Despite their success, mixing performance of existing methods when sampling from multimodal distributions can be less efficient with insufficient Monte Carlo samples; this is evidenced by slow convergence and insufficient exploration of posterior distributions. We propose a generalized framework to improve the sampling efficiency of stochastic gradient MCMC, by leveraging a generalized kinetics that delivers superior stationary mixing, especially in multimodal distributions, and propose several techniques to overcome the practical issues. We show that the proposed approach is better at exploring a complicated multimodal posterior distribution, and demonstrate improvements over other stochastic gradient MCMC methods on various applications.
originalAbstract: Scaling Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to estimate posterior distributions from large datasets has been made possible as a result of advances in stochastic gradient techniques. Despite their success, mixing performance of existing methods when sampling from multimodal distributions can be less efficient with insufficient Monte Carlo samples; this is evidenced by slow convergence and insufficient exploration of posterior distributions. We propose a generalized framework to improve the sampling efficiency of stochastic gradient MCMC, by leveraging a generalized kinetics that delivers superior stationary mixing, especially in multimodal distributions, and propose several techniques to overcome the practical issues. We show that the proposed approach is better at exploring a complicated multimodal posterior distribution, and demonstrate improvements over other stochastic gradient MCMC methods on various applications.

paragraphs: Stochastic-gradient methods make Markov chain Monte Carlo more practical for estimating posterior distributions from large datasets. However, a manageable number of samples may still explore a complicated distribution poorly. This is especially troublesome for multimodal distributions, where slow mixing can leave important regions insufficiently visited.

The paper proposes a generalized stochastic-gradient MCMC framework that changes the sampler's kinetics. The intended benefit is better stationary mixing, particularly when the posterior has multiple modes. The authors also introduce several techniques to address practical issues arising from this framework, connecting the proposed sampling dynamics with usable inference procedures.

The reported results show better exploration of a complicated multimodal posterior and improvements over other stochastic-gradient MCMC methods across various applications. These findings concern the quality of exploration as well as scalability. Making individual sampling steps affordable is only part of effective posterior estimation; the sampler must also move through the distribution sufficiently well for its collected samples to represent the structure being estimated.
summary.tldr: Generalized sampling kinetics improve stochastic-gradient MCMC exploration, especially for the multimodal posteriors examined in the paper.

title: Stochastic Gradient Monomial Gamma Sampler

abstract: Advances in deep generative networks have led to impressive results in recent years. Nevertheless, such models can often waste their capacity on the minutiae of datasets, presumably due to weak inductive biases in their decoders. This is where graphics engines may come in handy since they abstract away low-level details and represent images as high-level programs. Current methods that combine deep learning and renderers are limited by hand-crafted likelihood or distance functions, a need for large amounts of supervision, or difficulties in scaling their inference algorithms to richer datasets. To mitigate these issues, we present SPIRAL, an adversarially trained agent that generates a program which is executed by a graphics engine to interpret and sample images. The goal of this agent is to fool a discriminator network that distinguishes between real and rendered data, trained with a distributed reinforcement learning setup without any supervision. A surprising finding is that using the discriminator’s output as a reward signal is the key to allow the agent to make meaningful progress at matching the desired output rendering. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of an end-to-end, unsupervised and adversarial inverse graphics agent on challenging real world (MNIST, Omniglot, CelebA) and synthetic 3D datasets. A video of the agent can be found at https://youtu.be/iSyvwAwa7vk.
originalAbstract: Advances in deep generative networks have led to impressive results in recent years. Nevertheless, such models can often waste their capacity on the minutiae of datasets, presumably due to weak inductive biases in their decoders. This is where graphics engines may come in handy since they abstract away low-level details and represent images as high-level programs. Current methods that combine deep learning and renderers are limited by hand-crafted likelihood or distance functions, a need for large amounts of supervision, or difficulties in scaling their inference algorithms to richer datasets. To mitigate these issues, we present SPIRAL, an adversarially trained agent that generates a program which is executed by a graphics engine to interpret and sample images. The goal of this agent is to fool a discriminator network that distinguishes between real and rendered data, trained with a distributed reinforcement learning setup without any supervision. A surprising finding is that using the discriminator’s output as a reward signal is the key to allow the agent to make meaningful progress at matching the desired output rendering. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of an end-to-end, unsupervised and adversarial inverse graphics agent on challenging real world (MNIST, Omniglot, CelebA) and synthetic 3D datasets. A video of the agent can be found at https://youtu.be/iSyvwAwa7vk.

paragraphs: Graphics engines can express images through high-level programs, providing structure that a generic image decoder may lack. This paper uses that idea to address image interpretation and generation. It targets difficulties in previous renderer-based approaches, including hand-designed comparison functions, extensive supervision, and inference procedures that struggle with richer datasets.

SPIRAL trains an agent to produce programs that a graphics engine executes. A discriminator learns to distinguish real images from rendered ones, and the agent learns through distributed reinforcement learning to fool that discriminator. The system is trained without supervision, using the adversarial signal to guide the generation of image-producing programs.

The authors identify the discriminator's output as the key reward signal enabling meaningful progress toward matching the desired rendering. They demonstrate the approach on MNIST, Omniglot, CelebA, and synthetic 3D data. They describe it, to their knowledge, as the first end-to-end unsupervised adversarial inverse-graphics demonstration on such challenging datasets. The findings support learned visual feedback as a way to train program-generating image agents.
summary.tldr: SPIRAL uses adversarial rewards and reinforcement learning to generate graphics programs without supervision.

title: Synthesizing Programs for Images using Reinforced Adversarial Learning

abstract: Interacting systems are prevalent in nature, from dynamical systems in physics to complex societal dynamics. The interplay of components can give rise to complex behavior, which can often be explained using a simple model of the system’s constituent parts. In this work, we introduce the neural relational inference (NRI) model: an unsupervised model that learns to infer interactions while simultaneously learning the dynamics purely from observational data. Our model takes the form of a variational auto-encoder, in which the latent code represents the underlying interaction graph and the reconstruction is based on graph neural networks. In experiments on simulated physical systems, we show that our NRI model can accurately recover ground-truth interactions in an unsupervised manner. We further demonstrate that we can find an interpretable structure and predict complex dynamics in real motion capture and sports tracking data.

paragraphs: Complex collective behavior can arise from interactions among relatively simple components. Understanding such a system requires learning both how its components behave and which components influence one another. Neural relational inference addresses these two tasks together, using observational data without supervised labels for the underlying interaction structure.

The model is a variational autoencoder whose hidden representation is an interaction graph. A graph neural network uses that representation to reconstruct the observed dynamics. This connects the inferred relationships to their ability to explain the system's behavior, so learning the graph and learning the dynamics become parts of the same modeling process.

In simulated physical systems, the authors show that the model can accurately recover the known interactions without supervision. On motion capture and sports tracking data, they report interpretable structure and prediction of complex dynamics. The simulations support comparison with ground-truth relationships, while the real-data results demonstrate that the approach can produce understandable relational descriptions alongside useful predictions.
summary.tldr: Neural relational inference jointly learns interaction graphs and system dynamics from observations without supervised interaction labels.

title: Neural Relational Inference for Interacting Systems

abstract: We consider the problem of learning causal DAGs in the setting where both observational and interventional data is available. This setting is common in biology, where gene regulatory networks can be intervened on using chemical reagents or gene deletions. Hauser & Buhlmann (2012) previously characterized the identifiability of causal DAGs under perfect interventions, which eliminate dependencies between targeted variables and their direct causes. In this paper, we extend these identifiability results to general interventions, which may modify the dependencies between targeted variables and their causes without eliminating them. We define and characterize the interventional Markov equivalence class that can be identified from general (not necessarily perfect) intervention experiments. We also propose the first provably consistent algorithm for learning DAGs in this setting and evaluate our algorithm on simulated and biological datasets.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph often combines passive observations with experiments that intervene on selected variables. Many interventions, including biological manipulations, instead alter those dependencies without completely removing them.

This paper extends the theory to such general interventions. It defines and characterizes the interventional Markov equivalence class: the set of causal directed acyclic graphs that remain indistinguishable given the available experimental information. The characterization explains what causal structure can be identified when an intervention changes a mechanism but does not necessarily sever its incoming relationships.

The authors also propose a provably consistent algorithm for learning graphs in this setting and evaluate it on simulated and biological datasets. The contribution connects a broader experimental model to both an identifiability theory and a learning procedure. Its guarantee concerns recovery within the stated intervention setting; the abstract does not claim that every intervention design uniquely identifies a single causal graph.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes what general interventions reveal about causal graphs and gives a consistent learning algorithm.

title: Characterizing and Learning Equivalence Classes of Causal DAGs under Interventions

abstract: Zero-sum games such as chess and poker are, abstractly, functions that evaluate pairs of agents, for example labeling them ‘winner’ and ‘loser’. If the game is approximately transitive, then self-play generates sequences of agents of increasing strength. However, nontransitive games, such as rock-paper-scissors, can exhibit strategic cycles, and there is no longer a clear objective – we want agents to increase in strength, but against whom is unclear. In this paper, we introduce a geometric framework for formulating agent objectives in zero-sum games, in order to construct adaptive sequences of objectives that yield open-ended learning. The framework allows us to reason about population performance in nontransitive games, and enables the development of a new algorithm (rectified Nash response, PSRO_rN) that uses game-theoretic niching to construct diverse populations of effective agents, producing a stronger set of agents than existing algorithms. We apply PSRO_rN to two highly nontransitive resource allocation games and find that PSRO_rN consistently outperforms the existing alternatives.

paragraphs: Self-play can produce increasingly strong agents when a game is approximately transitive, meaning comparisons roughly support a consistent ordering of strength. Nontransitive games complicate that picture: strategies can defeat one another in cycles, as in rock-paper-scissors. Improving against one opponent therefore does not provide a clear, universal direction of progress.

The paper introduces a geometric framework for defining objectives in zero-sum games and adapting those objectives over time. It supports reasoning about the performance of whole populations in nontransitive settings. From this framework, the authors develop rectified Nash response, or PSRO_rN, which uses game-theoretic niching to construct diverse populations of effective agents.

The algorithm is tested on two highly nontransitive resource allocation games, where it consistently outperforms the alternatives evaluated. The results support organizing learning around population diversity and adaptive objectives when a single ordering of agent strength is inadequate. The empirical evidence concerns those games, while the framework supplies the broader way of formulating progress.
summary.tldr: A geometric framework and rectified Nash response algorithm support diverse agent populations, outperforming evaluated alternatives in two nontransitive games.

title: Open-ended learning in symmetric zero-sum games

abstract: Reducing the variance of estimators for policy gradient has long been the focus of reinforcement learning research. While classic algorithms like REINFORCE find an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point in $\OM({1}/{\epsilon^4})$ random trajectory simulations, no provable improvement on the complexity has been made so far. This paper presents a Hessian aided policy gradient method with the first improved sample complexity of $\OM({1}/{\epsilon^3})$. While our method exploits information from the policy Hessian, it can be implemented in linear time with respect to the parameter dimension and is hence applicable to sophisticated DNN parameterization. Simulations on standard tasks validate the efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods learn behavior from simulated trajectories, but the estimates used to update a policy can have high variance. This makes the number of trajectories needed for optimization an important concern. The paper introduces a Hessian-aided policy-gradient method that uses information about how the policy’s derivatives change to improve the theoretical sample complexity.

The stated comparison is with classic methods such as REINFORCE, which require on the order of one over epsilon to the fourth power in trajectory simulations to reach an epsilon-approximate first-order stationary point. The proposed method improves that dependence to one over epsilon cubed. The guarantee concerns reaching approximate stationarity, meaning a point with a sufficiently small first-order optimization signal, rather than guaranteeing the globally best policy.

Although the method uses Hessian information, the authors show that it can be implemented with computation linear in the number of policy parameters. That makes the approach applicable to policies parameterized by sophisticated deep neural networks. Simulations on standard tasks support its efficiency, complementing the theoretical improvement in trajectory requirements with empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: Hessian information improves policy-gradient trajectory complexity from an epsilon-to-the-minus-four dependence to epsilon-to-the-minus-three while retaining linear parameter-time implementation.

title: Hessian Aided Policy Gradient

abstract: We study the implicit regularization of mini-batch stochastic gradient descent, when applied to the fundamental problem of least squares regression. We leverage a continuous-time stochastic differential equation having the same moments as stochastic gradient descent, which we call stochastic gradient flow. We give a bound on the excess risk of stochastic gradient flow at time $t$, over ridge regression with tuning parameter $\lambda = 1/t$. The bound may be computed from explicit constants (e.g., the mini-batch size, step size, number of iterations), revealing precisely how these quantities drive the excess risk. Numerical examples show the bound can be small, indicating a tight relationship between the two estimators. We give a similar result relating the coefficients of stochastic gradient flow and ridge. These results hold under no conditions on the data matrix $X$, and across the entire optimization path (not just at convergence).

This paper studies that effect for mini-batch stochastic gradient descent in least-squares regression. It uses a continuous-time stochastic differential equation, called stochastic gradient flow, whose moments match those of the discrete optimization method.

The authors bound the excess risk of stochastic gradient flow at time t relative to ridge regression with regularization parameter 1/t. The bound uses explicit quantities, including mini-batch size, step size, and iteration count, showing how optimization choices affect the comparison. They also derive a related result comparing the fitted coefficient vectors.

These guarantees hold without conditions on the data matrix and cover the whole optimization path, rather than only its endpoint. Numerical examples show that the risk bound can be small, supporting a close relationship between the two estimators. The results give a quantitative link between progress along a stochastic optimization trajectory and the strength of explicit ridge regularization.
summary.tldr: Explicit risk and coefficient bounds connect stochastic gradient flow for least squares to ridge regression throughout the optimization path.

title: The Implicit Regularization of Stochastic Gradient Flow for Least Squares

abstract: Given data drawn from an unknown distribution, D, to what extent is it possible to “amplify” this dataset and faithfully output an even larger set of samples that appear to have been drawn from D? We formalize this question as follows: an (n,m) amplification procedure takes as input n independent draws from an unknown distribution D, and outputs a set of m > n “samples” which must be indistinguishable from m samples drawn iid from D. We consider this sample amplification problem in two fundamental settings: the case where D is an arbitrary discrete distribution supported on k elements, and the case where D is a d-dimensional Gaussian with unknown mean, and fixed covariance matrix. Perhaps surprisingly, we show a valid amplification procedure exists for both of these settings, even in the regime where the size of the input dataset, n, is significantly less than what would be necessary to learn distribution D to non-trivial accuracy. We also show that our procedures are optimal up to constant factors. Beyond these results, we describe potential applications of such data amplification, and formalize a number of curious directions for future research along this vein.

paragraphs: Can a dataset be enlarged so that the result looks like a genuinely larger independent sample from the same unknown distribution? This paper formalizes that question as sample amplification. A procedure receives n independent observations and must output more than n samples that are indistinguishable from an equally large collection of independent draws.

The authors study two settings: arbitrary discrete distributions supported on k elements, and d-dimensional Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and fixed covariance. In both cases, they show that valid amplification is possible even when the original dataset is substantially smaller than what would be required to learn the underlying distribution to nontrivial accuracy.

The procedures are optimal up to constant factors. The result separates two statistical capabilities: producing a somewhat larger sample-like dataset can be feasible with less information than learning the distribution itself. The paper also describes potential applications and further research questions, with its formal guarantees established for the two distribution families analyzed.
summary.tldr: For discrete distributions and fixed-covariance Gaussians, datasets can be faithfully amplified even with too few observations to learn the distribution accurately.

title: Sample Amplification: Increasing Dataset Size even when Learning is Impossible

abstract: We provide an end-to-end differentially private spectral algorithm for learning LDA, based on matrix/tensor decompositions, and establish theoretical guarantees on utility/consistency of the estimated model parameters. We represent the spectral algorithm as a computational graph. Noise can be injected along the edges of this graph to obtain differential privacy. We identify subsets of edges, named “configurations”, such that adding noise to all edges in such a subset guarantees differential privacy of the end-to-end spectral algorithm. We characterize the sensitivity of the edges with respect to the input and thus estimate the amount of noise to be added to each edge for any required privacy level. We then characterize the utility loss for each configuration as a function of injected noise. Overall, by combining the sensitivity and utility characterization, we obtain an end-to-end differentially private spectral algorithm for LDA and identify which configurations outperform others under specific regimes. We are the first to achieve utility guarantees under a required level of differential privacy for learning in LDA. We additionally show that our method systematically outperforms differentially private variational inference.

paragraphs: The paper develops a differentially private algorithm for learning latent Dirichlet allocation using matrix and tensor decompositions. Its central question is how to protect the input data throughout this spectral learning procedure while retaining useful parameter estimates. The authors establish theoretical guarantees covering both the utility and consistency of the estimated model parameters.

They represent the algorithm as a computational graph and identify collections of edges where injecting noise guarantees privacy for the complete procedure. These collections are called configurations. For each relevant edge, they analyze sensitivity to the input, which determines how much noise is needed for a specified privacy level.

The choice of where to add noise is therefore a consequential part of the learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: A private spectral LDA algorithm analyzes where to inject noise and how each choice affects privacy and parameter accuracy.

title: An end-to-end Differentially Private Latent Dirichlet Allocation Using a Spectral Algorithm

abstract: The main approach to defining equivalence among acyclic directed causal graphical models is based on the conditional independence relationships in the distributions that the causal models can generate, in terms of the Markov equivalence. However, it is known that when cycles are allowed in the causal structure, conditional independence may not be a suitable notion for equivalence of two structures, as it does not reflect all the information in the distribution that is useful for identification of the underlying structure. In this paper, we present a general, unified notion of equivalence for linear Gaussian causal directed graphical models, whether they are cyclic or acyclic. In our proposed definition of equivalence, two structures are equivalent if they can generate the same set of data distributions. We also propose a weaker notion of equivalence called quasi-equivalence, which we show is the extent of identifiability from observational data. We propose analytic as well as graphical methods for characterizing the equivalence of two structures. Additionally, we propose a score-based method for learning the structure from observational data, which successfully deals with both acyclic and cyclic structures.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph from observations requires understanding which structures the data can distinguish. For acyclic graphs, equivalence is commonly described through conditional independence relationships. When feedback cycles are allowed, however, those relationships may miss distributional information that helps identify structure. The paper addresses this mismatch within linear Gaussian causal models.

The authors define two structures as distributionally equivalent when they can generate exactly the same collection of data distributions. This gives a unified definition covering graphs with and without cycles. They also introduce the weaker concept of quasi-equivalence and show that it describes the extent to which structure can be identified from observational data.

Analytic and graphical methods provide ways to characterize equivalence between structures. The paper additionally proposes a score-based learning method that handles both cyclic and acyclic graphs successfully. Together, these contributions connect a definition of indistinguishability with a practical structure-learning approach, while retaining the observational identifiability boundary expressed through quasi-equivalence.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes distributional equivalence and observational identifiability for linear Gaussian causal graphs, including graphs with feedback cycles.

title: Characterizing Distribution Equivalence and Structure Learning for Cyclic and Acyclic Directed Graphs

abstract: Creating open-ended algorithms, which generate their own never-ending stream of novel and appropriately challenging learning opportunities, could help to automate and accelerate progress in machine learning. A recent step in this direction is the Paired Open-Ended Trailblazer (POET), an algorithm that generates and solves its own challenges, and allows solutions to goal-switch between challenges to avoid local optima. However, the original POET was unable to demonstrate its full creative potential because of limitations of the algorithm itself and because of external issues including a limited problem space and lack of a universal progress measure. Importantly, both limitations pose impediments not only for POET, but for the pursuit of open-endedness in general. Here we introduce and empirically validate two new innovations to the original algorithm, as well as two external innovations designed to help elucidate its full potential. Together, these four advances enable the most open-ended algorithmic demonstration to date. The algorithmic innovations are (1) a domain-general measure of how meaningfully novel new challenges are, enabling the system to potentially create and solve interesting challenges endlessly, and (2) an efficient heuristic for determining when agents should goal-switch from one problem to another (helping open-ended search better scale). Outside the algorithm itself, to enable a more definitive demonstration of open-endedness, we introduce (3) a novel, more flexible way to encode environmental challenges, and (4) a generic measure of the extent to which a system continues to exhibit open-ended innovation. Enhanced POET produces a diverse range of sophisticated behaviors that solve a wide range of environmental challenges, many of which cannot be solved through other means.

summary.tldr: Enhanced POET improves challenge novelty, goal switching, environment representation, and progress measurement for open-ended learning.

title: Enhanced POET: Open-ended Reinforcement Learning through Unbounded Invention of Learning Challenges and their Solutions

abstract: We study the problem of learning Granger causality between event types from asynchronous, interdependent, multi-type event sequences. Existing work suffers from either limited model flexibility or poor model explainability and thus fails to uncover Granger causality across a wide variety of event sequences with diverse event interdependency. To address these weaknesses, we propose CAUSE (Causality from AttribUtions on Sequence of Events), a novel framework for the studied task. The key idea of CAUSE is to first implicitly capture the underlying event interdependency by fitting a neural point process, and then extract from the process a Granger causality statistic using an axiomatic attribution method. Across multiple datasets riddled with diverse event interdependency, we demonstrate that CAUSE achieves superior performance on correctly inferring the inter-type Granger causality over a range of state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies relationships among different event types in sequences where events occur at irregular times and depend on one another. Its target is Granger causality: the predictive relationships between event histories and subsequent events. Existing approaches face a tension between representing varied dependencies flexibly and making those learned dependencies understandable.

CAUSE separates the task into two stages. It first fits a neural point process to capture dependencies in the event sequence. It then applies an attribution method governed by explanatory axioms to extract a Granger causality statistic from the fitted process. The model learns the event relationships implicitly, and the attribution step turns that knowledge into an explicit statistic.

This design makes explanation part of the process for recovering relationships between event types. Across multiple datasets containing different forms of event dependence, CAUSE identifies inter-type Granger causality more successfully than a range of leading comparison methods. The reported finding concerns inference of these predictive relationships across the evaluated event sequences.
summary.tldr: CAUSE combines neural event modeling with attribution methods to recover Granger causal relationships between event types.

title: CAUSE: Learning Granger Causality from Event Sequences using Attribution Methods

abstract: We consider the problem of optimizing hybrid structures (mixture of discrete and continuous input variables) via expensive black-box function evaluations. This problem arises in many real-world applications. For example, in materials design optimization via lab experiments, discrete and continuous variables correspond to the presence/absence of primitive elements and their relative concentrations respectively. The key challenge is to accurately model the complex interactions between discrete and continuous variables. In this paper, we propose a novel approach referred as Hybrid Bayesian Optimization (HyBO) by utilizing diffusion kernels, which are naturally defined over continuous and discrete variables. We develop a principled approach for constructing diffusion kernels over hybrid spaces by utilizing the additive kernel formulation, which allows additive interactions of all orders in a tractable manner. We theoretically analyze the modeling strength of additive hybrid kernels and prove that it has the universal approximation property. Our experiments on synthetic and six diverse real-world benchmarks show that HyBO significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Many expensive optimization problems combine discrete decisions with continuous quantities. In materials design, for example, choosing which elements to include is discrete, while choosing their concentrations is continuous. Modeling these choices separately can miss the interactions that determine the outcome. This paper addresses such hybrid search spaces within Bayesian optimization.

The proposed method, HyBO, builds its model using diffusion kernels, which can be defined for both discrete and continuous variables. An additive kernel construction combines them while allowing interactions of all orders in a tractable form. This gives the model a way to represent relationships involving different combinations of variables across the hybrid space.

The authors prove a universal approximation property for their additive hybrid kernels, establishing their theoretical expressive capacity. They also compare HyBO with existing methods on synthetic problems and six diverse real-world benchmarks, reporting significant improvements. The approximation result concerns what the kernel can represent; the experiments provide evidence that this modeling approach helps guide expensive black-box evaluations in practice.
summary.tldr: HyBO models interactions between discrete and continuous variables with expressive hybrid kernels and improves optimization on the reported benchmarks.

title: Bayesian Optimization over Hybrid Spaces

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with linear function approximation has received increasing attention recently. However, existing work has focused on obtaining $\sqrt{T}$-type regret bound, where $T$ is the number of interactions with the MDP. In this paper, we show that logarithmic regret is attainable under two recently proposed linear MDP assumptions provided that there exists a positive sub-optimality gap for the optimal action-value function. More specifically, under the linear MDP assumption (Jin et al., 2020), the LSVI-UCB algorithm can achieve $\tilde{O}(d^{3}H^5/\text{gap}_{\text{min}}\cdot \log(T))$regret; and under the linear mixture MDP assumption (Ayoub et al., 2020), the UCRL-VTR algorithm can achieve $\tilde{O}(d^{2}H^5/\text{gap}_{\text{min}}\cdot \log^3(T))$ regret, where $d$ is the dimension of feature mapping, $H$ is the length of episode, $\text{gap}_{\text{min}}$ is the minimal sub-optimality gap, and $\tilde O$ hides all logarithmic terms except $\log(T)$. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first logarithmic regret bounds for RL with linear function approximation. We also establish gap-dependent lower bounds for the two linear MDP models.

paragraphs: Regret measures the accumulated cost of learning instead of consistently acting optimally. Existing analyses of reinforcement learning with linear function approximation had emphasized bounds growing like the square root of the number of interactions. This paper shows that much slower, logarithmic-type growth is attainable under two specified models of linear structure.

The crucial condition is a positive minimum suboptimality gap in the optimal action-value function. Suboptimal actions must be separated from optimal ones by a nonzero value difference. Under the linear MDP assumption, the authors establish a bound for LSVI-UCB involving log(T); under the linear mixture MDP assumption, they establish a bound for UCRL-VTR involving log cubed(T). Both also depend on feature dimension, episode length, and the inverse minimum gap.

The authors additionally prove gap-dependent lower bounds for both model classes. These provide complementary limits on achievable performance. The main message is conditional: linear structure together with a positive action-value gap permits stronger regret guarantees than the previously emphasized square-root dependence, with explicit costs for problem dimension, horizon, and action separation.
summary.tldr: Under two linear MDP assumptions and a positive action-value gap, existing RL algorithms admit logarithmic-type regret bounds.

title: Logarithmic Regret for Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Understanding the complex structure of multivariate extremes is a major challenge in various fields from portfolio monitoring and environmental risk management to insurance. In the framework of multivariate Extreme Value Theory, a common characterization of extremes’ dependence structure is the angular measure. It is a suitable measure to work in extreme regions as it provides meaningful insights concerning the subregions where extremes tend to concentrate their mass. The present paper develops a novel optimization-based approach to assess the dependence structure of extremes. This support identification scheme rewrites as estimating clusters of features which best capture the support of extremes. The dimension reduction technique we provide is applied to statistical learning tasks such as feature clustering and anomaly detection. Numerical experiments provide strong empirical evidence of the relevance of our approach.

paragraphs: Understanding multivariate extremes means understanding how several variables behave together in extreme situations. This matters in applications such as environmental risk, insurance, and portfolio monitoring. The paper works within multivariate Extreme Value Theory, where an angular measure describes dependence and indicates the subregions in which extreme observations tend to concentrate.

The authors introduce an optimization-based method for identifying this support: the parts of the extreme region carrying the relevant mass. They reformulate support identification as finding clusters of features that best capture where extremes occur. This connects the structure of extreme dependence to a dimension-reduction problem organized around groups of variables.

The resulting technique is applied to feature clustering and anomaly detection. Numerical experiments provide strong empirical evidence for its relevance. Its contribution is to turn a difficult question about the arrangement of multivariate extremes into an optimization problem with a reduced representation, making the identified dependence structure useful for subsequent statistical learning tasks as well as for describing extreme behavior.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based feature-clustering method identifies where multivariate extremes concentrate and supports dimension reduction and anomaly detection.

title: Feature Clustering for Support Identification in Extreme Regions

abstract: Adversarial learning has emerged as one of the successful techniques to circumvent the susceptibility of existing methods against adversarial perturbations. However, the majority of existing defense methods are tailored to defend against a single category of adversarial perturbation (e.g. $\ell_\infty$-attack). In safety-critical applications, this makes these methods extraneous as the attacker can adopt diverse adversaries to deceive the system. Moreover, training on multiple perturbations simultaneously significantly increases the computational overhead during training. To address these challenges, we propose a novel meta-learning framework that explicitly learns to generate noise to improve the model’s robustness against multiple types of attacks. Its key component is \emph{Meta Noise Generator (MNG)} that outputs optimal noise to stochastically perturb a given sample, such that it helps lower the error on diverse adversarial perturbations. By utilizing samples generated by MNG, we train a model by enforcing the label consistency across multiple perturbations. We validate the robustness of models trained by our scheme on various datasets and against a wide variety of perturbations, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms the baselines across multiple perturbations with a marginal computational cost.

paragraphs: A model trained to resist one category of adversarial perturbation can still face other kinds of attacks. Training against several categories at once can also substantially increase computational cost. This paper addresses both issues with a meta-learning framework that learns how to generate training noise useful for robustness across multiple perturbation types.

Its central component, the Meta Noise Generator, produces noise that randomly perturbs a given sample. The generator is trained so that these perturbed samples help reduce error under diverse adversarial perturbations. The prediction model then learns from the generated samples while being encouraged to keep its labels consistent across multiple perturbations.

The authors evaluate models trained this way on several datasets and a wide variety of perturbations. They report significant improvements over the tested baselines across multiple perturbations, with only marginal computational cost. The findings support learning a noise generator as a practical training mechanism for broader attack coverage, with the reported robustness established by those experimental evaluations.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned noise generator improves empirical robustness to multiple attack types with marginal computational cost.

title: Learning to Generate Noise for Multi-Attack Robustness

abstract: In this paper we investigate the Follow the Regularized Leader dynamics in sequential imperfect information games (IIG). We generalize existing results of Poincar{é} recurrence from normal-form games to zero-sum two-player imperfect information games and other sequential game settings. We then investigate how adapting the reward (by adding a regularization term) of the game can give strong convergence guarantees in monotone games. We continue by showing how this reward adaptation technique can be leveraged to build algorithms that converge exactly to the Nash equilibrium. Finally, we show how these insights can be directly used to build state-of-the-art model-free algorithms for zero-sum two-player Imperfect Information Games (IIG).

paragraphs: Learning in a sequential game does not automatically make strategies settle at an equilibrium. This paper studies Follow the Regularized Leader dynamics in games where players have imperfect information. Its starting concern is recurrence: learning trajectories can return near earlier states, so continued updating need not produce convergence to a single solution.

The authors extend existing recurrence results from normal-form games to two-player zero-sum games with imperfect information and other sequential settings. They then examine a way to change this behavior by adding a regularization term to the game’s rewards. For monotone games, this reward adaptation provides strong convergence guarantees.

The paper further shows how the reward adaptation can be used to construct algorithms that converge exactly to a Nash equilibrium. This connects an analysis of why learning can keep revisiting earlier behavior with a method for obtaining convergence. The authors also use the insights to build model-free algorithms described as state of the art for two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. The convergence claims retain their stated game-class qualifications.
summary.tldr: Regularizing game rewards turns insights about recurring learning dynamics into equilibrium-convergent algorithms for specified game classes.

title: From Poincaré Recurrence to Convergence in Imperfect Information Games: Finding Equilibrium via Regularization

abstract: Choosing the right parameters for optimization algorithms is often the key to their success in practice. Solving this problem using a learning-to-learn approach—using meta-gradient descent on a meta-objective based on the trajectory that the optimizer generates—was recently shown to be effective. However, the meta-optimization problem is difficult. In particular, the meta-gradient can often explode/vanish, and the learned optimizer may not have good generalization performance if the meta-objective is not chosen carefully. In this paper we give meta-optimization guarantees for the learning-to-learn approach on a simple problem of tuning the step size for quadratic loss. Our results show that the naïve objective suffers from meta-gradient explosion/vanishing problem. Although there is a way to design the meta-objective so that the meta-gradient remains polynomially bounded, computing the meta-gradient directly using backpropagation leads to numerical issues. We also characterize when it is necessary to compute the meta-objective on a separate validation set to ensure the generalization performance of the learned optimizer. Finally, we verify our results empirically and show that a similar phenomenon appears even for more complicated learned optimizers parametrized by neural networks.

paragraphs: Learning-to-learn methods can tune an optimizer by differentiating an objective defined over its training trajectory. This paper studies the difficulties of that outer optimization through a simple setting: learning the step size for quadratic loss. Even here, the gradient used to tune the optimizer can become excessively large or small, and the learned choice may generalize poorly.

The authors establish guarantees for this setting and show that a naïve meta-objective suffers from exploding or vanishing meta-gradients. A redesigned objective can keep the meta-gradient polynomially bounded. However, calculating that gradient directly through backpropagation still produces numerical difficulties, distinguishing a mathematical bound on the gradient from the stability of the computation used to obtain it.

The analysis also characterizes when the meta-objective must be evaluated on a separate validation set to ensure generalization of the learned optimizer. Experiments verify the theoretical findings and reveal a similar phenomenon in more complex optimizers parameterized by neural networks. The results make objective design, numerical computation, and validation data central considerations when learning optimization parameters.
summary.tldr: Analysis of learned step sizes exposes meta-gradient instability and identifies when objective design and separate validation data are needed.

title: Guarantees for Tuning the Step Size using a Learning-to-Learn Approach

abstract: Using the framework of boosting, we prove that all impurity-based decision tree learning algorithms, including the classic ID3, C4.5, and CART, are highly noise tolerant. Our guarantees hold under the strongest noise model of nasty noise, and we provide near-matching upper and lower bounds on the allowable noise rate. We further show that these algorithms, which are simple and have long been central to everyday machine learning, enjoy provable guarantees in the noisy setting that are unmatched by existing algorithms in the theoretical literature on decision tree learning. Taken together, our results add to an ongoing line of research that seeks to place the empirical success of these practical decision tree algorithms on firm theoretical footing.

paragraphs: Decision tree methods such as ID3, C4.5, and CART have long been practical tools for machine learning. This paper investigates the theoretical basis of their ability to learn from noisy data. It treats these familiar methods as members of the broader family of impurity-based decision tree algorithms.

Using a boosting framework, the authors prove strong noise-tolerance guarantees for that family. The results hold under the nasty-noise model, described in the abstract as the strongest noise setting. They also establish nearly matching upper and lower bounds on the noise rate that can be tolerated, characterizing both achievable robustness and its limits.

The authors show that these practical algorithms have guarantees in the noisy setting that existing algorithms in the theoretical decision-tree literature do not match. The contribution is therefore a theoretical explanation for the robustness of established learning procedures. The near-matching bounds also make clear that tolerance has a quantitative boundary, rather than implying successful learning under arbitrarily large amounts of noise.
summary.tldr: A boosting-based analysis proves strong noise tolerance for impurity-based decision trees, with nearly matching bounds on allowable noise.

title: Popular decision tree algorithms are provably noise tolerant

abstract: Contrastively trained language-image models such as CLIP, ALIGN, and BASIC have demonstrated unprecedented robustness to multiple challenging natural distribution shifts. Since these language-image models differ from previous training approaches in several ways, an important question is what causes the large robustness gains. We answer this question via a systematic experimental investigation. Concretely, we study five different possible causes for the robustness gains: (i) the training set size, (ii) the training distribution, (iii) language supervision at training time, (iv) language supervision at test time, and (v) the contrastive loss function. Our experiments show that the more diverse training distribution is the main cause for the robustness gains, with the other factors contributing little to no robustness. Beyond our experimental results, we also introduce ImageNet-Captions, a version of ImageNet with original text annotations from Flickr, to enable further controlled experiments of language-image training.

paragraphs: Language-image models such as CLIP, ALIGN, and BASIC perform unusually well under several natural distribution shifts. Their training differs from earlier approaches in multiple ways, so observing this robustness does not by itself reveal its cause. This paper uses a systematic experimental investigation to separate several plausible explanations.

The authors examine five factors: training-set size, the training distribution, language supervision during training, language supervision during testing, and the contrastive loss. Their experiments identify diversity in the training distribution as the main source of the robustness gains. The other investigated factors contribute little or no robustness in those experiments.

This finding directs attention toward what examples training exposes a model to when explaining its behavior under distribution shifts. It does not establish that every ingredient has the same effect in every setting. The paper also introduces ImageNet-Captions, which pairs ImageNet with original Flickr text annotations. That resource supports further controlled experiments on language-image training, helping researchers study data and supervision together while disentangling their contributions.
summary.tldr: Controlled experiments identify training-distribution diversity as the main source of CLIP-style robustness gains among five investigated factors.

title: Data Determines Distributional Robustness in Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (CLIP)

abstract: We study offline reinforcement learning (RL) for partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with possibly infinite state and observation spaces. Under the undercompleteness assumption, the optimal policy in such POMDPs are characterized by a class of finite-memory Bellman operators. In the offline setting, estimating these operators directly is challenging due to (i) the large observation space and (ii) insufficient coverage of the offline dataset. To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel algorithm that constructs confidence regions for these Bellman operators via offline estimation of their RKHS embeddings, and returns the final policy via pessimistic planning within the confidence regions. We prove that the proposed algorithm attains an \(\epsilon\)-optimal policy using an offline dataset containing \(\tilde\cO(1 / \epsilon^2)\){episodes}, provided that the behavior policy has good coverage over the optimal trajectory. To our best knowledge, our algorithm is the first provably sample efficient offline algorithm for POMDPs without uniform coverage assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a policy from fixed data when the environment is only partially observable, including settings with potentially infinite state and observation spaces. Under an undercompleteness assumption, optimal policies can be characterized through finite-memory Bellman operators. Estimating those operators is difficult when observations are numerous and the dataset provides incomplete coverage.

The proposed algorithm estimates reproducing-kernel Hilbert space embeddings of the operators and uses them to construct confidence regions. It then plans pessimistically within those regions. This makes uncertainty from offline estimation part of the policy selection process, addressing the risk of relying on poorly supported operator estimates.

The authors prove an epsilon-optimal policy guarantee using approximately O(1/epsilon²) episodes, up to logarithmic factors, provided the behavior policy covers the optimal trajectory well. The guarantee therefore retains a specific coverage requirement without demanding uniform coverage. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first provably sample-efficient offline algorithm for partially observable Markov decision processes with that relaxation.
summary.tldr: Confidence regions and pessimistic planning yield a sample-efficiency guarantee for offline POMDP learning under undercompleteness and optimal-trajectory coverage.

title: Provably Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes

abstract: The problem of online learning with graph feedback has been extensively studied in the literature due to its generality and potential to model various learning tasks. Existing works mainly study the adversarial and stochastic feedback separately. If the prior knowledge of the feedback mechanism is unavailable or wrong, such specially designed algorithms could suffer great loss. To avoid this problem, \citet{erez2021towards} try to optimize for both environments. However, they assume the feedback graphs are undirected and each vertex has a self-loop, which compromises the generality of the framework and may not be satisfied in applications. With a general feedback graph, the observation of an arm may not be available when this arm is pulled, which makes the exploration more expensive and the algorithms more challenging to perform optimally in both environments. In this work, we overcome this difficulty by a new trade-off mechanism with a carefully-designed proportion for exploration and exploitation. We prove the proposed algorithm simultaneously achieves $\mathrm{poly} \log T$ regret in the stochastic setting and minimax-optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ in the adversarial setting where $T$ is the horizon and $\tilde{O}$ hides parameters independent of $T$ as well as logarithmic terms. To our knowledge, this is the first best-of-both-worlds result for general feedback graphs.

paragraphs: In online learning with graph feedback, the graph determines which outcomes become observable after an action. Algorithms specialized for stochastic or adversarial environments can perform poorly when the assumed environment is wrong. This paper seeks one algorithm with strong guarantees in both settings without requiring that prior choice.

The work handles general feedback graphs, extending beyond earlier assumptions of undirected edges and self-loops at every vertex. Without a self-loop, selecting an action may not reveal even that action's outcome. This makes exploration more costly and complicates the balance between gathering information and choosing actions that currently appear useful.

The proposed algorithm uses a carefully designed exploration-exploitation trade-off. The authors prove regret growing polynomially in log T in the stochastic setting and minimax-optimal regret of order T^(2/3), with logarithmic and horizon-independent factors suppressed, in the adversarial setting. They describe this as the first such best-of-both-worlds result for general feedback graphs, to their knowledge. The guarantee accommodates both environments within the same algorithm.
summary.tldr: One algorithm achieves strong stochastic and minimax-optimal adversarial regret guarantees with general graph feedback.

title: Simultaneously Learning Stochastic and Adversarial Bandits with General Graph Feedback

abstract: Few-Shot Learning (FSL) requires vision models to quickly adapt to brand-new classification tasks with a shift in task distribution. Understanding the difficulties posed by this task distribution shift is central to FSL. In this paper, we show that a simple channel-wise feature transformation may be the key to unraveling this secret from a channel perspective. When facing novel few-shot tasks in the test-time datasets, this transformation can greatly improve the generalization ability of learned image representations, while being agnostic to the choice of datasets and training algorithms. Through an in-depth analysis of this transformation, we find that the difficulty of representation transfer in FSL stems from the severe channel bias problem of image representations: channels may have different importance in different tasks, while convolutional neural networks are likely to be insensitive, or respond incorrectly to such a shift. This points out a core problem of the generalization ability of modern vision systems which needs further attention in the future.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification asks a model to adapt to new classification tasks using very little task-specific information. A central difficulty is that the new tasks can differ from those encountered during training. This paper studies that shift through the channels of learned image representations, asking whether the importance assigned to those channels transfers appropriately.

The authors show that a simple transformation applied channel by channel can substantially improve representation generalization on novel tasks at test time. The transformation is agnostic to the choice of dataset and training algorithm. Its significance is that a relatively simple change to existing features can expose a consequential weakness in how those features transfer between tasks.

Their analysis identifies severe channel bias: different tasks may require different channels to matter, while convolutional networks can fail to respond to that change or respond incorrectly. The findings connect transfer difficulty to the handling of channel importance, rather than treating a learned representation as equally suitable for every new task. They also motivate closer attention to this issue in the generalization of vision systems.
summary.tldr: A simple channel-wise transformation improves few-shot transfer and reveals that learned channel importance can be poorly matched to new tasks.

title: Channel Importance Matters in Few-Shot Image Classification

abstract: Adversarial training (AT) defends deep neural networks against adversarial attacks. One challenge that limits its practical application is the performance degradation on clean samples. A major bottleneck identified by previous works is the widely used batch normalization (BN), which struggles to model the different statistics of clean and adversarial training samples in AT. Although the dominant approach is to extend BN to capture this mixture of distribution, we propose to completely eliminate this bottleneck by removing all BN layers in AT. Our normalizer-free robust training (NoFrost) method extends recent advances in normalizer-free networks to AT for its unexplored advantage on handling the mixture distribution challenge. We show that NoFrost achieves adversarial robustness with only a minor sacrifice on clean sample accuracy. On ImageNet with ResNet50, NoFrost achieves $74.06%$ clean accuracy, which drops merely $2.00%$ from standard training. In contrast, BN-based AT obtains $59.28%$ clean accuracy, suffering a significant $16.78%$ drop from standard training. In addition, NoFrost achieves a $23.56%$ adversarial robustness against PGD attack, which improves the $13.57%$ robustness in BN-based AT. We observe better model smoothness and larger decision margins from NoFrost, which make the models less sensitive to input perturbations and thus more robust. Moreover, when incorporating more data augmentations into NoFrost, it achieves comprehensive robustness against multiple distribution shifts. Code and pre-trained models are public at https://github.com/amazon-research/normalizer-free-robust-training.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve resistance to attacks while reducing accuracy on ordinary, clean inputs. The paper targets batch normalization as a bottleneck because clean and adversarial samples have different statistics. A normalization mechanism that must accommodate both can struggle with their mixture, contributing to the performance tradeoff.

NoFrost removes all batch-normalization layers and adapts normalizer-free networks to adversarial training. On ImageNet with ResNet50, it achieves 74.06% clean accuracy, a two-percentage-point decrease from standard training. The batch-normalized adversarial-training comparison reaches 59.28%, a 16.78-point decrease. Against the evaluated PGD attack, NoFrost also improves adversarial robustness from 13.57% to 23.56%, showing gains on both reported measures in this setting.

The authors observe smoother models and larger decision margins, which they connect to reduced sensitivity to input perturbations. Incorporating additional data augmentations also produces robustness across multiple distribution shifts. The findings support removing normalization as a useful design choice for this training setting, with the quantitative results tied to the stated model, dataset, and attack rather than all adversarial conditions.
summary.tldr: NoFrost removes batch normalization from adversarial training and improves both clean accuracy and evaluated attack robustness.

title: Removing Batch Normalization Boosts Adversarial Training

abstract: Federated learning (FL) systems have an inherent vulnerability to adversarial backdoor attacks during training due to their decentralized nature. The goal of the attacker is to implant backdoors in the learned model with poisoned updates such that at test time, the model’s outputs can be fixed to a given target for certain inputs (e.g., if a user types “people from New York” into a mobile keyboard app that uses a backdoored next word prediction model, the model will autocomplete their sentence to “people in New York are rude”). Prior work has shown that backdoors can be inserted in FL, but these backdoors are not durable: they do not remain in the model after the attacker stops uploading poisoned updates because training continues, and in production FL systems an inserted backdoor may not survive until deployment. We propose Neurotoxin, a simple one-line backdoor attack that functions by attacking parameters that are changed less in magnitude during training. We conduct an exhaustive evaluation across ten natural language processing and computer vision tasks and find that we can double the durability of state of the art backdoors by adding a single line with Neurotoxin.

paragraphs: A backdoor inserted during federated training aims to make a shared model produce an attacker-chosen output for particular inputs. Earlier attacks can lose their effect after the attacker stops contributing poisoned updates, because normal training continues. This paper focuses on that persistence problem: whether a planted behavior remains long enough to affect a deployed model.

Neurotoxin targets model parameters whose changes during training are smaller in magnitude. The approach uses the pattern of ordinary training updates to choose where to place the malicious behavior. Its central idea connects durability to how strongly subsequent training changes the affected parameters, rather than evaluating only whether a backdoor can initially be inserted.

Across ten natural language processing and computer vision tasks, the authors report that adding Neurotoxin can double the durability of state-of-the-art backdoors. They describe the modification as requiring a single line. The finding highlights continued vulnerability after malicious participation ends and makes persistence through later training a central consideration in evaluating federated backdoor attacks.
summary.tldr: Neurotoxin targets less-changing parameters and can double backdoor durability in the paper's federated learning evaluations.

title: Neurotoxin: Durable Backdoors in Federated Learning

abstract: Spurious correlations pose a major challenge for robust machine learning. Models trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) may learn to rely on correlations between class labels and spurious attributes, leading to poor performance on data groups without these correlations. This is challenging to address when the spurious attribute labels are unavailable. To improve worst-group performance on spuriously correlated data without training attribute labels, we propose Correct-N-Contrast (CNC), a contrastive approach to directly learn representations robust to spurious correlations. As ERM models can be good spurious attribute predictors, CNC works by (1) using a trained ERM model’s outputs to identify samples with the same class but dissimilar spurious features, and (2) training a robust model with contrastive learning to learn similar representations for these samples. To support CNC, we introduce new connections between worst-group error and a representation alignment loss that CNC aims to minimize. We empirically observe that worst-group error closely tracks with alignment loss, and prove that the alignment loss over a class helps upper-bound the class’s worst-group vs. average error gap. On popular benchmarks, CNC reduces alignment loss drastically, and achieves state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy by 3.6% average absolute lift. CNC is also competitive with oracle methods that require group labels.

paragraphs: A classifier may rely on an attribute that correlates with a label in training but fails to identify examples from groups where that correlation breaks. Correct-N-Contrast, or CNC, addresses this problem without requiring spurious-attribute labels during training. It focuses on improving the representations used by the classifier, with particular attention to the worst-performing group.

CNC first uses a conventionally trained model's outputs to identify examples that share a class but appear to differ in spurious features. A second model then uses contrastive learning to bring those examples' representations closer together. The initial model's tendency to capture misleading attributes thus provides information for training a more robust representation.

The analysis connects representation alignment to an upper bound on the gap between a class's worst-group and average errors. Empirically, worst-group error closely follows alignment loss. On the evaluated benchmarks, CNC substantially reduces that loss and reports an average absolute worst-group accuracy improvement of 3.6%, while remaining competitive with oracle methods that require group labels.
summary.tldr: CNC improves worst-group accuracy without training attribute labels by aligning same-class representations across differing spurious features.

title: Correct-N-Contrast: a Contrastive Approach for Improving Robustness to Spurious Correlations

abstract: A prominent paradigm for graph neural networks is based on the message-passing framework. In this framework, information communication is realized only between neighboring nodes. The challenge of approaches that use this paradigm is to ensure efficient and accurate long-distance communication between nodes, as deep convolutional networks are prone to over smoothing. In this paper, we present a novel method based on time derivative graph diffusion (TIDE) to overcome these structural limitations of the message-passing framework. Our approach allows for optimizing the spatial extent of diffusion across various tasks and network channels, thus enabling medium and long-distance communication efficiently. Furthermore, we show that our architecture design also enables local message-passing and thus inherits from the capabilities of local message-passing approaches. We show that on both widely used graph benchmarks and synthetic mesh and graph datasets, the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.
