paragraphs: Many graph neural networks communicate information through messages exchanged between neighboring nodes. Reaching distant nodes through this framework is challenging because deep convolutional networks are prone to oversmoothing. TIDE addresses this structural problem with a method based on time derivative graph diffusion, aiming to support efficient communication over medium and long distances.

A central feature is that the spatial extent of diffusion can be optimized for different tasks and network channels. This allows the architecture to adjust how broadly information travels. The authors also show that the design supports local message passing, preserving capabilities associated with communication between nearby nodes while adding control over more distant interactions.

The paper evaluates TIDE on widely used graph benchmarks and synthetic mesh and graph datasets. It reports a significant performance margin over state-of-the-art methods in those comparisons. The approach matters because it places the range of communication directly within the architecture's adaptable behavior, while retaining local processing. Its empirical results support this combination of local capabilities and efficient longer-distance information exchange.
summary.tldr: TIDE learns the spatial reach of graph diffusion to support local and longer-distance communication, outperforming compared methods on the reported benchmarks.

title: TIDE: Time Derivative Diffusion for Deep Learning on Graphs

abstract: We study convergence lower bounds of without-replacement stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for solving smooth (strongly-)convex finite-sum minimization problems. Unlike most existing results focusing on final iterate lower bounds in terms of the number of components $n$ and the number of epochs $K$, we seek bounds for arbitrary weighted average iterates that are tight in all factors including the condition number $\kappa$. For SGD with Random Reshuffling, we present lower bounds that have tighter $\kappa$ dependencies than existing bounds. Our results are the first to perfectly close the gap between lower and upper bounds for weighted average iterates in both strongly-convex and convex cases. We also prove weighted average iterate lower bounds for arbitrary permutation-based SGD, which apply to all variants that carefully choose the best permutation. Our bounds improve the existing bounds in factors of $n$ and $\kappa$ and thereby match the upper bounds shown for a recently proposed algorithm called GraB.

paragraphs: This paper asks how fast stochastic gradient descent can converge when it processes finite-sum components without replacement. Its focus is lower bounds: theoretical limits on the convergence performance algorithms can guarantee. Unlike analyses restricted to the final iterate, it considers arbitrary weighted averages of iterates and tracks all factors, including the condition number.

For random reshuffling, the authors strengthen the dependence of existing lower bounds on the condition number, which reflects the optimization problem's conditioning. The resulting bounds match upper bounds for weighted average iterates in both smooth convex and smooth strongly convex settings. Closing that gap identifies the achievable convergence scale within the studied setting rather than leaving uncertainty between known guarantees and known obstacles.

The analysis also covers arbitrary permutation-based SGD, including methods that carefully select the ordering of components. Those lower bounds improve dependencies on the number of components and the condition number, matching upper bounds for GraB. Thus, the results constrain what sophisticated ordering and iterate averaging can achieve, while sharpening the theoretical assessment of an existing algorithm.
summary.tldr: Sharper lower bounds close convergence gaps for weighted averages in random-reshuffling SGD and match GraB's guarantees for permutation-based SGD.

title: Tighter Lower Bounds for Shuffling SGD: Random Permutations and Beyond

abstract: We consider a fundamental class of assortment optimization problems in an offline data-driven setting. The firm does not know the underlying customer choice model but has access to an offline dataset consisting of the historically offered assortment set, customer choice, and revenue. The objective is to use the offline dataset to find an optimal assortment. Due to the combinatorial nature of assortment optimization, the problem of insufficient data coverage is likely to occur in the offline dataset. Therefore, designing a provably efficient offline learning algorithm becomes a significant challenge. To this end, based on the principle of pessimism, we propose a novel algorithm called Pessimistic ASsortment opTimizAtion (PASTA for short), which can correctly identify the optimal assortment by only requiring the offline data to cover the optimal assortment under general settings. In particular, we establish the first regret bound for the offline assortment optimization problem under the celebrated multinomial logit model (MNL). We also propose an efficient computational procedure to solve our pessimistic assortment optimization problem. Our numerical studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the existing baseline method.

paragraphs: Assortment optimization chooses which products to offer to customers. In the offline setting studied here, a firm has historical records of offered assortments, customer choices, and revenue, but does not know the underlying choice model. Because there are many possible product combinations, the historical data may cover only a limited part of the decision space.

PASTA applies the principle of pessimism to this incomplete-data problem. The authors show that, under general settings, it can correctly identify the optimal assortment while requiring data coverage of that assortment, rather than coverage of every possible assortment. The coverage condition is central: the result describes what can be learned when the historical data support the optimal choice.

The paper establishes the first stated regret bound for offline assortment optimization under a multinomial logit choice model. It also supplies an efficient computational procedure for solving the pessimistic optimization problem. Numerical studies show better performance than the existing baseline, combining a theoretical account of limited coverage with a computationally usable approach.
summary.tldr: PASTA uses pessimistic offline optimization to learn assortments with guarantees that require coverage of the optimal assortment.

title: PASTA: Pessimistic Assortment Optimization

abstract: Optimization problems with nonlinear cost functions and combinatorial constraints appear in many real-world applications but remain challenging to solve efficiently compared to their linear counterparts. To bridge this gap, we propose $\textbf{\emph{\texttt{SurCo}}}$ that learns linear $\underline{\text{Sur}}$rogate costs which can be used in existing $\underline{\text{Co}}$mbinatorial solvers to output good solutions to the original nonlinear combinatorial optimization problem. The surrogate costs are learned end-to-end with nonlinear loss by differentiating through the linear surrogate solver, combining the flexibility of gradient-based methods with the structure of linear combinatorial optimization. We propose three $\texttt{SurCo}$ variants: $\texttt{SurCo}-\texttt{zero}$ for individual nonlinear problems, $\texttt{SurCo}-\texttt{prior}$ for problem distributions, and $\texttt{SurCo}-\texttt{hybrid}$ to combine both distribution and problem-specific information. We give theoretical intuition motivating $\texttt{SurCo}$, and evaluate it empirically. Experiments show that $\texttt{SurCo}$ finds better solutions faster than state-of-the-art and domain expert approaches in real-world optimization problems such as embedding table sharding, inverse photonic design, and nonlinear route planning.

paragraphs: Optimization with discrete constraints becomes especially difficult when the cost function is nonlinear. SurCo addresses this by learning linear surrogate costs that existing combinatorial solvers can use. The aim is for solutions obtained under the surrogate to perform well on the original nonlinear objective.

Training differentiates through the linear surrogate solver and evaluates the result using the nonlinear loss. This connects gradient-based learning to the structure handled by a combinatorial solver. SurCo-zero targets an individual problem, SurCo-prior learns across a distribution of problems, and SurCo-hybrid combines distribution-level knowledge with information specific to the current problem.

The paper provides theoretical intuition and evaluates the approach on embedding-table sharding, inverse photonic design, and nonlinear route planning. In these experiments, SurCo finds better solutions faster than the compared state-of-the-art and domain-expert approaches. The findings support learning a solver's linear objective as a practical route to nonlinear optimization, with the choice of variant reflecting whether reusable experience, individual adaptation, or both are available.
summary.tldr: SurCo learns linear costs for existing combinatorial solvers, producing better nonlinear-objective solutions faster in the reported applications.

title: SurCo: Learning Linear SURrogates for COmbinatorial Nonlinear Optimization Problems

abstract: Many problems in science and engineering involve optimizing an expensive black-box function over a high-dimensional space. In the offline model-based optimization (MBO) setting, we assume access to a fixed, offline dataset for pretraining and a small budget for online function evaluations. Prior approaches seek to utilize the offline data to approximate the function or its inverse but are not sufficiently accurate far from the data distribution. We propose BONET, a generative framework for pretraining a novel model-based optimizer using offline datasets. In BONET, we train an autoregressive model on fixed-length trajectories derived from an offline dataset. We design a sampling strategy to synthesize trajectories from offline data using a simple heuristic of rolling out monotonic transitions from low-fidelity to high-fidelity samples. Empirically, we instantiate BONET using a causally masked Transformer (Radford et al., 2019) and evaluate it on Design-Bench (Trabucco et al., 2022), where we rank the best on average, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Many scientific and engineering optimization problems involve expensive evaluations over large search spaces. This paper considers access to a fixed dataset for pretraining and only a small budget for new evaluations. It identifies a weakness in approaches that learn the objective function or its inverse: their predictions can be insufficiently accurate away from the offline data distribution.

BONET instead trains a generative model on sequences derived from the available dataset. Its sampling procedure constructs fixed-length trajectories with monotonic transitions from lower-fidelity to higher-fidelity samples. An autoregressive model learns these trajectories, turning the offline examples into training material for an optimizer that generates sequences.

The empirical implementation uses a causally masked Transformer and is evaluated on Design-Bench. BONET achieves the best average ranking and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The significance is that generative pretraining can learn an optimization procedure from existing data, rather than relying solely on an accurate function approximation throughout the search space. The reported advantage is an average benchmark result, not a claim of superiority on every optimization problem.
summary.tldr: BONET learns an optimizer by generatively pretraining on trajectories constructed from offline data and achieves the best average ranking on Design-Bench.

title: Generative Pretraining for Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Understanding the effect of a feature vector $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$ on the response value (label) $y\in \mathbb{R}$ is the cornerstone of many statistical learning problems. Ideally, it is desired to understand how a set of collected features combine together and influence the response value, but this problem is notoriously difficult, due to the high-dimensionality of data and limited number of labeled data points, among many others. In this work, we take a new perspective on this problem, and we study the question of assessing the difference of influence that the two given features have on the response value. We first propose a notion of closeness for the influence of features, and show that our definition recovers the familiar notion of the magnitude of coefficients in the parametric model. We then propose a novel method to test for the closeness of influence in general model-free supervised learning problems. Our proposed test can be used with finite number of samples with control on type I error rate, no matter the ground truth conditional law $\mathcal{L}(Y|X)$. We analyze the power of our test for two general learning problems i) linear regression, and ii) binary classification under mixture of Gaussian models, and show that under the proper choice of score function, an internal component of our test, with sufficient number of samples will achieve full statistical power. We evaluate our findings through extensive numerical simulations, specifically we adopt the datamodel framework (Ilyas, et al., 2022) for CIFAR-10 dataset to identify pairs of training samples with different influence on the trained model via optional black box training mechanisms.

paragraphs: Understanding how all input features jointly affect a prediction can be difficult when data are high dimensional and labeled examples are scarce. This paper takes a more focused approach: comparing the influence of two features on the response. It introduces a definition of closeness of influence that recovers the familiar comparison of coefficient magnitudes in parametric models.

The authors then develop a statistical test for this comparison without requiring a particular model for the relationship between inputs and responses. Its finite-sample guarantee controls the type I error rate regardless of the true conditional distribution of the response. This separates the validity of the test from assumptions about a specific prediction model.

The paper also studies when the test can reliably detect differences. For linear regression and binary classification under Gaussian mixture models, an appropriate internal score function and sufficiently many samples yield full statistical power. Numerical experiments include a CIFAR-10 datamodel application that identifies training examples with different influences on a trained model.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a model-free test for comparing two features’ influence, with finite-sample error control and conditional power guarantees.

title: A Model-free Closeness-of-influence Test for Features in Supervised Learning

abstract: We investigate the online bandit learning of the monotone multi-linear DR-submodular functions, designing the algorithm $\mathtt{BanditMLSM}$ that attains $O(T^{2/3}\log T)$ of $(1-1/e)$-regret. Then we reduce submodular bandit with partition matroid constraint and bandit sequential monotone maximization to the online bandit learning of the monotone multi-linear DR-submodular functions, attaining $O(T^{2/3}\log T)$ of $(1-1/e)$-regret in both problems, which improve the existing results. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to give a sublinear regret algorithm for the submodular bandit with partition matroid constraint. A special case of this problem is studied by Streeter et al.(2009). They prove a $O(T^{4/5})$ $(1-1/e)$-regret upper bound. For the bandit sequential submodular maximization, the existing work proves an $O(T^{2/3})$ regret with a suboptimal $1/2$ approximation ratio (Niazadeh et al. 2021).

paragraphs: This paper studies online optimization with bandit feedback for a class of functions exhibiting diminishing returns. The learner must make repeated choices while receiving limited feedback about their value. The authors focus on monotone, multilinear DR-submodular functions and introduce an algorithm called BanditMLSM.

BanditMLSM achieves O(T^(2/3) log T) regret relative to a benchmark scaled by 1−1/e, where T is the number of rounds. That approximation factor is part of the guarantee: the comparison is to a fraction of the optimum. Because the regret grows more slowly than T, its contribution per round decreases as the interaction continues.

The authors then reduce two other problems to this framework: submodular bandits with partition matroid constraints and sequential monotone maximization with bandit feedback. Both inherit the same guarantee. They describe the first result as, to their knowledge, the first sublinear-regret algorithm for the general partition-constrained problem. For sequential maximization, the result improves the approximation factor from the previously reported 1/2 to 1−1/e, while introducing a logarithmic factor in the stated regret rate.
summary.tldr: BanditMLSM provides sublinear approximation regret for diminishing-returns optimization and transfers its guarantee to two constrained bandit problems.

title: Bandit Multi-linear DR-Submodular Maximization and Its Applications on Adversarial Submodular Bandits

abstract: Differentiable physics-based simulators have witnessed remarkable success in robot learning involving contact dynamics, benefiting from their improved accuracy and efficiency in solving the underlying complementarity problem. However, when utilizing the First-Order Policy Gradient (FOPG) method, our theory indicates that the complementarity-based systems suffer from stiffness, leading to an explosion in the gradient variance of FOPG. As a result, optimization becomes challenging due to chaotic and non-smooth loss landscapes. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive Barrier Smoothing (ABS), which introduces a class of softened complementarity systems that correspond to barrier-smoothed objectives. With a contact-aware adaptive central-path parameter, ABS reduces the FOPG gradient variance while controlling the gradient bias. We justify the adaptive design by analyzing the roots of the system’s stiffness. Additionally, we establish the convergence of FOPG and show that ABS achieves a reasonable trade-off between the gradient variance and bias by providing their upper bounds. Moreover, we present a variant of FOPG based on complementarity modeling that efficiently fits the contact dynamics by learning the physical parameters. Experimental results on various robotic tasks are provided to support our theory and method.

paragraphs: Differentiable physics simulators allow robot policies to learn through gradients of simulated motion. Contact makes this difficult: the paper shows that complementarity-based contact systems can be stiff, causing the variance of first-order policy gradients to explode. Consequently, even an accurate contact model can produce an optimization landscape that is chaotic and nonsmooth.

Adaptive Barrier Smoothing, or ABS, softens the complementarity system through objectives smoothed by barriers. Its smoothing parameter adapts to contact conditions, reducing gradient variance while controlling the bias introduced by smoothing. This distinction matters because a more stable gradient is useful only if it still provides sufficiently faithful guidance about the underlying task.

The authors analyze the source of stiffness to justify their adaptive design, establish convergence of first-order policy gradient, and give upper bounds describing the variance–bias trade-off. They also introduce a related policy-gradient variant that learns physical parameters to fit contact dynamics efficiently. Experiments across robotic tasks support the theory and method, suggesting that adapting the simulator’s smoothness can improve the learning process.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Barrier Smoothing stabilizes policy gradients through contact dynamics by reducing gradient variance while controlling smoothing bias.

title: Adaptive Barrier Smoothing for First-Order Policy Gradient with Contact Dynamics

abstract: We propose Stacked Deep Sets and Quantile Pooling for learning tasks on set data. We introduce Quantile Pooling, a novel permutation-invariant pooling operation that synergizes max and average pooling. Just like max pooling, quantile pooling emphasizes the most salient features of the data. Like average pooling, it captures the overall distribution and subtle features of the data. Like both, it is lightweight and fast. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of tasks, showing that quantile pooling can outperform both max and average pooling in each of their respective strengths. We also introduce a variant of deep set networks that is more expressive and universal. While Quantile Pooling balances robustness and sensitivity, Stacked Deep Sets enhances learning with depth.

paragraphs: Learning from sets requires combining information without making the result depend on the order of the elements. This paper proposes Quantile Pooling as a permutation-invariant way to perform that combination. It aims to retain both prominent features and information about the broader distribution of features within a set.

The motivation comes from complementary strengths of familiar pooling operations. Max pooling emphasizes salient features, while average pooling captures more of the overall distribution and subtle information. Quantile Pooling brings these properties together while remaining lightweight and fast. Across a variety of tasks, the authors show that it can outperform both alternatives in the areas where each is typically strongest.

The paper also introduces Stacked Deep Sets, a more expressive and universal variant of deep set networks. This architectural contribution uses depth to enhance learning, complementing the pooling operation’s balance of robustness and sensitivity. Together, the proposals address two parts of set modeling: what information survives aggregation and how effectively the network can transform that information through multiple layers.
summary.tldr: Quantile Pooling combines salient and distributional set information, while Stacked Deep Sets adds depth for greater expressiveness.

title: Stacking Deep Set Networks and Pooling by Quantiles

abstract: Masked Video Autoencoder (MVA) approaches have demonstrated their potential by significantly outperforming previous video representation learning methods. However, they waste an excessive amount of computations and memory in predicting uninformative tokens/frames due to random masking strategies. (e.g., over 16 nodes with 128 NVIDIA A100 GPUs). To resolve this issue, we exploit the unequal information density among the patches in videos and propose EVEREST, a surprisingly efficient MVA approach for video representation learning that finds tokens containing rich motion features and discards uninformative ones during both pre-training and fine-tuning. We further present an information-intensive frame selection strategy that allows the model to focus on informative and causal frames with minimal redundancy. Our method significantly reduces the computation and memory requirements of MVA, enabling the pre-training and fine-tuning on a single machine with 8 GPUs while achieving comparable performance to computation- and memory-heavy baselines on multiple benchmarks and the uncurated Ego4D dataset. We hope that our work contributes to reducing the barrier to further research on video understanding.

paragraphs: Masked video autoencoders learn video representations by predicting missing portions of their inputs. Random masking can make them spend substantial computation and memory on patches or frames that provide little useful information. EVEREST starts from the observation that information is distributed unevenly across a video, so treating every region alike can waste resources.

The method identifies tokens rich in motion information and removes uninformative tokens during both pretraining and fine-tuning. It also introduces a frame-selection strategy designed to concentrate on informative, causal frames with little redundancy. Together, these choices focus processing on selected spatial and temporal content instead of relying only on random masking.

The authors report reduced computation and memory requirements sufficient to run pretraining and fine-tuning on one machine with eight GPUs. Performance remains comparable to resource-intensive baselines across multiple benchmarks and the uncurated Ego4D dataset. The findings suggest that more selective use of video content can preserve useful representations while reducing the hardware burden of learning them.
summary.tldr: EVEREST removes uninformative video tokens and frames to reduce training costs while maintaining comparable performance in the reported evaluations.

title: EVEREST: Efficient Masked Video Autoencoder by Removing Redundant Spatiotemporal Tokens

abstract: Despite impressive results, deep generative models require massive datasets for training, and as dataset size increases, effective evaluation metrics like precision and recall (P&R) become computationally infeasible on commodity hardware. In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing efficient P&R (eP&R) metrics that give almost identical results as the original P&R but with much lower computational costs. Specifically, we identify two redundancies in the original P&R: i) redundancy in ratio computation and ii) redundancy in manifold inside/outside identification. We find both can be effectively removed via hubness-aware sampling, which extracts representative elements from synthetic/real image samples based on their hubness values, i.e., the number of times a sample becomes a k-nearest neighbor to others in the feature space. Thanks to the insensitivity of hubness-aware sampling to exact k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) results, we further improve the efficiency of our eP&R metrics by using approximate k-NN methods. Extensive experiments show that our eP&R matches the original P&R but is far more efficient in time and space. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Byronliang8/Hubness_Precision_Recall

paragraphs: Precision and recall provide useful measurements for evaluating generative models, but their computational demands can become impractical as image datasets grow. This paper proposes efficient precision and recall, or eP&R, to preserve almost the same evaluation results while substantially reducing the time and memory needed to compute them.

The authors identify redundant work in two parts of the original calculation: computing ratios and deciding whether samples fall inside or outside the relevant manifold. They address both through hubness-aware sampling. A sample’s hubness counts how often it appears among other samples’ nearest neighbors in feature space. These counts guide the selection of representative real and generated images.

The sampling method is relatively insensitive to exact nearest-neighbor results, allowing the authors to use approximate nearest-neighbor methods for further efficiency. Extensive experiments show close agreement with the original precision and recall measurements, alongside substantially lower time and space costs. The finding supports a practical way to scale an existing evaluation approach while maintaining its reported results closely.
summary.tldr: Hubness-aware sampling makes generative-model precision and recall much cheaper to compute while producing nearly identical results.

title: Efficient Precision and Recall Metrics for Assessing Generative Models using Hubness-aware Sampling

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive reasoning abilities, but translating reasoning into actions in the real world remains challenging. In particular, it is unclear how to complete a given task provably within a minimum number of interactions with the external environment, e.g., through an internal mechanism of reasoning. To this end, we propose the first framework with provable regret guarantees to orchestrate reasoning and acting, which we call reason for future, act for now (RAFA). Specifically, we design a prompt template for reasoning that learns from the memory buffer and plans a future trajectory over a long horizon (reason for future). At each step, the LLM agent takes the initial action of the planned trajectory (act for now), stores the collected feedback in the memory buffer, and reinvokes the reasoning routine to replan the future trajectory from the new state. The key idea is to cast reasoning in LLMs as learning and planning in Bayesian adaptive Markov decision processes (MDPs). Correspondingly, we prompt LLMs with the memory buffer to estimate the unknown environment (learning) and generate an optimal trajectory for multiple future steps that maximize a value function (planning). The learning and planning subroutines are performed in an in-context manner to emulate the actor-critic update for MDPs. Our theoretical analysis establishes a $\sqrt{T}$ regret, while our experimental validation demonstrates superior empirical performance.

paragraphs: An LLM's ability to reason does not automatically determine how effectively it acts in an unfamiliar environment. It frames the agent's internal reasoning as learning about the environment and planning within a Bayesian adaptive Markov decision process.

A reasoning prompt uses a memory buffer of prior interactions to estimate the unknown environment and plan a trajectory over multiple future steps. The agent executes the first action, records the resulting feedback, and plans again from its updated state. This cycle lets longer-term reasoning inform the immediate decision while incorporating new evidence after each interaction.

Learning and planning take place in context, emulating actor-critic updates through the prompt and stored experience. The paper establishes a regret bound scaling as the square root of the interaction horizon T and reports superior empirical performance. The guarantee formalizes cumulative decision quality in the analyzed framework. The architectural contribution is a repeated connection between memory, future planning, immediate action, and replanning.
summary.tldr: RAFA combines memory-based learning, long-horizon planning, and one-step execution with a square-root regret guarantee.

title: Reason for Future, Act for Now: A Principled Architecture for Autonomous LLM Agents

abstract: DreamCoder is an inductive program synthesis system that, whilst solving problems, learns to simplify search in an iterative wake-sleep procedure. The cost of search is amortized by training a neural search policy, reducing search breadth and effectively "compiling" useful information to compose program solutions across tasks. Additionally, a library of program components is learnt to compress and express discovered solutions in fewer components, reducing search depth. We present a novel approach for library learning that directly leverages the neural search policy, effectively "decompiling" its amortized knowledge to extract relevant program components. This provides stronger amortized inference: the amortized knowledge learnt to reduce search breadth is now also used to reduce search depth. We integrate our approach with DreamCoder and demonstrate faster domain proficiency with improved generalization on a range of domains, particularly when fewer example solutions are available.

paragraphs: DreamCoder learns to solve problems by searching for programs, then using what it discovers to make later searches easier. It does this in two complementary ways. A neural search policy narrows which possibilities to explore, while a library of reusable program components shortens the sequences needed to express solutions.

This paper connects those two mechanisms. Instead of learning library components independently of the neural policy's accumulated knowledge, it extracts relevant components directly from that policy. The authors describe this as decompiling: knowledge previously absorbed into a neural search guide becomes explicit building blocks that can appear in newly synthesized programs.

The same learned information can therefore reduce both search breadth and search depth. Integrated into DreamCoder, the method reaches domain proficiency faster and improves generalization across several domains. The reported advantage is particularly pronounced when example solutions are scarce. These results suggest that a learned search policy can be useful both for directing search and for improving the language of components available to it.
summary.tldr: Extracting reusable program components from DreamCoder's neural search policy makes program learning faster and improves generalization, especially with few example solutions.

title: Bayesian Program Learning by Decompiling Amortized Knowledge

abstract: Robust Reinforcement Learning (RRL) is a promising Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm aimed at training robust to uncertainty or disturbances models, making them more efficient for real-world applications. Following this paradigm, uncertainty or disturbances are interpreted as actions of a second adversarial agent, and thus, the problem is reduced to seeking the agents’ policies robust to any opponent’s actions. This paper is the first to propose considering the RRL problems within the positional differential game theory, which helps us to obtain theoretically justified intuition to develop a centralized Q-learning approach. Namely, we prove that under Isaacs’s condition (sufficiently general for real-world dynamical systems), the same Q-function can be utilized as an approximate solution of both minimax and maximin Bellman equations. Based on these results, we present the Isaacs Deep Q-Network algorithms and demonstrate their superiority compared to other baseline RRL and Multi-Agent RL algorithms in various environments.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning can represent uncertainty and disturbances as the actions of an adversarial second agent. Learning then becomes a problem of choosing policies that withstand an opponent's actions. This paper develops that view using positional differential game theory to motivate a centralized Q-learning approach.

The key theoretical result concerns minimax and maximin Bellman equations, which reflect different orders of optimization between the two agents. Under Isaacs's condition, the authors prove that one Q-function can serve as an approximate solution to both equations. This conditional result provides a mathematical basis for sharing the value representation across the two opposing optimization perspectives.

Building on that connection, the paper introduces Isaacs Deep Q-Network algorithms. Experiments across several environments report superiority over evaluated robust reinforcement learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning baselines. The contribution links a game-theoretic condition to a concrete learning design, with empirical evidence that the resulting algorithms can improve robustness-oriented learning in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: Under Isaacs's condition, a shared Q-function supports both opposing Bellman formulations and motivates robust deep Q-learning algorithms.

title: Zero-Sum Positional Differential Games as a Framework for Robust Reinforcement Learning: Deep Q-Learning Approach

abstract: Weak-to-strong (W2S) generalization is a type of finetuning (FT) where a strong (large) student model is trained on pseudo-labels generated by a weak teacher. Surprisingly, W2S FT often outperforms the weak teacher. We seek to understand this phenomenon through the observation that FT often occurs in intrinsically low-dimensional spaces. Leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of FT, we analyze W2S in the ridgeless regression setting from a variance reduction perspective. For a strong student-weak teacher pair with sufficiently expressive low-dimensional feature subspaces $\mathcal{V}_s, \mathcal{V}_w$, we provide an exact characterization of the variance that dominates the generalization error of W2S. This unveils a virtue of discrepancy between the strong and weak models in W2S: the variance of the weak teacher is inherited by the strong student in $\mathcal{V}_s \cap \mathcal{V}_w$, while reduced by a factor of $\mathrm{dim}(\mathcal{V}_s)/N$ in the subspace of discrepancy $\mathcal{V}_w \setminus \mathcal{V}_s$ with $N$ pseudo-labels for W2S. Our analysis further casts light on the sample complexities and the scaling of performance gap recovery in W2S. The analysis is supported by experiments on synthetic regression problems, as well as real vision and NLP tasks.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a larger student learns from labels generated by a weaker teacher and can outperform that teacher. This paper investigates the phenomenon through the observation that fine-tuning often takes place in a space with relatively few effective dimensions. It analyzes a ridgeless regression setting to understand how training on teacher labels can reduce variance.

For sufficiently expressive, low-dimensional student and teacher feature spaces, the authors exactly characterize the variance that dominates generalization error. Teacher variance is inherited in the feature space shared by both models. In the part of the teacher’s feature space outside the student’s, it is reduced by a factor equal to the student space’s dimension divided by the number of pseudo-labels.

This distinction explains how differences between teacher and student representations can help under the analyzed conditions. It also connects the amount of training data to variance reduction and recovery of the performance gap. Experiments on synthetic regression, vision, and language tasks support the analysis, linking the theoretical account to observed weak-to-strong behavior.
summary.tldr: A low-dimensional regression analysis shows how differences between teacher and student feature spaces can reduce inherited variance in weak-to-strong learning.

title: Discrepancies are Virtue: Weak-to-Strong Generalization through Lens of Intrinsic Dimension

abstract: Unconscious bias has been shown to influence how we assess our peers, with consequences for hiring, promotions and admissions. In this work, we focus on affinity bias, the component of unconscious bias which leads us to prefer people who are similar to us, despite no deliberate intention of favoritism. In a world where the people hired today become part of the hiring committee of tomorrow, we are particularly interested in understanding (and mitigating) how affinity bias affects this feedback loop. This problem has two distinctive features: 1) we only observe the biased value of a candidate, but we want to optimize with respect to their real value 2) the bias towards a candidate with a specific set of traits depends on the fraction of people in the hiring committee with the same set of traits. We introduce a new bandits variant that exhibits those two features, which we call affinity bandits. Unsurprisingly, classical algorithms such as UCB often fail to identify the best arm in this setting. We prove a new instance-dependent regret lower bound, which is larger than that in the standard bandit setting by a multiplicative function of $K$. Since we treat rewards that are time-varying and dependent on the policy’s past actions, deriving this lower bound requires developing proof techniques beyond the standard bandit techniques. Finally, we design an elimination-style algorithm which nearly matches this regret, despite never observing the real rewards.

paragraphs: Affinity bias favors people similar to those making an assessment. The paper studies a feedback loop in which today’s hires influence tomorrow’s hiring committee, changing future bias. Decisions are difficult because the observed assessment is biased, while the objective is to select candidates according to their underlying value.

The authors formalize this as affinity bandits. Bias toward a set of traits depends on the fraction of committee members sharing those traits, so observed rewards change over time and depend on previous decisions. Classical methods such as UCB often fail to identify the best option in this setting. The challenge therefore involves both hidden true rewards and feedback altered by the decision-maker’s own history.

The paper proves an instance-dependent lower bound on regret that exceeds the standard bandit bound by a multiplicative function of the number of options. Establishing it requires techniques that handle this evolving feedback. An elimination-style algorithm nearly matches the bound despite never observing true rewards, showing that effective decision-making remains possible within the proposed model while quantifying its additional difficulty.
summary.tldr: Affinity bandits model decision-dependent biased feedback, and an elimination algorithm nearly matches the resulting regret lower bound without observing true rewards.

title: On Mitigating Affinity Bias through Bandits with Evolving Biased Feedback

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely used in various domains such as social networks, molecular biology, or recommendation systems. Concurrently, different explanations methods of GNNs have arisen to complement its blackbox nature. Explanations of the GNNs’ predictions can be categorized into two types—factual and counterfactual. Given a GNN trained on binary classification into “accept” and “reject” classes, a global counterfactual explanation consists in generating a small set of “accept” graphs relevant to all of the input “reject” graphs. The transformation of a “reject” graph into an “accept” graph is called a recourse. A common recourse explanation is a small set of recourse, from which every “reject” graph can be turned into an “accept” graph. Although local counterfactual explanations have been studied extensively, the problem of finding common recourse for global counterfactual explanation remains unexplored, particularly for GNNs. In this paper, we formalize the common recourse explanation problem, and design an effective algorithm, COMRECGC, to solve it. We benchmark our algorithm against strong baselines on four different real-world graphs datasets and demonstrate the superior performance of COMRECGC against the competitors. We also compare the common recourse explanations to the graph counterfactual explanation, showing that common recourse explanations are either comparable or superior, making them worth considering for applications such as drug discovery or computational biology.

paragraphs: A counterfactual explanation asks what would need to change for a model to make a different prediction. This paper considers graph neural networks that classify graphs as accepted or rejected. Its goal is to explain rejected inputs collectively, using a small collection of changes that can turn every rejected graph into an accepted one.

The authors call a transformation that changes rejection into acceptance a recourse. Their common recourse formulation focuses on a compact collection of such transformations that covers the rejected inputs. This differs from organizing a global explanation around a small collection of accepted example graphs. The paper formalizes this problem and introduces COMRECGC as an algorithm for solving it.

Across four real-world graph datasets, COMRECGC outperforms the competing baselines. The authors also find that common recourse explanations perform comparably to or better than graph counterfactual explanations. These results support considering shared transformations as a useful explanatory object, with potential applications in drug discovery and computational biology.
summary.tldr: COMRECGC explains graph classifications through compact sets of shared transformations that change rejected graphs into accepted ones.

title: COMRECGC: Global Graph Counterfactual Explainer through Common Recourse

abstract: Attention layers are the core component of transformers, the current state-of-the-art neural network architecture. Alternatives to softmax-based attention are being explored due to its tendency to hinder effective information flow. Even at initialisation, it remains poorly understood why the propagation of signals and gradients through these random networks can be pathological, resulting in issues known as (i) vanishing/exploding gradients and (ii) rank collapse in depth, i.e. when all tokens converge to a single representation along layers. While rank collapse in depth naturally arises from repeated matrix multiplications—a common pattern across various architectures—we identify an additional and previously unknown challenge unique to softmax attention layers: (iii) rank collapse in width, which occurs as the context length increases. Using Random Matrix Theory, we conduct a rigorous analysis that uncovers a spectral gap between the two largest singular values of the attention matrix as the cause of (iii), which in turn exacerbates (i) and (ii). Building on this insight, we propose a novel yet simple practical solution to mitigate rank collapse in width by removing the outlier eigenvalue(s). Our theoretical framework offers a fresh perspective on recent practical studies, such as (Ye et al., 2024; Ali et al., 2023), whose ad hoc solutions can now be interpreted as implicit efforts to address the spectral gap issue. This work provides valuable theoretical support for ongoing large-scale empirical research, bringing theory and practice one step closer in the understanding of transformers.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes why softmax attention can propagate information poorly even at initialization. Known problems include gradients that vanish or explode and representations that collapse across depth, leaving different tokens with essentially the same representation. The authors identify an additional form of collapse associated with increasing context length.

Using random matrix theory, they trace this collapse in width to a gap between the two largest singular values of the attention matrix. The analysis links that spectral imbalance to the loss of representational diversity. It also shows how this problem worsens gradient behavior and the already recognized collapse that occurs across layers.

The authors propose mitigating width-related collapse by removing outlier eigenvalues. Their framework also provides an interpretation of earlier practical interventions as implicitly addressing the spectral gap. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: it identifies a mechanism in random attention networks and motivates a simple intervention. Its stated role is to support continuing large-scale empirical research, connecting theoretical properties at initialization to practical questions about information flow in transformers.
summary.tldr: A spectral gap in softmax attention explains context-length-related rank collapse and motivates removing outlier eigenvalues.

title: Mind the Gap: a Spectral Analysis of Rank Collapse and Signal Propagation in Attention Layers

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization using static datasets, avoiding the risks and costs of extensive real-world exploration. However, it struggles with suboptimal offline behaviors and inaccurate value estimation due to the lack of environmental interaction. We present Video-Enhanced Offline RL (VeoRL), a model-based method that constructs an interactive world model from diverse, unlabeled video data readily available online. Leveraging model-based behavior guidance, our approach transfers commonsense knowledge of control policy and physical dynamics from natural videos to the RL agent within the target domain. VeoRL achieves substantial performance gains (over 100% in some cases) across visual control tasks in robotic manipulation, autonomous driving, and open-world video games. Project page: https://panmt.github.io/VeoRL.github.io.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from fixed datasets, avoiding the costs and risks of extensive real-world exploration. However, the recorded behavior may be suboptimal, and the lack of interaction can make value estimates inaccurate. VeoRL investigates whether diverse unlabeled videos available online can provide additional knowledge useful for learning control.

The method constructs an interactive world model from this video data and uses model-based behavior guidance to support the agent in its target domain. Its purpose is to transfer knowledge about physical dynamics and control behavior from natural videos. The world model supplies a route for applying that information within the offline learning process.

Experiments cover visual control in robotic manipulation, autonomous driving, and open-world video games. VeoRL reports substantial performance improvements, exceeding 100% in some cases. That qualification matters: the largest gains are specific reported cases, not a uniform improvement across every task. The results support using broad video data as a source of behavioral and physical knowledge for model-based offline reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: VeoRL builds an interactive world model from unlabeled videos to guide offline reinforcement learning, achieving substantial gains across several visual-control domains.

title: Video-Enhanced Offline Reinforcement Learning: A Model-Based Approach

abstract: Understanding the inner representation of a neural network helps users improve models. Concept-based methods have become a popular choice for explaining deep neural networks post-hoc because, unlike most other explainable AI techniques, they can be used to test high-level visual "concepts" that are not directly related to feature attributes. For instance, the concept of "stripes" is important to classify an image as a zebra. Concept-based explanation methods, however, require practitioners to guess and manually collect multiple candidate concept image sets, making the process labor-intensive and prone to overlooking important concepts. Addressing this limitation, in this paper, we frame concept image set creation as an image generation problem. However, since naively using a standard generative model does not result in meaningful concepts, we devise a reinforcement learning-based preference optimization (RLPO) algorithm that fine-tunes a vision-language generative model from approximate textual descriptions of concepts. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate our method’s ability to efficiently and reliably articulate diverse concepts that are otherwise challenging to craft manually.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations investigate whether a neural network responds to meaningful visual ideas, such as stripes when recognizing a zebra. Building these explanations normally requires practitioners to propose concepts and collect image sets representing them. That manual process takes effort and can overlook concepts that matter to the model but are difficult to anticipate or illustrate.

This paper treats the creation of concept image sets as an image generation task. A practitioner supplies an approximate textual description, and a vision-language generative model is adapted to produce useful examples. The authors find that simply using a standard generator does not yield meaningful concepts, motivating a reinforcement learning-based preference optimization algorithm for fine-tuning.

Experiments demonstrate that the method can efficiently and reliably express diverse concepts, including ones that are challenging to construct manually. Its contribution is to improve the material used for concept-based investigation: generated image sets make otherwise laborious concepts easier to examine. The work therefore connects generative modeling with post-hoc explanation, using preference learning to make generated images more suitable for understanding internal representations.
summary.tldr: Preference-tuned vision-language generation creates concept image sets that help explain neural representations with less manual collection.

title: Explainable Concept Generation through Vision-Language Preference Learning for Understanding Neural Networks’ Internal Representations

abstract: Text-to-3D generation automates 3D content creation from textual descriptions, which offers transformative potential across various fields. However, existing methods often struggle to align generated content with human preferences, limiting their applicability and flexibility. To address these limitations, in this paper, we propose DreamDPO, an optimization-based framework that integrates human preferences into the 3D generation process, through direct preference optimization. Practically, DreamDPO first constructs pairwise examples, then validates their alignment with human preferences using reward or large multimodal models, and lastly optimizes the 3D representation with a preference-driven loss function. By leveraging relative preferences, DreamDPO reduces reliance on precise quality evaluations while enabling fine-grained controllability through preference-guided optimization. Experiments demonstrate that DreamDPO achieves state-of-the-art results, and provides higher-quality and more controllable 3D content compared to existing methods. The code and models will be open-sourced.

paragraphs: Generating a 3D object from text does not automatically produce something people prefer. DreamDPO addresses this gap by making preference information part of the optimization process for the 3D representation. Its objective is to improve both the quality of generated content and the ability to steer it toward desired characteristics.

The framework first creates pairs of examples. Reward models or large multimodal models then assess whether those pairs align with human preferences. A preference-based loss uses the resulting comparisons to update the 3D representation. This makes relative judgments between alternatives the main guidance signal, reducing dependence on precise absolute assessments of quality.

The approach matters because preference comparisons provide a way to guide fine-grained changes during generation. The authors report state-of-the-art experimental results, with higher-quality and more controllable 3D content than existing methods. These findings support the use of direct preference optimization for text-to-3D generation, with model-based preference assessment serving as the connection between candidate outputs and the optimization objective.
summary.tldr: DreamDPO optimizes text-generated 3D content using pairwise preference judgments to improve quality and controllability.

title: DreamDPO: Aligning Text-to-3D Generation with Human Preferences via Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: As the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) expand, evaluating true inductive generalization on entirely unseen data becomes increasingly challenging. To this end, we introduce a modular in-context learning evaluation framework, that is scalable and extendable across its separate modules. This is based upon the notion of synthetic scenarios with controllable complexity across three independent axes: 1) the logic of the underlying data distribution (UDD) 2) their projection into diverse representations, and 3) the interaction dynamic determining how the model accesses and explores the data. For these scenarios, the model is tasked to perform in-context scientific discovery and produce an interpretable theory in natural language that explains the observations. In a separate conversation, the model is then tasked to convert this generated theory into executable code, which can be programmatically compared against the underlying data distribution. Using this modular framework we produce an initial suite of 600 diverse scenarios that we use to evaluate and analyze various state-of-the-art LLMs. Although these experiments show that Gemini 3.0 Pro achieves the best overall score, each model performs the best at different tasks. For example: GPT 5.2 is the clear winner on pure symbolic data, Claude Opus 4.5 is the best at working with files, Gemini is the strongest model for the non-dynamic scenarios, and Grok 4.1 is the strongest model when UDD complexity scales. Furthermore, all models struggle with active exploration and are seemingly incapable of identifying informative data points, resulting in less efficient exploration than a random baseline.

paragraphs: SEDRAS evaluates whether language models can infer an underlying rule from unfamiliar observations. It creates synthetic scenarios with separately controlled complexity in the data-generating logic, the representation of observations, and the way a model accesses or explores them. This modular design separates different demands involved in scientific discovery.

The model first develops an interpretable natural-language theory explaining the observations. In a separate conversation, it converts that theory into executable code, which is compared programmatically with the known data-generating distribution. This makes the proposed explanation testable against the mechanism that produced the data. The initial evaluation suite contains 600 scenarios.

Gemini 3.0 Pro achieves the best overall score, while strengths differ by task: GPT 5.2 leads on purely symbolic data, Claude Opus 4.5 on files, Gemini on non-dynamic scenarios, and Grok 4.1 as underlying-distribution complexity scales. All evaluated models struggle with active exploration and appear unable to select informative observations effectively, exploring less efficiently than a random baseline. The findings distinguish successful rule inference from the ability to decide what evidence to seek.
summary.tldr: SEDRAS tests model-generated scientific theories against synthetic ground truth and finds pronounced weaknesses in choosing informative observations.

title: SEDRAS: Symbolically Evaluated Deep Research And Science

abstract: Language models struggle to generalize beyond pretraining context lengths, limiting long-horizon reasoning and retrieval. Continued pretraining on long-context data can help but is expensive due to the quadratic scaling of Attention. We observe that most tokens do not require (Global) Attention over the entire sequence and can rely on local context. Based on this, we propose L2A (Learning To Attend), a layer that enables conditional (token-wise) long-range memory access by deciding when to invoke global attention. We evaluate L2A on Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3 models, extending their effective context length from 32K to 128K tokens. L2A matches the performance of standard long-context training to within 3% while skipping Global Attention for $\sim$80% of tokens, outperforming prior baselines. We also design custom Triton kernels to efficiently implement this token-wise conditional Attention on GPUs, achieving up to $\sim$2$\times$ improvements in training throughput and time-to-first-token over FlashAttention. Moreover, L2A enables post-training pruning of highly sparse Global Attention layers, reducing KV cache memory by up to 50% with negligible performance loss. Our code is released under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/awslabs/hybrid-model-factory/tree/main/examples/research/L2A.

paragraphs: Extending a language model's usable context through continued training is expensive because full attention scales quadratically with sequence length. This paper starts from the observation that most tokens can rely on nearby context. Learning To Attend, or L2A, adds a layer that decides separately for each token when access to the entire sequence is needed.

This conditional access makes global attention selective while retaining it where the model calls for long-range information. On Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3 models, the authors extend effective context from 32 thousand to 128 thousand tokens. L2A stays within 3% of standard long-context training performance while skipping global attention for approximately 80% of tokens and outperforming prior baselines.

Custom Triton kernels translate the token-level decisions into GPU efficiency, with reported improvements of up to about twofold in training throughput and time to first token over FlashAttention. After training, highly sparse global-attention layers can also be pruned, reducing key-value cache memory by up to 50% with negligible performance loss. The results connect selective memory access to both computational and storage savings.
summary.tldr: L2A learns which tokens need global attention, extending evaluated context length while reducing attention computation and key-value cache memory.

title: Learning When to Attend: Conditional Memory Access for Long-Context LLMs

abstract: In performative learning, the data distribution reacts to the deployed model—for example, because strategic users adapt their features to game it—which creates a more complex dynamic than in classical supervised learning. One should thus not only optimize the model for the current data but also take into account that the model might steer the distribution in a new direction, without knowing the exact nature of the potential shift. We explore how regularization can help cope with performative effects by studying its impact in high-dimensional ridge regression. We show that, while performative effects worsen the test risk in the population setting, when moving to the over-parameterized regime where the number of features exceeds the number of samples, the optimal regularization in the presence of performativity helps reduce the variance in the estimated parameters, thereby improving performance. We show that the optimal regularization scales with the overall strength of the performative effect, making it possible to set the regularization in anticipation of this effect. We illustrate this finding through empirical evaluations of the optimal regularization parameter on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Deploying a model can change the data it later encounters. For example, people may alter their features to influence its decisions. Performative learning studies this feedback, where fitting the current distribution is only part of the problem. This paper examines how regularization can help when the exact resulting distribution shift is unknown.

The analysis focuses on high-dimensional ridge regression. It finds that performative effects worsen test risk in the population setting, but the picture changes when the model has more features than training examples. In that over-parameterized regime, optimal regularization in the presence of performativity reduces variability in the estimated parameters, which can improve performance.

The authors show that the optimal regularization scales with the overall strength of the performative effect. This provides a way to choose regularization in anticipation of feedback, rather than considering only the currently observed data. Synthetic and real-world evaluations illustrate the finding. The contribution links distributional response and estimation variance within the studied ridge-regression setting, explaining why their interaction matters for regularization.
summary.tldr: In high-dimensional ridge regression, regularization tuned to performative feedback can reduce estimation variance and improve over-parameterized performance.

title: Optimal Regularization for Performative Learning

abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in streaming scenarios, rendering conventional post-hoc safeguards ineffective as they fail to interdict unsafe content in real-time. While streaming safeguards based on token-level supervised training could address this, they necessitate expensive annotations and suffer from severe overfitting. In this work, we challenge the paradigm that streaming safety must rely on token-level supervised training. Instead, it is an inherent capability of well-trained post-hoc safeguards, as they already encode token-level risk signals in hidden representations. Hence, we introduce NExT-Guard, a framework that achieves streaming safeguards by monitoring interpretable latent features from Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). It uses pretrained SAEs from publicly available base LLMs, enabling flexible, low-cost deployment without token-level supervision. Experimental results show that NExT-Guard outperforms both post-hoc and streaming safeguards based on supervised training, with superior robustness across models, SAE variants, and risk scenarios. These results make NExT-Guard a universal and scalable paradigm for real-time safety, accelerating the practical deployment of streaming safeguards.

paragraphs: NExT-Guard addresses safety monitoring when a language model streams its response before the entire answer is available. A safeguard that checks only completed responses cannot intervene at the moment unsafe content appears. Training a separate streaming monitor with token-level labels is one option, but the paper identifies annotation expense and severe overfitting as problems with that approach.

The authors argue that well-trained post-hoc safeguards already contain token-level risk signals in their hidden representations. NExT-Guard accesses interpretable latent features using sparse autoencoders and monitors those features during streaming. It uses pretrained autoencoders from publicly available base language models, avoiding the need for token-level supervision.

Experiments report stronger performance than the evaluated post-hoc and supervised streaming safeguards, with robustness across models, autoencoder variants, and risk scenarios. These findings support reusing internal representations for real-time monitoring. The practical significance is that an existing safeguard’s learned information can support earlier intervention without requiring a new dataset labeling risk at every token.
summary.tldr: NExT-Guard uses sparse-autoencoder features to monitor streaming safety without token-level training labels.

title: NExT-Guard: Streaming Safeguard without Token-Level Labels

abstract: Instruction data curation is central to improving the instruction-following ability of large language models. However, existing approaches often struggle to simultaneously maintain data quality, diversity, and distributional consistency, largely because they do not explicitly distinguish semantic redundancy from quality defects and rely on coarse-grained modeling of instruction data quality. To address this issue, we propose Cure-SFT, a coarse-to-fine, diagnostic-guided method for instruction data curation that explicitly disentangles semantic redundancy from quality defects. Specifically, Cure-SFT removes redundant samples via stratified semantic-geometric sampling, applies teacher models for diagnostic triage, and performs targeted defect remediation on fixable samples. Our experiments show that Cure-SFT can surpass full-data instruction tuning using only 10% of the data budget. Moreover, Cure-SFT consistently outperforms strong selection-based and rewriting-based baselines across data budgets, supporting the effectiveness of diagnostic-guided data curation.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuning data can be problematic for different reasons: an example may repeat information already present, or it may contain a quality defect. Cure-SFT treats these as separate curation problems. Its goal is to improve instruction-following training while balancing quality, diversity, and consistency with the data distribution.

The method works from coarse selection to finer diagnosis. It first removes redundant examples through stratified sampling based on semantic and geometric structure. Teacher models then diagnose the remaining examples, and targeted remediation repairs samples with fixable defects. This sequence gives redundancy reduction and quality repair distinct roles, rather than treating every undesirable example as a candidate for the same intervention.

In the reported experiments, Cure-SFT can exceed the performance of instruction tuning on the full dataset while using only 10% of the data budget. It also consistently outperforms strong selection and rewriting baselines across budgets. These findings support the value of diagnosing what is wrong with an example before deciding how to curate it.
summary.tldr: Cure-SFT separates redundant instructions from defective ones, enabling targeted curation that can outperform full-data tuning with 10% of the data budget.

title: Cure-SFT: Diagnostic-Guided Data Curation for Instruction Tuning

abstract: Understanding the multi-dimensional attributes and intensity nuances of image-evoked emotions is pivotal for advancing machine empathy and empowering diverse human-computer interaction applications. However, existing models are still limited to coarse-grained emotion perception or deficient reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce EEmoDB, the largest image-evoked emotion understanding dataset to date. It features $5$ analysis dimensions spanning $5$ distinct task categories, facilitating comprehensive interpretation. Specifically, we compile $1.2M$ question-answering (QA) pairs (EEmoDB-QA) from $125K$ images via automated generation, alongside a $36K$ dataset (EEmoDB-Assess) curated from $25K$ images for fine-grained assessment. Furthermore, we propose EEmo-Logic, an all-in-one multimodal large language model (MLLM) developed via instruction fine-tuning and task-customized group relative preference optimization (GRPO) with novel reward design. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EEmo-Logic achieves robust performance in in-domain and cross-domain datasets, excelling in emotion QA and fine-grained assessment. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/workerred/EEmo-Logic.

paragraphs: Assessing the emotions an image evokes requires more than assigning a broad emotion label. The paper targets multiple emotional attributes, differences in intensity, and the reasoning needed to explain an assessment. It introduces both a dataset and a multimodal language model to address the coarse emotion perception and limited reasoning of existing approaches.

The dataset, EEmoDB, covers five analysis dimensions across five task categories. Its question-answering portion contains 1.2 million automatically generated pairs based on 125,000 images. A separate assessment portion contains 36,000 examples curated from 25,000 images. Together, these components support emotion-related questions and more detailed assessment within a unified resource.

EEmo-Logic is trained through instruction fine-tuning followed by task-customized group relative preference optimization with a new reward design. Experiments report robust results on both in-domain and cross-domain datasets, including strong emotion question answering and fine-grained assessment. The work connects broader training coverage with task-specific optimization to improve how a single model describes and reasons about image-evoked emotion.
summary.tldr: EEmo-Logic combines a large emotion-understanding dataset with staged model training for detailed assessment of image-evoked emotions.

title: EEmo-Logic: A Unified Dataset and Multi-Stage Framework for Comprehensive Image-Evoked Emotion Assessment

abstract: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a growing threat to large language model (LLM) safety because they exploit feedback from auxiliary judge models to iteratively refine prompts toward harmful goals. Existing defenses largely detect or block unsafe content at individual turns or at the final response, leaving the judge-driven refinement loop intact and allowing attackers to extract informative feedback from intermediate interactions. We introduce D-Judge, a semantics-preserving output rewriting defense that intervenes directly in this loop by rewriting the victim LLM’s responses before they are evaluated by the attacker’s judge. By misaligning the judge’s feedback signal without changing the meaning of the original response, D-Judge derails the attacker’s prompt-refinement process, causing subsequent queries to be optimized against a distorted signal of attack progress. To improve D-Judge’s ability to produce such rewrites, we construct a dataset of semantically equivalent response pairs that induce different judge-assigned harmfulness scores, and use it for supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization. Experiments on HarmBench show that D-Judge reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art multi-turn jailbreaks while preserving performance on benign benchmarks.

paragraphs: Some multi-turn jailbreak attacks use an auxiliary judge to score a model’s responses and guide the next attack prompt. Even when defenses block unsafe content at individual turns, intermediate responses may still provide useful feedback for this iterative search. D-Judge targets that feedback process directly.

The defense rewrites the protected model’s responses before the attacker’s judge evaluates them. Its goal is to preserve the response’s meaning while changing how the judge assesses harmfulness. The attacker then refines subsequent prompts using a distorted indication of progress. This approach relies on the distinction between what a response means and the score a judge assigns to its particular wording.

To train the rewriter, the authors construct pairs of semantically equivalent responses that receive different harmfulness scores. They apply supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization. On HarmBench, D-Judge reduces the success rate of state-of-the-art multi-turn jailbreaks while preserving performance on benign benchmarks. The findings show that interfering with judge-driven adaptation can provide an additional defense against the evaluated attacks.
summary.tldr: D-Judge preserves response meaning while rewriting wording to disrupt the feedback that guides multi-turn jailbreak attacks.

title: D-Judge: Disrupting Multi-Turn Jailbreaks using Semantics-Preserving Output Rewriting

abstract: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism maximizes hardware utilization by eliminating the pipeline bubbles inherent in synchronous execution, offering a path toward efficient large-scale distributed training. However, this efficiency gain can be compromised by gradient staleness, where the immediate model updates with delayed gradients introduce noise into the optimization process. Crucially, we identify a critical, yet often overlooked, pathology: this delay scales linearly with pipeline depth, fundamentally undermining the very scalability that the method originally intends to provide. We trace this pathology to a specific property of the optimization landscape: the misalignment between the Hessian eigenbasis and the standard coordinate basis, which triggers oscillations in the update trajectories of coordinate-wise adaptive optimizers. We identify that these oscillations cause delayed updates to diverge from their true counterparts, invalidating their use for current iterations. This insight is formalized through theoretical analysis, including a convergence bound showing that basis misalignment amplifies the delay penalty, and substantiated with empirical evaluation. To address this, we propose basis rotation, a framework that rotates the optimizer’s coordinate system to align with the Hessian eigenbasis, keeping delayed updates useful. We theoretically demonstrate that basis rotation minimizes basis misalignment, thereby counteracting the conditions that amplify delay penalties. Empirically, in training up to a 3B-parameter LLM, basis rotation reduces the required iterations by 81.7% compared to the best-performing asynchronous baseline.

We trace this pathology to a specific property of the optimization landscape: the misalignment between the Hessian eigenbasis and the standard coordinate basis, which triggers oscillations in the update trajectories of coordinate-wise adaptive optimizers. We theoretically demonstrate that basis rotation minimizes basis misalignment, thereby counteracting the conditions that amplify delay penalties. Empirically, in training up to a 3B-parameter LLM, basis rotation reduces the required iterations by 81.7% compared to the best-performing asynchronous baseline.

paragraphs: Asynchronous pipeline training improves hardware utilization by avoiding idle gaps, but its updates can use gradients computed for older model states. The paper emphasizes that this delay grows linearly with pipeline depth. Increasing the pipeline’s scale can therefore intensify the optimization problem created by stale gradients.

The authors trace an important source of trouble to misalignment between the optimizer’s coordinates and the Hessian eigenbasis, which describes directions of loss curvature. For coordinate-wise adaptive optimizers, this mismatch triggers oscillations that make delayed updates differ from their current counterparts. A convergence bound formalizes how basis misalignment amplifies the penalty associated with delay.

title: Mitigating Staleness in Asynchronous Pipeline Parallelism via Basis Rotation

abstract: Understanding how cellular morphology, gene expression, and spatial context jointly shape tissue function is a central challenge in biology. Image-based spatial transcriptomics technologies now provide high-resolution measurements of cell images and gene expression profiles, but existing methods typically analyze these modalities in isolation or at limited resolution. We address the problem by introducing SPATIA, a multi-level generative and predictive model that learns unified, spatially aware representations by fusing morphology, gene expression, and spatial context from the cell to the tissue level. SPATIA also incorporates a spatially conditioned generative framework with confidence-aware OT reweighting and morphology-profile alignment for modeling target-state morphology distributions. Specifically, we propose a confidence-aware flow matching objective that reweights weak optimal-transport pairs based on uncertainty. We further apply morphology-profile alignment to encourage biologically meaningful image generation, enabling the modeling of microenvironment-dependent phenotypic transitions. We assembled a multi-scale dataset consisting of 25.9 million cell-gene pairs across 17 tissues. We benchmark SPATIA against 18 models across 12 tasks, spanning categories such as phenotype generation, annotation, clustering, gene imputation, and cross-modal prediction. SPATIA achieves improved performance over state-of-the-art models, improving generative fidelity by 8% and predictive accuracy by up to 3%.

paragraphs: Cell appearance, gene expression, and location within tissue provide related information about biological function. SPATIA combines these sources in one model rather than analyzing them separately or only at limited resolution. A confidence-aware flow-matching objective reweights weak optimal-transport pairings according to uncertainty.
