title: SPATIA: Multimodal Generation and Prediction of Spatial Cell Phenotypes

abstract: It is folklore that reusing training data more than once can improve the statistical efficiency of gradient-based learning. While this phenomenon has been extensively studied in linear regression, the benefit of multi-pass gradient descent (GD, which reuses all the data) over one-pass stochastic gradient descent (online SGD, which uses each data point only once) is not well-understood in nonlinear and non-convex settings, except for a loss modification mechanism achieved by the first two passes on the data. In this work, we consider learning a $d$-dimensional single-index model with a quadratic activation, for which it is known that one-pass SGD requires $n\gtrsim d\log d$ samples to achieve weak recovery. We first show that this $\log d$ factor in the sample complexity persists for full-batch spherical GD on the correlation loss; however, by simply truncating the activation, full-batch GD exhibits a favorable optimization landscape at $n \simeq d$ samples, thereby outperforming one-pass SGD (with the same activation) in statistical efficiency. We complement this result with a trajectory analysis of full-batch GD on the squared loss from small initialization, showing that $n \gtrsim d$ samples and $T \gtrsim\log d$ gradient steps suffice to achieve strong (exact) recovery.

paragraphs: Reusing training examples can improve learning efficiency, but the benefit is harder to characterize in nonlinear, nonconvex problems. This paper studies a quadratic single-index model in d dimensions. It compares full-batch gradient descent, which repeatedly uses the dataset, with online stochastic gradient descent, which sees each example only once.

For the original quadratic activation, one-pass SGD needs on the order of d log d samples for weak recovery. The authors show that full-batch spherical gradient descent on correlation loss retains this logarithmic factor. summary.tldr: For a studied single-index problem, full-batch gradient descent can achieve recovery with fewer samples than one-pass SGD under specified training choices.

title: Full-Batch Gradient Descent Outperforms One-Pass SGD: Sample Complexity Separation in Single-Index Learning

abstract: Recent neural methods, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting, have achieved state-of-the-art rendering quality and speed. However, these methods frequently encounter challenges in regions with overlapping Gaussians, leading to blurring and artifacts in the rendered images. We observed that widely used view-space positional gradients are insufficient for handling such circumstances. To address this, we introduce PCGS, a Patch Comparison Gaussian Splatting method to control the densification of corresponding Gaussians adaptively. Specifically, PCGS divides the rendered image into patches and identifies those with significant errors by comparing the loss between the rendered and ground truth images. Additional densification operations are then applied to the Gaussians in these error-prone regions. Furthermore, to prevent over-densification and redundant Gaussians, we design a Gaussian control strategy to regulate the densification process. Specifically, we set a Gaussian number budget that dynamically changes according to the progress of densification, and sample the Gaussians required for each densification step based on their importance scores. Our method results in significantly fewer artifacts and less blur while maintaining a Gaussian count approximately equal to that of 3DGS. Extensive experiments on multiple standard benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

paragraphs: 3D Gaussian Splatting can render scenes quickly and accurately, yet regions with overlapping Gaussians may remain blurry or contain artifacts. The authors find that commonly used view-space positional gradients provide insufficient guidance in these cases. PCGS adds image-patch comparisons to decide where the scene representation needs additional detail.

The method divides a rendered image into patches and compares each against the corresponding ground-truth image to identify high-error regions. It applies extra densification to Gaussians associated with those regions. To avoid uncontrolled growth, a separate strategy adjusts the Gaussian-count budget as densification progresses and samples additions according to importance scores.

Across multiple standard benchmarks, the authors report reduced blur and fewer artifacts while keeping the Gaussian count approximately equal to ordinary 3DGS. The contribution is more selective allocation of scene primitives, combining local image-error evidence with explicit control over representation size. The results suggest that directing refinement toward problematic regions can improve rendering quality without requiring a substantially larger Gaussian representation.
summary.tldr: PCGS reduces rendering blur by directing Gaussian densification toward high-error image patches while controlling the total Gaussian count.

title: PCGS: Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting with Patch Comparison

abstract: Symmetry is central to modern machine learning and physics: invariances and equivariances improve sample efficiency, robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization, while symmetry principles guide scientific modeling. Yet for stochastic dynamical systems the relevant continuous symmetries are rarely known, and symmetry discovery for SDEs has remained essentially unexplored. We introduce LieStoNet, an end-to-end, template-free framework for discovering Lie-point symmetries of SDEs directly from spatiotemporal trajectories, without prespecifying symmetry groups, templates, or canonical coordinates. Building on the seminal SDE Lie-symmetry theory of Gaeta and Quintero (1999), which formalizes Lie-point SDE symmetries and their relation to Fokker-Planck symmetries, LieStoNet learns neural surrogates for drift and diffusion from increments, then learns projectable generators by enforcing the SDE determining equations, separately regularizing for closure under Lie brackets, adherence to the Lie algebra axioms (bilinearity, antisymmetry, Jacobi), and a non-redundant independent basis. The surrogate also defines an associated Fokker-Planck equation, enabling optional discovery of its Lie-point symmetries in parallel. Across multiple canonical SDEs with known analytic symmetries, LieStoNet recovers generators consistent with the ground-truth symmetry algebra, providing interpretable symmetry discovery for noisy dynamics. Code is available at this link.

Such symmetries describe transformations compatible with the dynamics and can make scientific models more interpretable. The framework does not require a predefined symmetry group, template, or canonical coordinate system, addressing settings where the relevant transformations are initially unknown.

It first learns neural approximations of drift and diffusion from trajectory increments. It then learns projectable symmetry generators by enforcing the equations that characterize SDE Lie-point symmetries. Separate regularizers encourage closure under Lie brackets, compliance with Lie algebra axioms, and an independent, nonredundant basis. This provides evidence for recovering interpretable structure from noisy dynamics in those systems, without requiring the symmetry family to be specified beforehand.
summary.tldr: LieStoNet learns continuous symmetries of stochastic dynamics from trajectories without prespecifying symmetry groups or templates.

title: LieStoNet: Learning Lie Symmetries from Spatiotemporal Data for Stochastic Dynamical Systems

abstract: Logical reasoning encompasses deduction, induction, and abduction. However, while Large Language Models (LLMs) have effectively mastered the former two, abductive reasoning remains significantly underexplored. Existing frameworks, predominantly designed for static deductive tasks, fail to generalize to abductive reasoning due to unstructured state representation and lack of explicit state control. Consequently, they are inevitably prone to Evidence Fabrication, Context Drift, Failed Backtracking, and Early Stopping. To bridge this gap, we introduce Graph of States (GoS), a general-purpose neuro-symbolic framework tailored for abductive tasks. GoS grounds multi-agent collaboration in a structured belief states, utilizing a causal graph to explicitly encode logical dependencies and a state machine to govern the valid transitions of the reasoning process. By dynamically aligning the reasoning focus with these symbolic constraints, our approach transforms aimless, unconstrained exploration into a convergent, directed search. Extensive evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that GoS significantly outperforms all baselines, providing a robust solution for complex abductive tasks. Code repo and all prompts: https://github.com/gaorch85/Graph-of-States.

paragraphs: Abductive reasoning seeks explanations for observed evidence. The paper argues that language-model reasoning frameworks designed around static deduction handle this poorly because they do not explicitly organize or control the evolving reasoning state. The resulting failure patterns include invented evidence, loss of context, unsuccessful backtracking, and stopping before the task is resolved.

Graph of States gives collaborating agents a structured representation of their beliefs. A causal graph records logical dependencies, while a state machine specifies which transitions in the reasoning process are valid. The framework continually aligns the agents’ focus with these symbolic constraints, turning exploration into a more directed search through possible explanations.

Evaluations on two real-world datasets show significant improvements over all tested baselines. The contribution lies in combining language-model exploration with explicit machinery for tracking dependencies and governing progress. In this design, reasoning state becomes something the system can control directly, rather than leaving the entire process implicit in generated text. The empirical results support this structured approach for the complex abductive tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: Graph of States uses causal dependencies and explicit state transitions to guide multi-agent language models through abductive reasoning.

title: Graph of States: Solving Abductive Tasks with Large Language Models

abstract: Programming adaptive behaviors at the cellular level is a long-standing goal that raises the question of how probabilistic computation can be implemented in biochemical systems. Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) provide such a substrate and have been shown to realize probabilistic models, including hidden Markov models and factor graphs, with dynamics reproducing Bayesian inference and belief propagation. However, encoding these algorithms typically requires prohibitively large reaction networks, and classical CRN reduction techniques do not directly apply. By recovering the factor graph structure encoded in Napp–Adams-compiled CRNs, we transport recent factor-graph reduction results to their chemical implementations, obtaining significantly smaller CRNs while preserving the belief-propagation fixed points on surviving variables.

paragraphs: Chemical reaction networks can implement probabilistic computations, offering a route toward programming adaptive behavior in biochemical systems. Existing constructions can represent hidden Markov models and factor graphs, with reaction dynamics carrying out Bayesian inference or belief propagation. The difficulty is size: encoding these algorithms can require reaction networks too large to be practical.

This paper reduces such networks by recovering the computational structure behind them. Specifically, it identifies the factor graph encoded in reaction networks produced by the Napp–Adams compilation method. Once that structure is recovered, recent factor-graph reduction results can be transferred to the corresponding chemical implementation. This creates a route around the mismatch between these compiled networks and classical chemical-network reduction techniques.

The resulting reaction networks are significantly smaller while preserving belief-propagation fixed points for variables that remain after reduction. That preservation statement is precise: it concerns the surviving variables’ fixed points, rather than asserting that every aspect of the original reaction dynamics is unchanged. The contribution links simplification of a probabilistic computation to simplification of the biochemical system that implements it.
summary.tldr: Recovering factor-graph structure enables smaller probabilistic chemical networks while preserving belief-propagation fixed points on retained variables.

title: Reduction of Probabilistic Chemical Reaction Networks

abstract: Bayesian inference provides principled uncertainty quantification but is often limited by the challenges of prior and likelihood elicitation. The martingale posterior (MGP) (Fong et al., 2023) offers an alternative by replacing these requirements with a predictive rule. In addition, the MGP focuses inference on parameters defined through a loss function. This framework is especially resonant in the era of foundation transformers; practitioners increasingly leverage models like TabPFN for their state-of-the-art capabilities, yet often require epistemic uncertainty for a scientific estimand $\theta$ that need not parameterise the implicit latent model. The MGP provides a mechanism to recover these posterior distributions. We introduce TabMGP, an MGP built on TabPFN for tabular data. TabMGP produces credible sets with near-nominal coverage and often outperforms both handcrafted MGP constructions and standard Bayesian baselines.

paragraphs: Bayesian analysis usually requires specifying a prior and likelihood, which can be difficult when a powerful predictive model is already available. Martingale posteriors offer another route: use a predictive rule to obtain uncertainty about a quantity defined through a loss. TabMGP applies that idea to TabPFN for tabular data.

The target scientific parameter need not be a parameter of TabPFN’s implicit model. Instead, the martingale-posterior construction uses its predictions to recover a distribution for the estimand of interest. This separates the choice of a useful predictive engine from the choice of the scientific quantity whose uncertainty matters.

The resulting credible sets have near-nominal coverage and often outperform handcrafted martingale-posterior constructions and standard Bayesian baselines. The contribution makes a tabular foundation model usable for inferential tasks beyond point prediction, while evaluating whether its uncertainty sets have the intended empirical coverage rather than assuming predictive accuracy automatically supplies calibrated inference.
summary.tldr: TabMGP turns TabPFN’s predictive rule into posterior uncertainty for scientific estimands, with near-nominal reported coverage.

title: TabMGP: Martingale Posterior with TabPFN

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for downstream tasks is an essential stage of modern AI deployment. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the dominant fine-tuning paradigm, underpinning many state-of-the-art LLMs. In contrast, evolution strategies (ES) has largely been overlooked due to the widespread belief that it does not scale to modern model sizes. This paper overturns this assumption by demonstrating the first successful application of ES to full-parameter fine-tuning of LLMs at the billion-parameter scale, without dimensionality reduction. ES can indeed search over extremely high-dimensional parameter spaces and outperform established RL implementations across multiple axes, including improved tolerance to long-horizon and delayed rewards, robustness across diverse base LLMs, reduced susceptibility to reward hacking, and improved training stability. These findings suggest that ES is not merely a viable alternative to RL, but a fundamentally different and powerful backpropagation-free post-training paradigm that opens a new direction for LLM fine-tuning beyond current RL-based approaches.

paragraphs: Evolution strategies optimize parameters through population-based evaluations rather than backpropagating through the model. They are often assumed to scale poorly to very large language models. This paper challenges that assumption by applying evolution strategies to full-parameter fine-tuning at the billion-parameter scale without dimensionality reduction.

The study compares this approach with established reinforcement-learning implementations across several aspects of post-training. Reported advantages include tolerance of long-horizon and delayed rewards, robustness across base models, improved stability, and reduced susceptibility to reward hacking. These tests examine how the optimization paradigm behaves, not simply whether it can update a large parameter vector.

The findings establish a viable alternative direction for large-model fine-tuning in the evaluated settings. The abstract does not supply training-cost comparisons or claim that evolution strategies dominate every reinforcement-learning method. Its contribution is a large-scale demonstration and comparative evidence that a backpropagation-free approach deserves consideration for tasks where its different optimization behavior is useful.
summary.tldr: Full-parameter evolution strategies successfully fine-tune billion-parameter language models and show advantages over the evaluated RL implementations.

title: Evolution Strategies at Scale: LLM Fine-Tuning Beyond Reinforcement Learning

abstract: When evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) in question-answering domains, multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) is widely used because it enables automatic grading. However, MCQA also exposes models to answer options that can be exploited in ways that inflate reasoning ability. We study this phenomenon across $15$ question-answering benchmarks and $27$ LLMs by systematically varying how and when models are exposed to answer options. For non-reasoning LLMs, MCQA can remain a good proxy for free-text performance when any chain-of-thought is produced only before the options are revealed. However, this "decoupled" format is not realizable for most reasoning models: they are designed to emit reasoning tokens whenever they are prompted, so if options are present they inevitably "reason over" the options. In practice, this makes reasoning models particularly effective at extracting signal from options, and can create large, misleading gains over free-text baselines. To characterize how models exploit MCQA, we introduce diagnostic probes that isolate option-only and question-plus-option exploitation pathways, and we quantify how design choices such as distractor strength and "none-of-the-above" answers effect exploitability. Finally, we examined the practice of multiple choice as an error diagnostic: inferring a model’s mistake from the wrong option it picks. On benchmarks where reasoning can be expressed as code, we ask models to output code, we then executed it varying the inputs, and compared the resulting input–output behavior, revealing failure modes that MCQA diagnostics obscure. Lastly, we offer practical guidelines when analyzing results from MCQA that better reflect LLMs’ genuine reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Multiple-choice tests simplify grading, but their answer options also provide information a model can use to reach an answer. This paper investigates how that changes apparent reasoning ability across 15 question-answering benchmarks and 27 language models. The experiments systematically alter when and how answer options become visible.

For non-reasoning models, multiple-choice performance can remain a useful proxy for free-text performance when reasoning occurs only before options are revealed. Most reasoning models cannot readily follow that separation because they produce reasoning tokens whenever prompted. Their ability to reason over visible options can therefore create large gains relative to free-text answers that give a misleading impression of independent problem-solving ability.

The authors introduce probes separating exploitation of options alone from exploitation involving both questions and options. They also examine distractor strength and none-of-the-above choices. On tasks expressible as code, executing model-generated programs with varied inputs reveals failure modes hidden by the selected wrong answer. The work argues for interpreting both multiple-choice scores and error diagnoses in light of these option-driven effects.
summary.tldr: Answer options can inflate apparent reasoning performance, and selected wrong answers can obscure the underlying mistakes models make.

title: Reasoning Models Are Test Exploiters: Rethinking Multiple Choice

abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of specified data from a trained model. While the unlearning accuracy provides a widely used metric for assessing unlearning performance, it falls short in assessing the reliability of forgetting. In this paper, we find that the forgetting data points misclassified by unlearning accuracy still have their ground truth labels included in the conformal prediction set from the uncertainty quantification perspective, leading to a phenomenon we term fake forgetting. To address this issue, we propose a novel metric CR, inspired by conformal prediction, that offers a more reliable assessment of forgetting quality. Building on these insights, we further propose an unlearning framework CPU that incorporates conformal prediction into the Carlini & Wagner adversarial attack loss, enabling the ground truth label to be effectively removed from the conformal prediction set. Through extensive experiments on image classification tasks, we demonstrate both the effectiveness of our proposed metric and the superior forgetting quality achieved by our framework. Code is available at https://github.com/TIML-Group/Conformal-Prediction-Unlearning.
originalAbstract: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of specified data from a trained model. While the unlearning accuracy provides a widely used metric for assessing unlearning performance, it falls short in assessing the reliability of forgetting. In this paper, we find that the forgetting data points misclassified by unlearning accuracy still have their ground truth labels included in the conformal prediction set from the uncertainty quantification perspective, leading to a phenomenon we term fake forgetting. To address this issue, we propose a novel metric CR, inspired by conformal prediction, that offers a more reliable assessment of forgetting quality. Building on these insights, we further propose an unlearning framework CPU that incorporates conformal prediction into the Carlini & Wagner adversarial attack loss, enabling the ground truth label to be effectively removed from the conformal prediction set. Through extensive experiments on image classification tasks, we demonstrate both the effectiveness of our proposed metric and the superior forgetting quality achieved by our framework. Code is available at https://github.com/TIML-Group/Conformal-Prediction-Unlearning.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning is often evaluated by checking whether a model stops correctly classifying the examples it was asked to forget. This paper shows why that test can give an incomplete picture. A forgotten example may be misclassified even though its true label remains among the labels retained by a conformal prediction set.

The authors call this behavior fake forgetting. Their proposed CR metric uses conformal prediction to assess forgetting through uncertainty-aware label sets, rather than relying only on the single selected label. This changes the evaluation target: removing the correct answer from first place is distinguishable from removing it from the model’s conformal prediction set.

The CPU unlearning framework incorporates conformal prediction into a Carlini & Wagner adversarial attack loss to push the true label out of that set. Image-classification experiments support both the proposed metric and the framework’s improved forgetting quality. The findings establish a more demanding assessment of forgetting in these experiments, centered on whether the original label remains plausible under the chosen uncertainty procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper detects fake forgetting through uncertainty-aware prediction sets and trains models to exclude the labels they should forget.

title: Tackling Fake Forgetting through Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: Despite the rapid advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), a critical gap remains in their ability to handle structured, controllable diagrammatic tasks essential for professional workflows, as existing methods predominantly rely on pixel-based synthesis which operates in probabilistic pixel spaces and is inherently limited in editability and fidelity; instead, we propose a new "Diagram-as-Code" paradigm with symbolic logic that leverages mxGraph Extensible Markup Language (XML) for precise diagram generation and editing, and we present VCG-Bench, a unified benchmark for visual-centric mxGraph tasks comprising (1) a taxonomized dataset of 1,449 diverse diagrams spanning 6 domains and 15 sub-domains, (2) a paradigm definition that integrates Generation (Vision-to-Code) and Editability (Code-to-Code), and (3) a Tailored Evaluation Protocol employing multi-dimensional metrics such as mxGraph Execution Success Rate and Style Consistency Score (SCS), where experimental results highlight the challenges faced by current State-of-the-Art (SOTA) VLMs in structured fidelity and instruction compliance, reflecting their vision and reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Professional diagrams need to be controllable and editable as well as visually convincing. This paper argues that pixel-based generation does not adequately support those requirements and proposes representing diagrams as code using mxGraph XML. That representation makes structured generation and editing explicit tasks for vision-language models.

VCG-Bench contains 1,449 diagrams organized into six domains and 15 subdomains. It evaluates two connected capabilities: generating diagram code from visual input and editing existing diagram code. Bringing both tasks into one benchmark links initial reconstruction with subsequent changes, reflecting the need to work with diagram structure throughout an editing workflow.

The evaluation protocol measures several dimensions, including whether the generated mxGraph executes successfully and whether visual style remains consistent. Experiments show that current state-of-the-art vision-language models still struggle with structural fidelity and following instructions in this setting. The contribution is a dataset, task definition, and evaluation framework that make those difficulties measurable, with emphasis on usable diagram structure rather than visual appearance alone.
summary.tldr: VCG-Bench evaluates diagram generation and editing through mxGraph code, exposing structural-fidelity and instruction-following challenges in current vision-language models.

title: VCG-Bench: Towards A Unified Visual-Centric Benchmark for Structured Generation and Editing

abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by using a smaller draft model to propose draft tokens that are subsequently verified by a larger target model. However, the performance of standard SD is often limited by the strictly sequential execution of these drafting and verification stages. To address this, this paper proposes MineDraft, a batch parallel speculative decoding (PSD) framework designed to effectively hide drafting latency by overlapping it with verification. Our theoretical analysis shows that PSD is substantially more efficient than standard SD. MineDraft realizes the PSD through a novel batch-parallel design that maintains two batches of requests, overlapping drafting for one batch with verification for the other. Our experimental results show significant improvements of MineDraft in both throughput (up to 75%) and end-to-end latency (up to 39%) over standard SD. Furthermore, we have implemented MineDraft as a plugin for vLLM, demonstrating its practicality for production-ready inference systems. The code is publicly available in the MineDraft GitHub repository.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model generation by having a smaller model propose tokens for a larger model to verify. Standard implementations run these stages sequentially, so drafting remains part of the waiting time before verification can proceed. MineDraft addresses this scheduling bottleneck by overlapping work across request batches.

The framework maintains two batches. While the target model verifies proposals for one batch, the draft model prepares proposals for the other. This batch-parallel organization is designed to hide drafting latency behind verification. The paper’s theoretical analysis finds substantially greater efficiency for parallel speculative decoding than for the standard sequential approach.

Experiments report throughput improvements of up to 75% and end-to-end latency improvements of up to 39% over standard speculative decoding. The authors also implement MineDraft as a vLLM plugin, demonstrating integration with an inference system used for serving models. The contribution shows how coordinating the drafting and verification stages across requests can improve both service capacity and response time.
summary.tldr: MineDraft overlaps drafting and verification across two request batches, improving throughput and latency over standard speculative decoding.

title: MineDraft: A Framework for Batch Parallel Speculative Decoding

abstract: Deep forecasting models often suffer from attenuated periodic perception and entangled trend–noise representations as network depth increases. Moreover, the widely adopted channel-independent paradigm, while improving training stability, disrupts intrinsic dynamic coordination among variables, hindering the modeling of cross-variable consistency in multivariate time series. To address these issues, we propose PESD-TSF, a physics-inspired structured decomposition framework for long-term time series forecasting that jointly emphasizes interpretability and predictive accuracy. PESD-TSF introduces three key designs. First, a Multiplicative Periodic Gating mechanism incorporates continuous-time priors to dynamically modulate signal amplitudes, preserving periodic structures across deep layers. Second, a multi-scale structured encoder integrates detrended attention with hierarchical sampling to explicitly decouple long-term trends from high-frequency variations while retaining fine-grained temporal semantics. Third, to recover disrupted inter-variable dependencies, we propose Cross-Scale Collaborative Attention (CSCA) together with an RLC regularization scheme, which reconstructs global inter-variable topology in deep feature spaces and enforces physically consistent collaboration through orthogonality and consistency constraints. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets from multiple domains demonstrate that PESD-TSF consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains on multivariate forecasting tasks involving complex inter-variable coupling, highlighting its superior structural modeling capability and generalization.

paragraphs: Long-term forecasting requires models to preserve repeating patterns, distinguish trends from rapid fluctuations, and track relationships between variables. This paper argues that increasing network depth can weaken periodic information and entangle trend and noise. It also identifies a tradeoff in treating channels independently: training may become more stable, but coordination among variables can be disrupted.

PESD-TSF addresses these issues through three connected designs. Multiplicative Periodic Gating uses continuous-time priors to modulate amplitudes and retain periodic structure across layers. A multi-scale encoder combines detrended attention with hierarchical sampling to separate longer-term trends from high-frequency variation. Cross-Scale Collaborative Attention and RLC regularization then reconstruct relationships among variables in deep representations, using orthogonality and consistency constraints to encourage physically consistent coordination.

Experiments across multiple domains report consistently state-of-the-art forecasting performance, with particularly strong gains when variables have complex coupling. The results support the framework’s emphasis on explicitly preserving different kinds of temporal structure. Its contribution combines periodic modeling, structured decomposition, and inter-variable collaboration within one forecasting architecture, rather than leaving these relationships implicit in deeper representations.
summary.tldr: PESD-TSF improves long-term forecasting by explicitly preserving periodicity, separating temporal components, and modeling coordination between variables.

title: PESD-TSF: A Period-Aware and Explicit Structured Decomposition Framework for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Watermarking embeds statistical signatures in AI-generated text for detection and attribution. We reveal a fundamental vulnerability: when users access multiple models (today’s reality), watermarks trivially fail. Watermarks perturb output distributions away from the original, and in competitive markets, these perturbations are typically independent across providers. We theoretically prove that averaging output probability distributions recovers the unwatermarked distribution with up to a second-order error term. Empirically, simply averaging 3-5 models cancels out these perturbations. We introduce WASH (Watermark Attenuation via Statistical Hybridisation), which solves practical challenges in ensemble generation: vocabulary misalignment and tokenisation differences across heterogeneous models. Experiments across six watermarking schemes and three LLMs show that averaging across 3 models suppresses detection z-scores from 5-300 to below 2 (below the detection threshold of 4) and reduces TPR@5%FPR to below 50%, while improving quality by 27.5% and running 6$\times$ faster than the best baseline on the long sequence generation. Our results suggest that robust AI-text detection via watermarking requires either accepting this fundamental vulnerability or unprecedented coordination among model providers.

paragraphs: Text watermarks alter a model’s output probabilities to leave a detectable statistical signature. This paper studies what happens when a user combines outputs at the probability level across multiple models. Its central argument is that provider-specific perturbations, typically independent across providers, can cancel when averaged.

The authors theoretically show recovery of the unwatermarked distribution up to a second-order error term and empirically observe cancellation with three to five models. Their WASH method handles practical obstacles to combining heterogeneous models, including mismatched vocabularies and tokenization. These components make probability averaging usable across models whose output units do not directly align.

The findings expose a vulnerability in the tested distributional watermarks and motivate attention to coordination between providers.
summary.tldr: WASH averages output probabilities across models to attenuate text watermarks, exposing a vulnerability when provider-specific perturbations cancel.

title: Linear Ensembles Wash Away Watermarks: On the Fragility of Distributional Perturbations in LLMs

abstract: Research on continual learning for LLMs seeks to acquire new skills without catastrophic forgetting of established prior knowledge. However, domain-specific fine-tuning still triggers severe, long-tailed forgetting issues even under narrow updates, particularly when the pre-training data is inaccessible. To tackle this challenge, we propose ALER, a data-free continual learning framework that adversarially searches for a small set of latent prompt embeddings to maximize logit divergence from a frozen reference model, proactively exposing high-risk forgetting modes at each step. It then performs online distillation from the frozen reference using the discovered embeddings to retain prior behaviors while preserving target-domain adaptation. We provide theoretical guarantees on the efficiency of our targeted repair, and extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in the retention–adaptation frontier over representative baselines across $2$ domain-specific fine-tuning datasets and $6$ general-purpose benchmarks, suggesting a more proactive approach for LLM continual learning.

To tackle this challenge, we propose ALER, a data-free continual learning framework that adversarially searches for a small set of latent prompt embeddings to maximize logit divergence from a frozen reference model, proactively exposing high-risk forgetting modes at each step. It then performs online distillation from the frozen reference using the discovered embeddings to retain prior behaviors while preserving target-domain adaptation. paragraphs: Teaching a language model a specialized skill can damage abilities it already had, even when the update is narrow. ALER addresses this continual-learning problem when the original pretraining data is unavailable. Its central idea is to actively search for behaviors at risk of being forgotten during adaptation.

The method keeps a frozen reference model and searches for a small collection of latent prompt embeddings: internal representations that act as inputs. This search deliberately maximizes disagreement between the adapting model’s output scores and those of the reference. The resulting embeddings expose vulnerable behaviors. ALER then uses online distillation on these inputs to bring the adapting model closer to the reference while continuing target-domain learning.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees concerning the efficiency of this targeted repair. Experiments across two specialized fine-tuning datasets and six general-purpose benchmarks show a consistently better balance between retaining previous abilities and acquiring new ones than the evaluated baselines. The findings support proactive repair as a way to improve that balance without needing access to pretraining examples.
summary.tldr: ALER searches for internal inputs that expose forgetting, then distills a frozen model’s behavior to preserve prior abilities during fine-tuning.

title: Adversarial Latent Embedding Repair for LLM Continual Learning

abstract: Segment Anything Models (SAMs) often struggle with certain specialized tasks. A common approach is to fine-tune models with specific task labels, but this often leads to overfitting, introduces model bias and significantly degrades their generalization ability. To overcome these challenges, we propose SHERPA, a novel framework that leverages a smaller SAM to guide the fine-tuning of a larger SAM via task-relevant features. Specifically, we first leverage the Fisher Ratio Separation (FRS) module to separate high task-relevant features and preserve the ability of the large SAM to perform other general tasks. Then, the Guiding Feature Extraction (GFE) module is used to extract representative guiding features from the fine-tuned small SAMs. We leverage small SAMs tailored for specific tasks (including natural image segmentation, biomedical image segmentation, and video object segmentation) as guidance and then evaluate the SHERPA scheme to fine-tune larger SAM series models. Our experiments demonstrate that SHERPA enhances the retention of generalization ability across those diverse tasks, by up to 11.1%, and improves specific task performance by up to 2.2%.

paragraphs: Segment Anything Models can struggle on specialized segmentation tasks. Fine-tuning with task labels may help specialization but also cause overfitting, bias, and loss of generalization. SHERPA addresses this tension by using a smaller, task-adapted SAM to guide the fine-tuning of a larger model through features relevant to the target task.

Its Fisher Ratio Separation module separates highly task-relevant features, with the aim of preserving the larger model’s ability to handle other general tasks. These are reported upper gains across the evaluations, supporting the use of task-relevant guidance to improve specialization while better retaining broader segmentation abilities.
summary.tldr: SHERPA uses features from a smaller specialized SAM to improve a larger SAM’s task performance while better retaining generalization.

title: SHERPA: Fine-tuning Segment Anything Models with Task-relevant Guidance

abstract: We present a comprehensive benchmarking dataset and empirical scaling law analysis for neural network wavefunctions by matching them to a wide spectrum of famous many body target wavefunctions. The dataset, WF-Bench, spans multiple distinct regimes of strongly correlated quantum matter, including topological states, Wigner crystals, and superconducting wavefunctions, providing a diverse and challenging test bed for neural network wavefunction expressivity. We introduce a systematic and reproducible benchmarking protocol for target wavefunction matching, enabling consistent performance evaluation across different neural network wavefunction architectures. By using wavefunction fidelity as the uniform metric, we discover empirical scaling laws that characterize how representability depends on system size and key model parameters, including number of determinant and model depth. By applying our benchmark protocol on Psiformer and Ferminet, we show that WF-Bench establishes a unified dataset driven framework for evaluating and comparing neural network wavefunctions and for guiding the design of future architectures.

paragraphs: WF-Bench evaluates how well neural networks can represent quantum many-body wavefunctions. It does this by asking models to match target wavefunctions across several distinct regimes of strongly correlated matter, including topological states, Wigner crystals, and superconducting wavefunctions. The diversity of targets makes representational ability the central object of comparison.

The paper introduces a systematic, reproducible matching protocol and uses wavefunction fidelity as a common measure of agreement. This provides a consistent basis for comparing different neural-network wavefunction architectures. The authors apply the protocol to Psiformer and Ferminet, placing both within the same dataset-driven evaluation framework.

The analysis finds empirical scaling laws relating representability to physical system size and model choices, including the number of determinants and network depth. These laws summarize observed scaling behavior rather than asserting universal guarantees. The benchmark therefore serves two connected purposes: measuring which target states architectures can represent, and investigating how increasing particular model resources changes that ability. Both can inform the design of future wavefunction models.
summary.tldr: WF-Bench compares neural-network wavefunctions through target matching and identifies empirical relationships between representability, system size, and model capacity.

title: WF-Bench: A Benchmark for Neural-Network WaveFunction Expressivity and Scaling Laws

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with diverse user preferences is a critical yet challenging task. While post-training methods can adapt models to specific needs, they often require costly data curation and additional training. Test-time scaling (TTS) presents an efficient, training-free alternative, but its application has been largely limited to verifiable domains like mathematics and coding, where response correctness is easily judged. To extend TTS to preference alignment, we introduce a novel framework that models the task as a realignment problem, since the base model often fails to sufficiently align with the stated preference. Our key insight is to decompose the underlying reward function into two components: one related to the question and the other to preference information. This allows us to derive a REAlignment Reward (REAR) that selectively rescales the proportions of these two reward terms. We then show that REAR can be formulated as a linear combination of token-level policy log-probabilities, making it computationally efficient and easy to integrate with various TTS algorithms such as best-of-$N$ sampling and tree search. Experiments show that compared to other test-time baselines, REAR not only enables scable test-time realignment for preference alignment tasks under diverse user requirements, but also generalizes to mathematical and visual tasks under appropriate preference settings.

paragraphs: Adapting a language model to different user preferences through additional training can require expensive data preparation and computation. REAR explores adaptation during inference instead. It treats the problem as realignment because a base model may respond to a question without adequately reflecting the preference supplied alongside it.

The framework separates the underlying reward into a question-related component and a preference-related component. Its realignment reward selectively changes the balance between them. The authors show that this reward can be expressed as a linear combination of token-level policy log-probabilities, making it computationally convenient to use with methods such as best-of-N sampling and tree search.

The contribution is a reward construction that makes inference-time search sensitive to the desired balance between answering the question and following user preferences, extending test-time scaling beyond settings organized primarily around verifiable correctness.
summary.tldr: REAR rebalances question and preference rewards during inference to improve preference alignment without additional model training.

abstract: We compute a common feature selection or kernel selection configuration formultiple support vector machines (SVMs) trained on different yet inter-relateddatasets. The method is advantageous when multiple classification tasks anddifferently labeled datasets exist over a common input space. Differentdatasets can mutually reinforce a common choice of representation or relevantfeatures for their various classifiers. We derive a multi-task representationlearning approach using the maximum entropy discrimination formalism. Theresulting convex algorithms maintain the global solution properties of supportvector machines. However, in addition to multiple SVMclassification/regression parameters they also jointly estimate an optimalsubset of features or optimal combination of kernels. Experiments are shown onstandardized datasets.

paragraphs: This paper learns a common feature selection or kernel selection configuration for several support vector machines. The setting involves related tasks with differently labeled datasets over the same input space. By learning the representation jointly, the datasets can reinforce a shared choice of useful features or kernels for their respective classifiers.

The authors derive the approach using maximum entropy discrimination. The resulting algorithms jointly estimate the parameters of multiple SVM classification or regression models and an optimal feature subset or kernel combination. Individual task models therefore have their own parameters while participating in the shared representation choice.

The algorithms are convex and retain the global solution properties associated with SVMs. This is a central computational feature of the formulation because representation selection and task learning are optimized together. Experiments on standardized datasets illustrate the approach. The contribution is a framework in which related tasks can inform a common representation while preserving the stated optimization properties.
summary.tldr: A convex multitask method jointly learns SVM parameters and a shared feature subset or kernel combination across related datasets.

title: Multi-task feature and kernel selection for SVMs

abstract: This paper presents a Support Vector Method for optimizing multivariate nonlinear performance measures like the F1 score. Taking a multivariate prediction approach, we give an algorithm with which such multivariate SVMs can be trained in polynomial time for large classes of potentially non-linear performance measures, in particular ROCArea and all measures that can be computed from the contingency table. The conventional classification SVM arises as a special case of our method.

Taking a multivariate prediction approach, we give an algorithm with which such multivariate SVMs can be trained in polynomial time for large classes of potentially non-linear performance measures, in particular ROCArea and all measures that can be computed from the contingency table. The conventional classification SVM arises as a special case of our method.

paragraphs: Classification performance is often judged using a measure that depends on a collection of predictions. F1 is one example: its value reflects the combined pattern of correct and incorrect decisions. This paper presents a support vector method designed to optimize such multivariate measures, including measures that are nonlinear.

The approach treats prediction as a multivariate problem, allowing the training formulation to account for the performance measure across predictions. The authors provide a polynomial-time training algorithm for broad classes of measures. These include ROC area and every measure computable from a contingency table, which summarizes the counts of different prediction outcomes.

The significance is that a broad range of evaluation goals can be brought into a support vector training framework with a stated computational guarantee. Conventional classification SVMs appear as a special case, connecting the proposal to an established method. The polynomial-time result applies to the supported classes of performance measures; the abstract does not claim coverage of every conceivable evaluation objective.
summary.tldr: A multivariate support vector framework supports polynomial-time training for broad classes of performance measures, including F1 and ROC area.

title: A support vector method for multivariate performance measures

abstract: We introduce a novel approach to incorporating domain knowledge into Support Vector Machines to improve their example efficiency. Domain knowledge is used in an Explanation Based Learning fashion to build justifications or explanations for why the training examples are assigned their given class labels. Explanations bias the large margin classifier through the interaction of training examples and domain knowledge. We develop a new learning algorithm for this Explanation-Augmented SVM (EA-SVM). It naturally extends to imperfect knowledge, a stumbling block to conventional EBL. Experimental results confirm desirable properties predicted by the analysis and demonstrate the approach on three domains.

It naturally extends to imperfect knowledge, a stumbling block to conventional EBL. paragraphs: This paper investigates how domain knowledge can help a support vector machine learn more efficiently from examples. The proposed Explanation-Augmented SVM uses knowledge to construct explanations for why training examples receive their assigned labels. Those explanations provide additional guidance for learning a large-margin classifier, connecting the observed examples with knowledge about the task.

The approach draws on Explanation Based Learning, where explanations help determine what a learner should infer from an example. Here, the interaction between domain knowledge and training examples biases the SVM’s classifier. The authors develop a new learning algorithm for this purpose. The explanations therefore participate in training, giving the method a concrete mechanism for incorporating knowledge into the learned decision rule.

The algorithm also extends naturally to imperfect domain knowledge, which the abstract identifies as a difficulty for conventional Explanation Based Learning. Experiments across three domains confirm desirable properties predicted by the analysis and demonstrate the approach in use. The contribution is a way to integrate explanatory knowledge with large-margin learning while allowing that knowledge to be imperfect.
summary.tldr: Explanation-Augmented SVM uses domain-knowledge explanations to guide large-margin learning and accommodates imperfect knowledge.

title: Explanation-Augmented SVM: an approach to incorporating domain knowledge into SVM learning

paragraphs: The paper studies linear regression when the model's parameter is a matrix whose rank must remain fixed. This requirement constrains the set of allowable regression models. The authors approach the problem by studying the geometry of that set, treating fixed-rank matrices as a Riemannian manifold on which optimization can be performed.

Using this geometric view, they develop efficient line-search algorithms. The rank restriction becomes part of the space being searched, giving a principled basis for designing updates within the constrained problem. The approach also provides a geometric interpretation of recent work on learning fixed-rank matrices, connecting algorithm design to the structure of the parameter space.

The proposed methods scale to high-dimensional problems and have local convergence properties. That qualification places the convergence claim near a solution rather than asserting guaranteed discovery of a global optimum. Benchmark experiments suggest performance competitive with leading alternatives. Together, the geometry and numerical results support manifold optimization as a versatile framework for constructing machine-learning algorithms with fixed-rank constraints.
summary.tldr: Riemannian geometry yields efficient line-search algorithms for fixed-rank linear regression with local convergence properties and competitive benchmark results.

title: Linear Regression under Fixed-Rank Constraints: A Riemannian Approach
